abstract: Construction project management faces persistent challenges in optimizing resource allocation under uncertainty, particularly when integrating real-time environmental, supply chain, and workforce data. Traditional scheduling and risk mitigation approaches often rely on static models that inadequately account for dynamic disruptions such as material shortages, weather variability, or regulatory changes. This project proposes the development of a high-resolution simulation framework to model complex construction workflows using agent-based modeling (ABM) and hybrid machine learning techniques. By integrating multi-source data streams—including IoT sensor outputs from equipment, real-time climate forecasts, and supplier API feeds—the computational system will simulate emergent project risks and propose adaptive resource reallocation strategies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process large-scale spatiotemporal datasets, train graph neural networks to predict cascading delays, and run parallel Monte Carlo simulations evaluating thousands of scenario permutations. The research will advance computational sustainability in construction by embedding carbon accounting metrics and circular economy constraints directly into optimization algorithms. Expected outcomes include a novel decision-support tool capable of balancing cost, timeline, and environmental impact tradeoffs under volatility, validated against historical project data from highway infrastructure and modular housing developments. This work bridges gaps between operations research, industrial ecology, and construction informatics, offering a scalable computational methodology to improve capital project resilience while reducing avoidable waste in the built environment. Results will provide both methodological contributions to stochastic project scheduling and practical frameworks for implementing data-driven adaptive management in construction enterprises.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply project management knowledge, skills, tools, and techniques in the construction and facility management industries. Includes instruction in facilities operations and maintenance, construction estimating, OSHA standards, sustainability, drafting, construction plans, project planning, risk management, cost and time management, contracts and procurement, accounting, statistics, decision making, and human resources.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a multiscale computational framework to predict the nonlinear dynamic response of magneto-elastic metamaterials under coupled mechanical and electromagnetic loading. These engineered materials, which integrate soft polymer matrices with embedded ferromagnetic particles, exhibit tunable stiffness and damping properties when exposed to magnetic fields, enabling adaptive vibration control in real time. However, their complex multiphysics behavior—spanning microscale particle interactions, mesoscale domain reconfiguration, and macroscale structural dynamics—poses significant modeling challenges. Existing approaches often decouple electromagnetic and mechanical effects or rely on oversimplified homogenization, limiting predictive accuracy for design optimization. To address this gap, we propose a high-fidelity simulation strategy combining finite element methods (FEM) for macroscale deformation, discrete element modeling (DEM) for particle-scale magnetic interactions, and hybrid machine learning surrogates to bridge time-scale disparities. The computational workflow will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to resolve transient coupling phenomena across three spatial orders of magnitude while maintaining numerical stability through implicit time integration. Key objectives include quantifying the energy dissipation mechanisms arising from magnetic domain wall motion during cyclic loading, characterizing frequency-dependent damping capacity as a function of particle morphology, and establishing design maps for targeted stiffness modulation. The simulations will be validated against in-house experimental measurements of prototype metamaterials under combined harmonic excitation and variable magnetic fields. Successful completion will yield an open-source computational toolkit for designing next-generation adaptive damping systems, with potential applications in precision manufacturing equipment, wearable assistive devices, and sensitive instrumentation platforms. This work advances the emerging frontier of smart mechanical metamaterials by providing a physics-informed framework to harness magneto-mechanical coupling effects, directly contributing to the Engineering Mechanics discipline through its integration of continuum dynamics, material nonlinearity, and coupled field analysis.
cip_definition: A program with a general focus on the application of the mathematical and scientific principles of classical mechanics to the analysis and evaluation of the behavior of structures, forces and materials in engineering problems. Includes instruction in statics, kinetics, dynamics, kinematics, celestial mechanics, stress and failure, and electromagnetism.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to address the challenge of modeling emergent behavior in hybrid bio-physical systems, where biological components (e.g., enzymatic networks, cellular aggregates) interact with synthetic materials (e.g., responsive polymers, nanostructured substrates) under dynamic environmental conditions. Such systems exhibit complex, nonlinear feedback loops that defy reductionist approaches, yet their study is critical for advancing applications in adaptive biomedical devices, environmental remediation, and programmable biomaterials. Current computational frameworks struggle to reconcile the disparate spatiotemporal scales and heterogeneous data types inherent to these systems, particularly when integrating stochastic biological processes with deterministic physical models. To overcome these limitations, this project will develop a multiscale computational framework combining agent-based modeling, coarse-grained molecular dynamics, and machine learning-driven parameter optimization. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable parallelized simulations of system evolution across scales—from nanoscale molecular interactions to mesoscale collective behaviors—while iterative learning algorithms will identify critical coupling mechanisms between biological and material components. The computational pipeline will leverage GPU-accelerated simulations for real-time analysis of phase transitions and pattern formation, validated against experimental datasets from collaborating laboratories. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible codebase for hybrid system simulation, quantitative design rules for tuning bio-physical interfaces, and predictive models of emergent stability in mixed systems subjected to thermal or chemical gradients. This work will establish a foundational methodology for engineering biologically integrated materials, with implications for sustainable technology and adaptive medical implants. The requested HPC allocation is essential to manage the high memory demands of multiscale coupling algorithms and the computational cost of parameter space exploration, which exceeds the capacity of local cluster resources.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply advanced computational methods and analysis to science, mathematics, and engineering practice. Includes instruction in applied mathematics and statistics, data science, numerical analysis and scientific computing, computational mechanics and physics, parallel computing and computer architecture, and mathematical modeling.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address computational bottlenecks in optimizing dynamic design workflows for high-resolution digital and print media. As demand grows for complex, data-rich visual content in prepress and digital imaging, traditional desktop publishing tools struggle with latency and scalability when processing large-scale assets, multi-layered compositions, or AI-driven design automation tasks. The research problem centers on developing adaptive computational methods to enhance real-time rendering, automated layout optimization, and color management for heterogeneous output devices (e.g., commercial printers, interactive web platforms). Proposed work includes parallelizing resource-intensive tasks such as raster image processor (RIP) simulations, GPU-accelerated typographic analysis, and machine learning models trained on design pattern datasets to predict layout efficiency. Computational experiments will benchmark workflows using distributed memory systems for batch processing of high-fidelity image sets and parameter sweeps for print preparation scenarios. Outcomes aim to establish scalable protocols for reducing processing time in design iteration cycles by 40–60%, while maintaining industry-standard color accuracy and resolution requirements. The project also explores energy-efficient rendering strategies to align computational workflows with sustainability goals in publishing. By integrating HPC capabilities into desktop publishing research, this work will provide novel frameworks for handling emerging challenges in cross-platform digital design, such as variable-data printing and responsive multimedia layouts. Results will be disseminated through open-source toolkits for academic programs in communication design, enabling reproducible studies on computational creativity and resource-aware design practices. This initiative bridges a critical gap between traditional graphic design pedagogy and advanced computing, fostering innovation in non-STEM disciplines reliant on high-throughput visual computation.
cip_title: Prepress/ Desktop Publishing and Digital Imaging Design
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the layout, design and typographic arrangement of printed and/or electronic graphic and textual products. Includes instruction in printing and lithographic equipment and operations, computer hardware and software, digital imaging, print preparation, page layout and design, desktop publishing, and applicable principles of graphic design and web page design.

abstract: Palliative care and pain management require personalized treatment strategies to address the complex interplay of biological, psychological, and social factors influencing patient outcomes. Current approaches often rely on generalized protocols, which may fail to account for individual variability in pain perception, treatment response, and disease progression. This project proposes to develop a computational framework integrating multimodal patient data—including electronic health records, genomic profiles, and longitudinal symptom reports—to identify predictive biomarkers and optimize dynamic treatment regimens. The research problem centers on overcoming the computational challenges of analyzing high-dimensional, heterogeneous datasets while preserving clinical interpretability. To address this, we will implement machine learning models (e.g., Bayesian hierarchical clustering, recurrent neural networks) and causal inference methods to model temporal relationships between interventions and outcomes. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential for training these models on a cohort of 15,000+ palliative care patients, enabling parallel processing of genomic association studies, real-time simulation of treatment pathways, and sensitivity analyses across diverse demographic subgroups. Key computational steps include dimensionality reduction of multi-omics data, reinforcement learning for adaptive treatment recommendation systems, and validation through in silico clinical trials. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated predictive algorithm for opioid response phenotypes, (2) dynamic decision-support tools for titrating multimodal therapies, and (3) mechanistic insights into neuroimmune pathways influencing refractory pain. By leveraging HPC capabilities to handle complex interactions at scale, this work aims to advance precision palliative care, reduce trial-and-error prescribing, and establish a computational infrastructure for translating large-scale clinical data into actionable treatment protocols. The results will directly inform the design of a forthcoming multicenter clinical trial evaluating algorithm-guided pain management strategies.
cip_definition: Research focused on Palliative Care/Pain Management

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model the biomechanical and biochemical interactions of advanced facial treatment protocols on heterogeneous skin types, with the goal of optimizing personalized skincare regimens. While facialists rely on empirical knowledge to select treatments, current practice lacks robust predictive tools to account for individual variations in skin elasticity, microbial ecosystems, and biochemical response kinetics. The research problem centers on bridging this gap through high-fidelity simulations of treatment outcomes across diverse demographic and physiological profiles. Using high-performance computing resources, we will implement multiscale models integrating 1) finite element analysis of mechanical stress distributions during facial massage techniques, 2) agent-based simulations of topical product absorption through stratified skin layers, and 3) machine learning-driven predictions of microbiome equilibrium states post-treatment. The computational pipeline will process clinical datasets spanning hyperspectral imaging of skin topography, metagenomic profiles, and longitudinal client outcome records from collaborating licensed practitioners. By parallelizing fluid-structure interaction solvers and employing graph neural networks to model dynamic skin-product-microbiome interfaces, the project aims to establish quantitative correlations between treatment parameters and client-specific biomarkers. Expected outcomes include a decision-support system capable of recommending optimized combinations of manual techniques, product formulations, and post-treatment care intervals. This work represents the first systematic computational investigation of facial treatment dynamics at mechanobiological and ecological scales, offering potential to transform evidence-based practice in skincare. The resource-intensive nature of modeling three-dimensional tissue deformation coupled with stochastic biochemical networks necessitates dedicated computing infrastructure to achieve clinically relevant resolution and cohort sizes. Results will advance both the technical rigor of aesthetic practice and foundational understanding of human skin as a complex adaptive system under therapeutic intervention.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to massage and treat the face, neck, and scalp with chemical and cosmetic preparations, and to function as licensed facial specialists in specialized and full service salons.  Includes instruction in facial surface anatomy; skin properties; skin decontamination and infection control; facial massage; facial makeup; facial wrapping; selection and application of creams, lotions, oils, and other chemicals and cosmetics; European and other facial techniques; client evaluation and care; applicable laws and regulations; and business practices.

abstract: The increasing complexity of modern energy systems, driven by the integration of distributed renewable generation, multi-vector storage technologies, and dynamic demand profiles, necessitates advanced computational tools to optimize grid stability and efficiency. Current optimization frameworks struggle to reconcile real-time operational constraints with long-term planning objectives, particularly in systems with high penetrations of intermittent resources. This project proposes the development of a quantum-inspired hybrid optimization platform to address the multi-scale, non-convex challenges inherent in next-generation energy systems. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, the research will implement tensor network algorithms and metaheuristic solvers to approximate quantum computing advantages on classical architectures, enabling the simultaneous resolution of temporal, spatial, and economic decision variables across microgrid-to-national-scale networks. The computational methodology integrates graph neural networks with decentralized optimization protocols to model demand-response interactions while preserving data privacy constraints. Key innovations include the formulation of adaptive receding horizon control schemes that dynamically adjust optimization fidelity based on real-time grid stress indicators and the creation of digital twin interfaces for scenario testing under extreme weather contingencies. Expected outcomes include a scalable software framework capable of reducing computational latency in day-ahead markets by 40% compared to conventional mixed-integer programming approaches, validated through co-simulation with operational data from three international grid operators. By bridging quantum computing principles with classical energy system optimization, this work aims to establish new benchmarks for computational efficiency in grid management while providing open-source tools to accelerate the clean energy transition. The requested HPC resources will enable large-scale parallelization of stochastic scenario analyses and facilitate the development of machine learning surrogates for rapid decision support in time-critical applications.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in energy systems engineering, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Ocular diseases in animals present complex diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to the intricate anatomy and physiology of the eye, as well as interspecies variations. This project seeks to advance the understanding and management of vision-threatening conditions in companion and livestock animals, such as glaucoma, cataracts, and immune-mediated keratitis, through high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled modeling and data analysis. A critical barrier in veterinary ophthalmology is the lack of species-specific biomechanical models for ocular tissues and predictive tools for treatment outcomes, which limits the precision of surgical planning and pharmacological interventions. To address this, we propose a computational pipeline integrating finite element modeling (FEM) of ocular biomechanics, machine learning (ML)-based analysis of multimodal imaging data (e.g., optical coherence tomography, ultrasound biomicroscopy), and molecular dynamics simulations of drug-cornea interactions. HPC resources will be essential to process high-resolution 3D imaging datasets, simulate tissue deformation under surgical or pathological stress, and train deep neural networks to detect subclinical disease features across diverse animal species. The FEM simulations will parameterize species-specific ocular geometries derived from clinical imaging, while molecular dynamics will model drug diffusion kinetics in corneal tissues with varying disease states. Concurrently, ML algorithms will correlate longitudinal clinical data with computational predictions to refine therapeutic protocols. Expected outcomes include open-access computational tools for predicting intraocular pressure dynamics post-surgery, optimizing corneal drug delivery, and automating lesion detection in ocular imaging. This work will directly inform clinical guidelines for animal-specific ocular surgeries and medical therapies, reducing complications and improving visual outcomes. By leveraging HPC to bridge translational gaps in veterinary ophthalmology, the project aims to establish a framework for precision medicine approaches that benefit both animal health and comparative ophthalmology research.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of ophthalmic diseases and disorders in animals, and related ocular pathology procedures. May included related research in animal eye surgery.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in understanding how multi-species interactions and environmental heterogeneity jointly shape ecosystem resilience under climate-driven disturbances. A key challenge in ecology lies in scaling organismal responses to landscape-level dynamics, particularly when incorporating feedbacks between biotic communities (e.g., plant-pollinator networks, predator-prey systems) and abiotic factors (e.g., nutrient fluxes, microclimate variability). Traditional analytical models struggle to capture the nonlinear, spatially explicit nature of these interactions across decadal timescales. Our research integrates individual-based modeling (IBM) with high-resolution environmental datasets to simulate community assembly and disassembly processes in disturbance-prone ecosystems. The computational framework couples (1) trait-mediated species interactions informed by paleoecological records and contemporary field data, (2) dynamic biogeochemical cycling across soil and aquatic matrices, and (3) stochastic disturbance regimes mimicking projected climate extremes. HPC resources are essential for executing parallelized simulations across parameter spaces encompassing >10^6 possible species combinations and 1km-scale landscape grids over 100-year horizons. Expected outcomes include identifying threshold ratios of functional diversity to habitat connectivity that buffer against regime shifts, and quantifying how legacy effects from prior disturbances alter recovery pathways in fire- and flood-adapted ecosystems. Results will directly inform regional conservation strategies targeting ecological memory preservation in critical watersheds. By resolving scale-dependent feedbacks between evolutionary adaptations and ecosystem processes, this work advances theoretical foundations in resilience ecology while providing testable frameworks for managing biodiverse landscapes under anthropogenic change.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the relationships and interactions of small-scale biological systems, such as organisms, to each other, to complex and whole systems, and to the physical and other non-biological aspects of their environments. Includes instruction in biogeochemistry; landscape and/or marine/aquatic dynamics; decomposition; global and regional elemental budgets; biotic and abiotic regulation of nutrient cycles; ecophysiology; ecosystem resilience, disturbance, and succession; community and habitat dynamics; organismal interactions (co-evolution, competition, predation); paleoecology; and evolutionary ecology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a large-scale computational analysis of phonetic, syntactic, and lexical variation across French dialects and creoles, with a focus on under-resourced varieties such as Caribbean Creoles and Acadian French. The research problem centers on the challenges of modeling linguistic evolution and contact phenomena in these varieties, which involve complex, multidimensional data spanning historical texts, contemporary speech corpora, and sociolinguistic metadata. Traditional comparative methods struggle to systematically analyze such datasets due to their scale, heterogeneity, and the non-linear interactions between linguistic features over time. The proposed computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) pipelines optimized for historical and regional French variants, machine learning classifiers to detect patterns of language contact, and acoustic-phonetic modeling to quantify shifts in pronunciation. HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based models on distributed textual corpora (15th–21st centuries), parallelizing comparative analyses across 20+ dialects/creoles, and running agent-based simulations of language change scenarios. Expected outcomes include (1) the first unified digital atlas mapping phonetic convergence between Metropolitan French and its creoles, (2) probabilistic models identifying syntactic innovations driven by language contact in North American French varieties, and (3) open-access tools for automated parsing of non-standard French orthographies. By enabling the synthesis of fragmented regional datasets, this work will advance theoretical understanding of dialect formation in Francophone contexts while supporting preservation initiatives for endangered varieties. The computational frameworks developed will also provide a template for similar studies in other under-documented language families.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the French language and related dialects and creoles. Includes instruction in philology; Metropolitan French; Canadian French; African and Caribbean Creoles; dialects; and applications in business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: Veterinary anesthesiology faces significant challenges in optimizing anesthetic protocols due to interspecies variability, complex physiological responses, and the scarcity of species-specific pharmacological data. Current approaches often rely on extrapolation from human medicine or trial-and-error adjustments, leading to suboptimal outcomes such as inadequate analgesia, adverse drug reactions, and increased perioperative risks. This project proposes to develop a computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to create predictive models for personalized anesthesia management in diverse animal species. The research will integrate pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) modeling with machine learning algorithms trained on multi-institutional clinical datasets encompassing physiological parameters, drug responses, and patient outcomes across common domestic species and exotic animals. HPC infrastructure will enable large-scale simulations to account for biological variability, simultaneous optimization of multiple anesthetic parameters, and analysis of high-dimensional data from electronic health records and multi-omics sources. The project will specifically focus on modeling interactions between anesthetic agents, analgesics, and cardiovascular stability in critical care scenarios, as well as predicting recovery trajectories in patients with comorbid conditions. Expected outcomes include species-specific dosing recommendations, real-time decision support tools for dynamic intraoperative adjustments, and quantitative safety profiles for novel drug combinations. Validation will occur through retrospective analysis of clinical cases and prospective observational studies in partnership with veterinary teaching hospitals. By establishing computational methods to address the unique physiological diversity in veterinary patients, this work aims to reduce anesthetic complications, improve pain management outcomes, and enhance safety in both routine and complex surgical procedures. The developed models will serve as a foundation for evidence-based protocol development in a field where controlled clinical trials are often logistically challenging or ethically constrained.
cip_definition: Research focused on the application of anesthesia for general and specialized surgery and obstetrics, critical animal care and the care of pain problems. May included related research in surgical procedures, current monitoring procedures, fluid therapy, pain management, diagnostic and therapeutic procedures outside the operating room, and operating room safety.

abstract: The emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens at the interface of wildlife, livestock, and human populations present complex challenges to global public health and food security. Current epidemiological models often lack the resolution to account for dynamic, multi-host transmission networks, environmental drivers, and heterogeneous data sources, limiting their utility in predicting outbreak trajectories or optimizing intervention strategies. This project seeks to develop a high-resolution, multi-scale computational framework to model zoonotic disease transmission dynamics, with a focus on pathogens impacting both animal health and food safety (e.g., Salmonella, avian influenza). Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will implement spatially explicit agent-based models (ABMs) integrating real-world datasets on livestock movements, wildlife habitat overlap, climate variables, and genomic surveillance data. These models will simulate pathogen spread across species barriers, incorporating stochastic transmission events, host immunity landscapes, and anthropogenic factors such as agricultural practices. Parallelized parameter sweeps and Bayesian calibration methods will be used to infer transmission pathways and identify high-risk spatiotemporal interfaces. Additionally, machine learning approaches will analyze model outputs to prioritize surveillance targets and forecast intervention efficacy under varying scenarios. The computational demands of these tasks—particularly the ABMs operating at regional scales with millions of agents and the integration of high-dimensional genomic and environmental data—necessitate access to HPC infrastructure for feasible runtime and storage. Outcomes will advance predictive capacity for zoonotic hotspots, inform One Health policies to mitigate cross-species transmission, and provide actionable insights for veterinary public health practitioners. This work will also establish an open-source toolkit for adaptive disease modeling, enhancing collaborative responses to emerging threats at the intersection of animal and human health.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_title: Veterinary Preventive Medicine, Epidemiology, and Public Health
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of the prevention and control of communicable animal diseases, diseases affecting humans, and prepares veterinarians to function as public health specialists. Includes instruction in animal epidemiology, biostatistics, food safety and quality assurance, food toxicology, zoonotic and infectious diseases, disease vectors and transference, production medicine, animal health, veterinary public health practice, and inspection and evaluation methods.

abstract: The brewing industry faces persistent challenges in optimizing fermentation processes, where microbial dynamics and metabolic interactions critically influence product quality, consistency, and efficiency. Traditional experimental approaches struggle to resolve the complexity of microbial ecosystems in brewing, particularly under varying raw material inputs and environmental conditions. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop multiscale computational models that simulate yeast metabolism and microbial community interactions during fermentation. By integrating genome-scale metabolic models of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and non-Saccharomyces species with dynamic fermentation parameters (e.g., temperature, pH, sugar profiles), we aim to predict metabolic fluxes, stress responses, and byproduct formation under diverse brewing scenarios. Computational workflows will employ constraint-based modeling, agent-based simulations, and machine learning to analyze multi-omics datasets (transcriptomics, metabolomics) from experimental fermentations. HPC resources are essential to handle the combinatorial complexity of microbial interactions, parameterize models using high-dimensional data, and conduct sensitivity analyses across thousands of simulated conditions. Expected outcomes include predictive frameworks for strain selection, process optimization, and contamination mitigation, directly addressing industry needs for precision in scaling novel beer styles and reducing production losses. The project will also advance methodologies for modeling microbial ecosystems in food systems, with broader applications in agricultural biotechnology. By bridging brewing science with computational biology, this work aligns with agricultural innovation goals, emphasizing sustainable resource use and value-added product development within the food and beverage sector.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the business, science, and technology of beer brewing operations. Includes instruction in biology, biochemistry, brewing, entrepreneurship, fermentation, malting, marketing, microbiology, quality control, and sanitation.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize decision-making in agricultural supply chains under climate and market volatility. Agricultural enterprises face increasing risks from fluctuating commodity prices, resource constraints, and climate-driven yield variability, yet existing operational models often lack the resolution to integrate real-time environmental and economic data. To address this gap, we propose an agent-based modeling (ABM) system coupled with machine learning to simulate multi-stakeholder interactions across production, distribution, and retail phases. The ABM will parameterize heterogeneous agents (e.g., farms, processors, retailers) using historical data on crop yields, soil health metrics, input costs, and regional market trends. Machine learning components will train on climate projection ensembles (CMIP6 datasets) and commodity futures data to forecast adaptive pricing and inventory strategies. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve the high-dimensional parameter space, including stochastic weather events, geographic variability in soil carbon dynamics, and nonlinear price-demand relationships at regional scales. Computational workflows will leverage parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to quantify risk distributions under 10,000+ scenarios, evaluating interventions such as dynamic crop rotation plans, cooperative bulk purchasing agreements, and distributed storage networks. Expected outcomes include a decision support tool that identifies context-specific strategies to buffer against revenue losses, reduce input waste, and improve supply chain resilience. The results will advance precision agriculture economics by demonstrating how computationally intensive, systems-level models can inform adaptive business planning. All code and anonymized simulation outputs will be shared via an open-access repository to support replication in diverse agribusiness contexts. This work directly addresses the USDA priority area of "Sustainable Agricultural Systems" by linking computational innovation to operational scalability for farm-to-market enterprises.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
detailed_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences nec
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on modern business and economic principles involved in the organization, operation, and management of agricultural enterprises.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in digital rhetoric and multimodal composition, addressing the challenge of analyzing large-scale, heterogeneous datasets of written and visual texts in online environments. Current methods for studying digital writing practices, particularly in social media, collaborative platforms, and multimedia-rich educational contexts, are constrained by the limited scalability of manual text analysis and off-the-shelf computational tools. The proposed research will employ NLP techniques, machine learning models, and network analysis to examine patterns in rhetorical strategies, genre evolution, and audience engagement across diverse digital communities. Key computational tasks include training custom transformer-based models to detect rhetorical moves in multimodal texts (e.g., image-text interactions in memes or infographics), clustering discourse communities based on stylistic and argumentative features, and simulating the diffusion of compositional norms in networked writing environments. These analyses will utilize existing corpora of 10M+ public forum posts, educational portfolios, and social media artifacts, requiring GPU-accelerated processing for transformer model fine-tuning and large-scale graph computations. Anticipated outcomes include new frameworks for understanding how digital platforms reshape persuasive communication, data-driven insights into cross-cultural literacy practices, and open-source tools for computational rhetoric analysis. The project will directly inform pedagogical innovations in composition studies, particularly for teaching multimodal writing in technologically mediated contexts, while contributing methodological advances to humanities computing. By integrating HPC capabilities with humanistic inquiry, this work aims to bridge gaps between traditional rhetorical theory and the computational demands of studying contemporary digital discourse at scale.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the humanistic and scientific study of rhetoric, composition, literacy, and language/linguistic theories and their practical and pedagogical applications. Includes instruction in historical and contemporary rhetoric/composition theories; composition and criticism of written, visual, and mixed-media texts; analysis of literacy practices in cultural and cross-cultural contexts; and writing program administration.

abstract: This project seeks to develop adaptive tactile interface systems that dynamically optimize user interaction patterns across heterogeneous hardware platforms, including wearable devices, touch-enabled industrial controls, and augmented reality (AR) environments. Current tactile feedback systems employ static response models, limiting their effectiveness in scenarios requiring real-time adaptation to user behavior, environmental sensor inputs, or variable hardware constraints. The research addresses this gap by integrating biomechanical simulation, sensor fusion algorithms, and reinforcement learning to create platform-agnostic tactile optimization frameworks. The computational challenge lies in modeling high-dimensional interactions between user input patterns, material deformation physics, and device-specific actuator responses at millisecond timescales. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable parallel execution of finite element analysis for synthetic tactile surface modeling, coupled with distributed training of neural networks that map multi-modal sensor data (pressure, capacitive, inertial) to adaptive feedback policies. Key innovations include a differentiable physics engine for co-optimizing hardware parameters and interaction logic, as well as a federated learning architecture that preserves user privacy while aggregating interaction patterns across devices. Expected outcomes include open-source libraries for cross-platform tactile interface development, validated through human-subject testing on three target platforms: assistive technologies for visually impaired users, AR maintenance guides with haptic cues, and industrial control systems with safety-adaptive responsiveness. The resource request supports GPU-accelerated material simulations, large-scale hyperparameter optimization for reinforcement learning agents, and real-time validation of tactile response models across heterogeneous computing architectures. Results will advance the design of context-aware human-computer interfaces while establishing computational methods for hardware-software co-adaptation in embedded systems.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to design, develop, and implement software-based solutions for specific business and consumer platforms including industrial, game, mobile, tactile, and web platforms. Includes instruction in computer programming, computer hardware, data structures, database theory, maintenance, operating systems, project management, software development, and systems analysis.

abstract: Maternal and neonatal health outcomes are significantly influenced by timely identification of risk factors during the prenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum periods. Current risk stratification tools in nurse midwifery practice often rely on static clinical guidelines, which may fail to account for complex, dynamic interactions between biological, socioeconomic, and environmental variables. This project seeks to develop a predictive computational framework to optimize personalized risk assessment and intervention strategies for childbearing individuals. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will integrate heterogeneous datasets—including electronic health records, longitudinal vital sign monitoring, genetic markers, and geographic health disparities data—to train ensemble machine learning models. These models will identify multivariate patterns associated with adverse outcomes such as preterm birth, preeclampsia, and postpartum hemorrhage. Computational workflows will employ federated learning techniques to preserve patient confidentiality while aggregating data from multiple health systems. Sensitivity analyses will quantify the relative contributions of modifiable risk factors, enabling midwives to prioritize targeted interventions. The scalability of these models requires HPC infrastructure to manage terabyte-scale datasets, parallelize hyperparameter optimization, and simulate population-level outcomes under different care scenarios. Expected outcomes include validated risk prediction algorithms deployable in clinical decision support systems, dynamic risk visualization tools for patient-provider communication, and evidence-based recommendations for resource allocation in underserved communities. By enhancing predictive accuracy and intervention timing, this research aligns with nurse midwifery’s preventive care paradigm, aiming to reduce maternal morbidity, neonatal intensive care admissions, and systemic healthcare costs. The computational framework will be disseminated as open-source software to support reproducibility and equitable adoption across diverse clinical settings.
cip_definition: A program that prepares registered nurses to independently deliver babies and treat mothers in the prenatal, delivery, and post-delivery periods. Includes instruction in pre-delivery screening, physician referral, and the care of infants during the delivery and immediate post-delivery phases.

abstract: Understanding the mechanisms driving species coexistence and extinction under rapid environmental change is a central challenge in ecology and evolutionary biology. This project addresses critical gaps in predicting how interspecific interactions and adaptive evolution shape biodiversity resilience in fragmented landscapes. We propose an integrative computational framework combining agent-based models, genomic vulnerability indices, and phylogenetic comparative methods to simulate multi-species metapopulation dynamics under climate warming scenarios. The research will parameterize models with empirical data from 12 insect-plant systems experiencing range shifts, incorporating trait evolution rates derived from whole-genome resequencing of 50 populations. High-performance computing resources are essential for running spatially explicit simulations at continental scales (1km² resolution across 10⁶ km² landscapes), tracking 10⁶+ individuals with evolving dispersal and phenology traits over 500-generation horizons. Parallelized likelihood-free inference methods will statistically match simulation outputs to observed range boundary shifts from 40 years of monitoring data. A novel module will quantify eco-evolutionary rescue potential by coupling quantitative genetics models with community network stability analyses. Expected outcomes include: 1) identification of critical thresholds in habitat connectivity that prevent evolutionary rescue in mutualistic networks, 2) predictive maps of extinction cascades under IPCC climate scenarios, and 3) open-source software for integrating phylogenetic constraints into spatial conservation prioritization. This work will directly inform management strategies for 14 ESA-listed species in our study regions while advancing theoretical synthesis across ecological and evolutionary timescales. The requested 500,000 CPU-hour allocation enables computationally intensive sensitivity analyses of nonlinear genotype-environment-phenotype interactions that cannot be feasibly explored through desktop computing.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on how evolution shapes biodiversity, and how organisms interact with each other and their environments. Includes instruction in animal, plant, population, functional, evolutionary, and ecosystem ecology; ecological and evolutionary genetics; molecular evolution; population and conservation biology; animal and plant diversity; biometry; and scientific and research ethics.

abstract: Structural biology faces a critical challenge in resolving the dynamic, multi-scale interactions of biomolecular systems, particularly those involving large macromolecular assemblies and transient states that evade conventional experimental techniques. This project seeks to address this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to perform atomic-level molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and hybrid modeling of key structural processes, including the assembly mechanisms of viral capsid proteins and the conformational dynamics of membrane-bound receptors. Current computational limitations restrict the timescales and system sizes that can be feasibly modeled, hindering insights into allosteric regulation, ligand-binding pathways, and structural transitions central to cellular function. To overcome these barriers, we propose a multi-tiered computational approach integrating enhanced sampling techniques (e.g., metadynamics, replica exchange) with coarse-grained modeling to map free-energy landscapes of protein folding and aggregation. Large-scale MD simulations will utilize GPU-optimized software (AMBER, GROMACS) to achieve microsecond-to-millisecond timescales for systems exceeding 1 million atoms, including explicit solvent and membrane environments. Concurrently, cryo-EM density maps and X-ray crystallography data will inform flexible fitting algorithms to refine structural models of disordered regions in cytoskeletal proteins. The requested HPC allocation will enable parallel processing of ensemble-based simulations, machine learning-aided analysis of conformational clusters, and validation against experimental biophysical data (SAXS, FRET). Expected outcomes include atomic-resolution models of metastable intermediate states in chaperone-mediated folding, predictive frameworks for mutational impacts on protein stability, and mechanistic insights into how microtubule-associated proteins regulate polymerization kinetics. These results will advance fundamental understanding of molecular recognition and assembly principles, with direct implications for targeting structural vulnerabilities in neurodegenerative diseases and viral pathogenesis. By bridging computational and experimental structural biology, this work will establish scalable protocols for simulating multi-component cellular machinery, fostering collaboration across biochemistry and biophysics disciplines.
detailed_field: Biochemistry, biophysics, and molecular biology nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of submolecular and molecular components and assemblies of living systems and how they are organized into functional units such as cells and anatomic tissues. Includes instruction in glycoprotein, carbohydrate, protein, and nucleic acid structures and chemistry; cytoskeletal structure; nuclear and intracellular structures; molecular recognition; molecular chaperones; transcription and folding; multicellular organization; microtubules and microfilaments; cell differentiation; immunophysics; and DNA sequencing.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model and optimize hybrid bio-electrochemical systems for sustainable carbon capture and conversion, integrating principles from microbial ecology, electrochemistry, and materials science. Current approaches to carbon utilization face challenges in scalability and energy efficiency due to the complex interplay between biological communities, electrochemical interfaces, and transport phenomena at multiple spatiotemporal scales. To address this, we propose a multi-physics modeling strategy combining lattice Boltzmann methods for fluid dynamics, kinetic Monte Carlo simulations for surface reactions, and genome-scale metabolic network models for microbial consortia behavior. The computational workflow will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to couple these disparate modeling paradigms through adaptive time-stepping and spatially resolved data exchange, enabling investigation of emergent system behaviors inaccessible through single-scale approaches. Key challenges include maintaining numerical stability across solvers with differing discretization schemes and scaling parallel efficiency for heterogeneous compute workloads. The project will validate models against experimental datasets from flow-cell bioreactors and conduct parameter sweeps to identify optimal operational regimes for carbon conversion efficiency. Expected outcomes include predictive insights into community-driven electron transfer mechanisms, design principles for scalable reactor architectures, and open-source software tools for simulating multi-domain bio-electrochemical systems. This work bridges critical gaps between biological carbon capture technologies and renewable energy storage systems, with potential applications in carbon-negative manufacturing and distributed energy infrastructure. Successful implementation requires sustained access to HPC resources capable of handling memory-intensive multiscale simulations, with anticipated usage of 500,000 core-hours annually for ensemble modeling and sensitivity analyses.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of computing and its application for solving challenges in science and engineering fields, with a focus on principles from mathematics, science, engineering and computing.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize industrial safety protocols by modeling complex interactions between human behavior, equipment dynamics, and environmental factors in high-risk workplaces. Current risk assessment methods often rely on static, compartmentalized analyses that inadequately capture real-time system interdependencies, limiting proactive hazard mitigation. To address this gap, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate multi-agent scenarios integrating ergonomic stressors, equipment failure probabilities, and worker decision-making patterns. The computational approach will combine agent-based modeling, Monte Carlo simulations, and machine learning techniques to process large-scale datasets from industrial sensor networks, incident reports, and human performance studies. Key objectives include quantifying cascading risks in manufacturing workflows, predicting rare but high-consequence safety events, and dynamically optimizing evacuation routes or equipment shutdown protocols. The simulations will account for variables such as toxic exposure thresholds, fatigue-driven error rates, and spatially distributed thermal or vibrational hazards. By parallelizing these computationally intensive workflows across HPC nodes, we aim to achieve near-real-time risk forecasting capabilities scalable to large facilities. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for accident precursors, a digital twin framework for safety training simulations, and evidence-based recommendations for revising equipment maintenance schedules and personnel deployment strategies. This work will advance industrial safety technology by enabling data-driven, systems-level interventions that traditional experimental methods cannot feasibly replicate. The requested computing resources will directly support the creation of open-source tools for probabilistic risk assessment, benefiting both academic research and industry partners in hazardous sectors such as chemical processing and heavy machinery operations.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills to assist engineers and other professionals in implementing and enforcing industrial safety standards to mitigate damage, reduce risks, and prevent accidents. Includes instruction in industrial processes, industrial hygiene, injury prevention, toxicology, ergonomics, risk analysis, system and process safety, safety performance measurement, human factors, human behavior, and applicable law and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamic interplay between cultural practices and social resilience in small-scale societies, with a focus on how ritual behaviors adapt to environmental and demographic stressors. Anthropological research on cultural transmission often relies on qualitative ethnography or limited quantitative models, but the complexity of multi-generational cultural systems—particularly when integrating ecological, demographic, and symbolic variables—exceeds the capacity of conventional computational tools. We propose developing agent-based models (ABMs) to simulate cultural evolution across hypothetical and historically informed scenarios, incorporating high-resolution ethnographic data on kinship networks, ritual participation, and resource-sharing practices. The models will parameterize variables such as environmental shocks, migration rates, and intergroup conflict to test hypotheses about cultural persistence and transformation. A second component employs natural language processing (NLP) to analyze comparative ethnographic texts from the Human Relations Area Files (HRAF), training transformer-based models to detect patterns in ritual descriptions that correlate with societal-scale adaptive outcomes. HPC resources are critical for scaling ABM simulations to realistic population sizes (10^4–10^5 agents) over multi-century timeframes, conducting parameter sweeps across diverse cultural configurations, and processing terabytes of unstructured textual data with deep learning architectures. Expected outcomes include (1) identifying computational signatures of cultural resilience, (2) generating testable frameworks for linking micro-scale ritual behaviors to macro-scale social durability, and (3) advancing methodological integration between ethnographic fieldwork and computational anthropology. Results will contribute to theoretical debates about cultural adaptation while providing open-source tools for simulating culturally-grounded decision-making processes, with implications for understanding societal responses to contemporary crises.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of culture and the relationship of culture to other aspects of social life. Includes instruction in cultural anthropology, anthropological theory, ethnography, linguistics, and quantitative and qualitative research methods.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational research in cross-linguistic analysis and large-scale literary pattern detection across understudied languages. While digital humanities tools have transformed text-based research in widely spoken languages, many low-resource and non-Indo-European languages remain computationally marginalized due to structural complexity, limited digitized corpora, and a lack of adaptable NLP frameworks. Our research addresses this gap by developing scalable methods to analyze syntactic, morphological, and semantic features across 15+ languages from diverse families (e.g., Uralic, Niger-Congo, Austronesian), using parallel corpora of folktales and oral narratives as a controlled comparative dataset. The computational approach combines transformer-based models for cross-lingual embedding alignment with graph-based algorithms to map narrative structures, requiring distributed training across GPU nodes and iterative optimization of memory-intensive alignment matrices. A second phase employs HPC-enabled topic modeling at scale to trace the diffusion of literary motifs through multilingual translation networks spanning the 18th–20th centuries, integrating OCR-processed primary texts in scripts including Cyrillic, Arabic, and Devanagari. The project’s computational demands stem from processing terabyte-scale multilingual text datasets, running parallelized feature extraction pipelines, and maintaining model reproducibility across heterogeneous language inputs. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for comparative literary analysis in low-resource languages, novel metrics for quantifying narrative divergence in translation traditions, and a publicly accessible database linking linguistic features to cultural-context metadata. By enabling systematic computational study of under-represented languages and their literary outputs, this work aims to reshape digital humanities methodologies while preserving linguistic diversity in algorithmic frameworks. Successful implementation directly supports pedagogical initiatives in computational literary studies and provides infrastructure for future collaborative research on global language traditions.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on one or more modern foreign languages that is not specific as to the name of the language(s) studied; that is otherwise undifferentiated; or that introduces students to language studies at the basic/elementary level.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize urban air quality management systems using advanced modeling and machine learning techniques. Urban environments face escalating challenges from airborne pollutants, exacerbated by dynamic factors such as traffic patterns, industrial emissions, and meteorological variability. Existing predictive models often lack the resolution and adaptability needed to inform real-time mitigation strategies, particularly in heterogeneous urban landscapes. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled approach integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations with graph neural networks (GNNs) to predict pollutant dispersion at hyperlocal scales. The CFD models will resolve micro-scale airflow and chemical transport over city domains, while GNNs will assimilate real-time sensor data to dynamically adjust predictions. This hybrid methodology requires substantial computational resources due to the iterative coupling of multi-physics simulations (1–10 m resolution) with data assimilation workflows across large spatial domains. The HPC allocation will support parallelized simulations, distributed training of GNN architectures, and uncertainty quantification through ensemble modeling. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework capable of recommending optimized emission control strategies, such as traffic rerouting or industrial activity modulation, under varying atmospheric conditions. This work will advance environmental control technologies by enabling responsive, data-informed decision-making for urban air quality management. The resulting tools and datasets will be shared with municipal planning agencies to support policy development, with broader applications in environmental health risk assessment. Successful implementation will demonstrate the critical role of HPC in scaling next-generation environmental control systems for sustainable cities.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in environmental control technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Chronic pain remains a poorly understood condition with complex interactions between neurophysiological, psychological, and environmental factors. Current treatment protocols often rely on generalized approaches that fail to account for individual variability in pain perception and treatment response. This project seeks to address this gap by developing patient-specific computational models of pain processing networks to predict optimal pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we aim to integrate multimodal neuroimaging data (fMRI, DTI), electrophysiological recordings, and patient-reported outcomes into a unified simulation framework. The research will focus on two interrelated objectives: (1) constructing dynamic whole-brain models that map pain signal propagation across thalamocortical and limbic pathways under varying pharmacological conditions, and (2) employing machine learning algorithms to identify biomarkers predictive of intervention success in heterogeneous patient populations. Computational workflows will utilize GPU-accelerated neural mass modeling and Bayesian inference techniques to simulate neurotransmitter dynamics across pain-related networks at unprecedented spatiotemporal resolution. The project requires HPC resources for large-scale parameter space exploration, parallel processing of high-dimensional neuroimaging datasets, and validation against clinical trial data from 500+ chronic pain patients. Expected outcomes include a novel computational platform for personalized pain therapy selection and mechanistic insights into interindividual differences in opioid response variability. By bridging computational neuroscience with clinical pain management, this work could fundamentally shift treatment paradigms from trial-and-error approaches to mechanism-driven precision medicine. The resulting models and algorithms will be made available through an open-source toolkit, enabling broader investigation of pain pathophysiology and accelerating development of targeted therapies.
cip_definition: A post-residency program of study that prepares physicians in the diagnosis, management, and treatment of acute and chronic pain. Includes instruction in anesthesiology, pain assessment, pain classification and diagnosis, pain neuroscience, palliative and end-of-life care, physical medicine and rehabilitation, psychiatry of pain, pain pharmacology, public policy, and legal issues of pain management.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a novel computational legal analytics framework aimed at modeling the evolution of judicial reasoning in U.S. appellate courts. Traditional legal research methods struggle to systematically analyze the growing volume and complexity of case law, particularly in identifying subtle patterns in judicial argumentation, citation networks, and the interplay between legal doctrine and sociopolitical context. By integrating natural language processing (NLP), temporal graph analysis, and transformer-based language models, this research will process a corpus of 10 million judicial opinions (1790–present) to trace doctrinal shifts, quantify the influence of non-legal factors on decision-making, and simulate the propagation of legal concepts across jurisdictions. The computational pipeline will involve entity recognition for legal constructs, dynamic network modeling of precedent hierarchies, and attention-based classification of rhetorical strategies in majority and dissenting opinions. HPC resources are critical for training domain-specific legal language models, conducting large-scale graph traversals to map precedent cascades, and running Monte Carlo simulations to assess the stability of inferred doctrinal patterns. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible knowledge graph of legal reasoning trajectories, predictive models of judicial outcomes under hypothetical policy scenarios, and methodological innovations in applying computational social science techniques to legal texts. This work bridges gaps between legal theory, computational linguistics, and complex systems analysis, offering pre-law scholars tools to study law as a dynamic, data-driven system. Results will inform curricular advancements in legal education, particularly in teaching students to navigate rapidly evolving areas like algorithmic accountability and digital rights, while providing a foundation for interdisciplinary research at the intersection of law, ethics, and emergent technologies.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the professional study of law at the post-baccalaureate level.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the biomechanical and molecular drivers of idiopathic condylar resorption (ICR), a rare but debilitating degenerative disorder affecting the temporomandibular joint (TMJ). ICR disproportionately impacts young adults, leading to chronic pain, facial deformity, and functional impairment, yet its etiology remains poorly understood due to the complex interplay of biomechanical stress, inflammatory signaling, and genetic susceptibility. Current clinical interventions are largely reactive and lack mechanistic precision. To address this gap, we propose an integrative computational framework combining finite element modeling (FEM) of TMJ biomechanics with multi-omic analysis of synovial fluid-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs). FEM simulations will model stress distributions under varying occlusal loads using patient-specific 3D reconstructions from cone-beam CT scans, while parallel EV proteomic and miRNA sequencing data will be analyzed via graph neural networks to identify mechanosensitive signaling pathways. The HPC environment is critical for scaling these analyses across a cohort of 200 patients and controls, enabling real-time coupling of mechanical simulations with dynamic biological network inference. Expected outcomes include the identification of load-dependent molecular biomarkers predictive of resorption progression and the development of a computational risk stratification tool to guide early intervention. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational biomechanics, systems biology, and precision medicine, offering a novel paradigm for understanding osteoarthritic disorders in mechanically active joints. By elucidating ICR’s multiscale pathophysiology, the work has broader implications for personalized management of understudied musculoskeletal diseases.
cip_definition: Any program in medicine, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Nursing assistants and patient care aides play a critical role in monitoring patients and ensuring timely interventions in clinical and long-term care settings. However, staffing constraints, high patient-to-staff ratios, and reliance on intermittent manual assessments often delay the detection of subtle physiological changes that precede adverse events such as falls, infections, or clinical deterioration. This project proposes the development of a machine learning framework to analyze multimodal patient data—including electronic health records (EHR), real-time vital signs, and mobility patterns from wearable sensors—to predict early signs of patient decline and optimize care workflows. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process large-scale, heterogeneous datasets spanning thousands of patient-days, train deep learning models for time-series prediction, and simulate care delivery scenarios under varying staffing conditions. The computational pipeline will integrate convolutional and recurrent neural networks to identify risk patterns from temporal data, while agent-based modeling will evaluate the impact of dynamic task prioritization strategies on care quality and aide workload. Successful implementation will generate two key outcomes: (1) a predictive analytics tool to alert nursing assistants to high-risk patients, enabling proactive interventions, and (2) evidence-based recommendations for balancing patient acuity with staff assignments in real time. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this project addresses the intersection of workforce challenges and patient safety in resource-constrained environments. The resulting tools have the potential to reduce preventable adverse events, improve care efficiency, and inform scalable training protocols for nursing assistants, ultimately enhancing outcomes for vulnerable populations in acute and long-term care settings.
cip_title: Nursing Assistant/ Aide and Patient Care Assistant/ Aide
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform routine nursing-related services to patients in hospitals or long-term care facilities, under the training and supervision of a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing resource allocation in public policy implementation through advanced computational modeling of complex, multi-stakeholder systems. Public administrators often face dynamic, large-scale decisions—such as balancing budgetary constraints with equity in service delivery or simulating long-term impacts of infrastructure investments—that involve interconnected economic, social, and political variables. Traditional analytical tools struggle to account for nonlinear interactions, feedback loops, and heterogeneous population behaviors inherent in these scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we propose developing an agent-based model (ABM) simulating resource distribution outcomes under varying policy conditions, integrated with machine learning techniques to identify high-impact decision pathways. The ABM framework will incorporate geospatial data, demographic records, and historical fiscal datasets to represent regional populations, government agencies, and external economic pressures. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to running thousands of parallelized simulations testing diverse policy combinations, scaling to granular municipal-level analyses across multi-year horizons. Expected outcomes include a validated decision-support tool for quantifying trade-offs in public spending priorities, predicting secondary effects of regulatory changes, and assessing vulnerability gaps in service access. This work directly contributes to evidence-based methods in public administration by enabling rapid, data-driven scenario testing that accounts for systemic complexity—a capability absent in current policy evaluation practices. Results will be shared with state-level planning agencies to inform equitable disaster relief fund distribution strategies and Medicaid expansion protocols, demonstrating how computational social science can bridge gaps between theoretical policy design and practical implementation constraints. The project underscores the growing role of HPC in non-STEM fields by advancing methodological rigor in participatory governance and institutional resource management.
cip_definition: A program that combines the fields of Public Administration and Public Policy and with an emphasis the administration and management of public policies. Includes instruction in the roles, development, and principles of public administration; the management of public policy; executive-legislative relations; public budgetary processes and financial management; administrative law; public personnel management; professional ethics; research methods; role of economic and political factors in public decision-making and policy formulation; and resource allocation.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to conduct a large-scale computational analysis of thematic and stylistic patterns in understudied 19th-century British novels, with a focus on serialized fiction published in periodicals. While traditional literary scholarship has examined canonical works from this era, the vast majority of serialized texts—often exceeding 1,000 words per installment and spanning decades of publication—remain unanalyzed due to their sheer volume and fragmented archival availability. The research problem centers on identifying latent thematic networks and stylistic shifts across this corpus, which may reveal overlooked cultural anxieties and narrative strategies tied to industrialization and class dynamics. The computational approach combines natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based language models fine-tuned on historical texts, with network analysis to map recurring motifs, character interactions, and lexical changes over time. Custom pipelines will process OCR-corrected texts from digitized archives, addressing challenges such as inconsistent formatting and historical orthography. HPC resources are critical for training domain-specific embeddings, running distributed topic modeling (e.g., BERTopic), and simulating keyword co-occurrence networks across a projected corpus of 15,000 installments (≈50 million tokens). Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible dataset of annotated serials, visualizations of theme evolution across publication decades, and statistical models quantifying the relationship between narrative structures and sociohistorical contexts. This work aims to redefine the scope of Victorian literary studies by demonstrating how computational methods can recover marginalized voices and subgenres while providing humanities scholars with reproducible workflows for analyzing large, heterogeneous text corpora. The project’s interdisciplinary framework bridges literary theory and data science, offering a template for resource-intensive digital humanities research that prioritizes both cultural interpretation and computational rigor.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in English language literature, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model and optimize decentralized marketplace dynamics, an emerging interdisciplinary niche at the intersection of computational economics, algorithmic game theory, and blockchain-enabled commerce. Traditional market structures rely on centralized intermediaries to facilitate trust and efficiency, but advances in distributed ledger technologies and autonomous smart contracts have enabled novel peer-to-peer (P2P) trading ecosystems. However, the combinatorial complexity of decentralized markets—including multi-agent strategic behavior, dynamic pricing under uncertainty, and real-time resource allocation—poses significant computational challenges. This study aims to develop agent-based simulation frameworks to evaluate equilibrium states, incentive mechanisms, and failure modes in large-scale P2P markets, with a focus on energy trading platforms and fractional asset exchanges. Using parallelized Monte Carlo methods and reinforcement learning algorithms, we will simulate heterogeneous agent strategies under varying regulatory and topological constraints. The computational models will integrate real-world datasets on transaction networks, liquidity patterns, and behavioral biases to parameterize agent interactions. Key outcomes include predictive metrics for market stability, protocol designs to mitigate collusion risks, and adaptive pricing algorithms for illiquid assets. By addressing the scalability limitations of existing economic simulations, this work will provide actionable insights for designing resilient decentralized market infrastructures, bridging gaps between theoretical mechanism design and practical implementation. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the high-dimensional optimization space and stochastic variability inherent to these systems, enabling simulations at scales previously unattainable with conventional computing infrastructure. Results will contribute to the nascent field of decentralized commerce, offering frameworks applicable to industries exploring blockchain-based market solutions while advancing computational methods for complex economic systems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the general study of business, including the processes of interchanging goods and services (buying, selling and producing), business organization, and accounting as used in profit-making and nonprofit public and private institutions and agencies. The programs may prepare individuals to apply business principles and techniques in various occupational settings.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the precision and customization of ophthalmic lens fabrication by integrating biomechanical modeling, optical simulation, and machine learning. Current lens manufacturing processes rely on static optical models that inadequately account for dynamic interactions between lenses, corneal biomechanics, and individual patient physiology, leading to suboptimal visual outcomes for patients with complex ocular conditions such as keratoconus or post-surgical corneas. To address this, we propose a computational framework that simulates real-time, patient-specific interactions between custom-fabricated lenses and ocular surfaces under varying mechanical and environmental conditions. The project will employ finite element analysis (FEA) to model corneal deformation and stress distribution, coupled with ray-tracing algorithms to predict optical aberrations introduced by lens-cornea interactions. Machine learning models will be trained on multi-modal datasets—including corneal topography, wavefront aberrometry, and patient-reported comfort metrics—to optimize lens curvature, edge design, and material properties. HPC resources are critical for resolving the computational intensity of iterative simulations across thousands of parametric combinations and large-scale data integration. Expected outcomes include a novel predictive tool for lens customization that reduces trial-and-error prototyping in laboratory settings and improves visual acuity outcomes by ≥15% in simulated cohorts. Additionally, the project will generate open-access datasets correlating lens design parameters with biomechanical strain metrics, fostering innovation in adaptive optics for ocular prosthetics. By bridging computational optics, materials science, and ocular biomechanics, this work aims to establish a new paradigm in precision ophthalmic device fabrication, with implications for emerging fields such as augmented reality eyewear and biocompatible smart lenses.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of ophthalmologists and optometrists, to cut, grind, edge, and finish corrective lenses and to fabricate eyewear. Includes instruction in optical theory, applied mathematics, lens surfacing and finishing, tinting and coating, impact resistance treatment and testing, frame construction and repair, prescription interpretation, equipment operation and maintenance, follow-up adjustment, record-keeping, and laboratory safety procedures.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable optimization framework for complex industrial systems under uncertainty, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to address computational bottlenecks in real-time decision-making.
