Includes instruction in biomechanics, gait analysis, pathomechanics, kinesiology, pathology, neuroanatomy, materials science, diagnostic imaging, patient analysis and measurement, impression taking, model rectification, assistive/restorative technology and engineering applications, product finishing, diagnostic and definitive fitting and alignment, power devices, postoperative management, and patient counseling and follow-up.

abstract: The study of plant structural adaptations to mechanical stress has remained underexplored due to the lack of integrative computational frameworks bridging cellular architecture, tissue-level mechanics, and environmental interactions. This project seeks to resolve how specialized cell wall compositions in mechanically stressed plants (e.g., wind-prone coastal species) enable energy dissipation and structural resilience, a question unaddressed by traditional biomechanical or physiological approaches. We propose a multiscale computational model integrating molecular dynamics simulations of cellulose-microfibril networks, finite element analysis of tissue deformation under dynamic loads, and machine learning-driven optimization of hypothetical cell wall architectures. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to parameterize these models using empirical data from atomic force microscopy, tensile testing, and live-cell imaging of stress-responsive lignocellulosic reconfiguration in *Calystegia soldanella*, a model species exhibiting extreme dune habitat adaptation. Simulations will iteratively predict optimal wall compositions under stochastic wind regimes, validated via 4D X-ray tomography of living shoots under controlled turbulence. The project’s computational workflow—leveraging GPU-accelerated molecular modeling and distributed finite element solvers—requires parallelized processing of terabyte-scale datasets to resolve nanoscale-to-macroscale mechanical feedback loops. Anticipated outcomes include (1) identification of evolutionary design principles governing plant mechanical resilience, (2) predictive algorithms for cell wall engineering in bioinspired materials, and (3) open-source tools for simulating plant-environment mechanical interactions. This work establishes a novel paradigm for studying plant adaptation through computational mechanics, advancing both fundamental knowledge and applications in sustainable material design, while circumventing traditional disciplinary boundaries in plant biology research.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in botany/plant biology, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the co-evolution of scientific methodologies and industrial technologies in 19th-century Europe through computational analysis of historical texts, patent records, and socio-economic datasets. The research problem centers on identifying how epistemic shifts in scientific practice—such as the rise of experimental standardization—interacted with technological innovation cycles, and how these dynamics were shaped by broader cultural and economic forces. Traditional historiographic methods struggle to systematically analyze the scale and complexity of these interactions across dispersed archives, necessitating a computational approach. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will apply natural language processing (NLP) to a curated corpus of 250,000 pages of scientific journals, technical manuals, and industrial correspondence from 1800–1900, supplemented by structured data from patent registries and trade ledgers. Custom transformer-based models will be trained to detect semantic shifts in terminology related to measurement, precision, and material processes, while graph network analyses will map temporal and geographic patterns of knowledge exchange between academic institutions and industries. A key innovation involves agent-based modeling to simulate how resource allocation in emerging engineering disciplines (e.g., thermodynamics, metallurgy) influenced regional technological adoption rates. Computational demands include large-scale parallelized text embedding, dynamic network visualization of citation clusters, and Monte Carlo simulations assessing counterfactual developmental scenarios. Expected outcomes include: (1) a quantitative framework for evaluating the material constraints on scientific theory formation, (2) identification of previously overlooked institutional actors in cross-disciplinary innovation, and (3) open-access tools for computational historiography. By integrating HPC-driven analytics with philosophical models of epistemic change, this work aims to establish new methodologies for studying technoscientific evolution while critically examining assumptions about linear progress in standard narratives of the Industrial Revolution.
detailed_field: History/ philosophy of science, technology, and society
cip_title: History and Philosophy of Science and Technology
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the historical evolution of scientific theories, science applications and technologies, and the scientific, medical, and technological disciplines, as well as the philosophy of science and its historical socio-economic context. Includes instruction in the concepts and methods of philosophical inquiry; historiography of science; history of science, medicine, and technology; and research methods in the history of the scientific and engineering disciplines, including mathematics.

abstract: Hematological disorders involving clotting pathologies, such as hereditary thrombophilias or acquired coagulation dysregulation, present significant diagnostic challenges due to the dynamic interplay of cellular, molecular, and hemodynamic factors. Current clinical assays often fail to capture the real-time spatial and temporal complexity of clot formation and dissolution, limiting predictive accuracy for thrombotic events. This project proposes a computational framework to model multiscale clot dynamics by integrating molecular interactions of coagulation proteins, platelet activation mechanics, and fluid-structure interactions within physiologically realistic vascular geometries. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we will simulate three-dimensional clot propagation under varying shear conditions and biochemical perturbations, parameterized by patient-derived hematologic data. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations will resolve conformational changes in fibrinogen and thrombin at near-atomic resolution, while continuum-scale models will couple these results with cellular-scale platelet adhesion dynamics. A custom lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) solver will model whole-blood rheology in anatomically accurate vessel networks reconstructed from clinical imaging data. Machine learning techniques will be employed to identify critical thresholds in clot stability and embolization risks from the simulation ensemble. The computational pipeline will be validated against microfluidic flow chamber experiments measuring clot morphology under controlled shear gradients. Successful implementation will establish a predictive platform for stratifying thrombosis risk in complex hematologic conditions, enabling personalized anticoagulant therapy optimization. This work bridges gaps between mechanobiology, computational fluid dynamics, and clinical hematology technology, offering a novel paradigm for interpreting laboratory coagulation tests within their physiological context. The requested HPC resources will support large-scale parameter sweeps, high-fidelity MD trajectories, and GPU-accelerated LBM simulations, which are computationally prohibitive on local infrastructure. Anticipated outcomes include open-source simulation tools for the hematology community and clinically actionable biomarkers derived from multiscale modeling.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of clinical laboratory scientists and health care professionals, to perform tests and analyses of blood samples. Includes instruction in clinical laboratory procedures; blood anatomy and physiology; cellular and molecular biology; blood pathology and disease indicators; quantitative, qualitative, and coagulation testing methodologies; equipment operation and maintenance; and record-keeping.

abstract: The integration of traditional herbal medicine with modern molecular science remains underexplored, despite its widespread global use and potential for novel therapeutic discovery. This project addresses the critical gap in understanding the polypharmacological mechanisms of multi-herb formulations used in Traditional East Asian Medicine (TEAM) systems. While clinical studies suggest efficacy for conditions such as chronic inflammation and metabolic disorders, the combinatorial effects of phytochemical ensembles on cellular signaling networks remain computationally intractable with conventional methods. We propose a multi-scale computational framework to model herb-herb-target-pathway interactions using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Molecular docking simulations will screen 8,000+ phytochemicals from a curated database of 120 TEAM formulations against 320 human protein targets implicated in immunometabolic regulation. Network pharmacology analyses will map synergistic and antagonistic relationships between compounds, followed by dynamic simulations of prioritized multi-target systems using all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) to characterize binding stability and conformational changes. A machine learning pipeline will then identify predictive patterns linking traditional formulation principles (e.g., herb pairing rules) to measurable bioactivity profiles. The computational workflow leverages GPU-accelerated docking (AutoDock-GPU), distributed MD (NAMD), and ensemble learning architectures (PyTorch), requiring 1.2 million core-hours and 40 TB of temporary storage for parallel batch processing. Expected outcomes include 1) the first quantitative map of cross-herb target modulation networks, 2) validated predictive models for formulation bioactivity, and 3) a public database of simulated herb-target interaction kinetics. This work establishes a computational bridge between empirical traditional medicine knowledge and systems biology, enabling data-driven optimization of integrative treatment strategies while preserving historical therapeutic paradigms. Results will directly inform ongoing preclinical studies of formulation safety and biomarker responses.
cip_title: Alternative and Complementary Medicine and Medical Systems, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in alternative and complementary medicine and medical systems, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in healthcare facility operations through the development of advanced computational models to optimize resource allocation, staffing, and patient flow management. Healthcare facilities face complex challenges in balancing dynamic patient demands with finite resources, which are exacerbated by unpredictable variables such as fluctuating admission rates, staff availability, and equipment utilization. Traditional management approaches often rely on static protocols or heuristic decision-making, leading to suboptimal outcomes in cost, wait times, and care quality. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes a data-driven framework integrating agent-based modeling, discrete-event simulation, and machine learning to dynamically predict and adapt to operational stressors in real time. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process large-scale datasets—including historical patient admission records, staff schedules, equipment telemetry, and real-time sensor data—and to simulate facility-wide scenarios under diverse constraints. The models will incorporate multi-objective optimization algorithms to evaluate trade-offs between cost, resource utilization, and patient outcomes, while accounting for regulatory and labor policy requirements. Validation will occur through retrospective analysis of anonymized operational data from partner hospitals and iterative testing of intervention strategies. Expected outcomes include actionable insights for reducing patient wait times, improving staff-to-patient ratios, and minimizing equipment downtime, as well as a generalizable computational toolkit for healthcare administrators. By enabling rapid, evidence-based decision-making, this work aims to enhance operational resilience, reduce preventable delays in care delivery, and lower institutional costs. The project will also contribute methodological advances in applying HPC to healthcare management problems, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration between computational science and health administration. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publications and open-source tools to support broader adoption in the field.
cip_title: Hospital and Health Care Facilities Administration/ Management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply managerial principles to the administration of hospitals, clinics, nursing homes, and other health care facilities. Includes instruction in facilities planning, building and operations management, business management, financial management and insurance, fund-raising and marketing, public relations, human resources management and labor relations, health care facilities operations, principles of health care delivery, and applicable law and regulations.

abstract: Osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) is a cornerstone of osteopathic medicine, yet the biomechanical and neurophysiological mechanisms underlying its therapeutic effects remain incompletely characterized. This project seeks to address this gap by developing multiscale computational models to simulate the biomechanical interactions of OMT techniques on human tissues and their downstream effects on physiological systems. A key challenge lies in integrating heterogeneous clinical data—including patient-specific imaging, motion capture, electromyography, and electronic health records—into predictive models that account for anatomical variability, tissue viscoelasticity, and neural feedback loops. To achieve this, we propose a two-phase computational approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. First, finite element modeling will simulate the three-dimensional mechanical deformation of musculoskeletal structures during representative OMT protocols, incorporating anisotropic material properties derived from diffusion tensor imaging and ultrasound elastography. Second, machine learning algorithms will analyze longitudinal clinical outcomes data to identify patterns linking specific mechanical inputs to neuroinflammatory modulation and autonomic nervous system responses. The computational workflow requires parallel processing capabilities for iterative parameter optimization in finite element simulations (estimated at 10⁶ core-hours) and GPU acceleration for training deep neural networks on multimodal datasets (>50 TB). Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models quantifying force transmission pathways during OMT, (2) mechanistic insights into how manual interventions influence systemic biomarkers such as cytokine profiles and heart rate variability, and (3) a computational framework for optimizing OMT protocols based on individual patient characteristics. This research will advance evidence-based practice in osteopathic medicine by establishing quantitative relationships between manual interventions and their clinical effects while demonstrating how HPC resources can catalyze innovation in hands-on therapeutic disciplines. The resulting models and datasets will be made available to the research community through an open-access portal, fostering collaborative investigations into osteopathic principles.
cip_definition: Research focused on Osteopathic Medicine

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address the growing computational demands of advanced digital arts research, particularly in the creation and optimization of large-scale, interactive, and AI-driven visual media. Current workflows in digital arts face significant bottlenecks when generating high-resolution 3D environments, simulating dynamic physics-based effects, or training generative neural networks for procedural content creation. These tasks require intensive parallel processing, real-time rendering capabilities, and vast memory allocation—requirements that exceed the capacity of standard desktop workstations. The research will focus on three core areas: (1) developing AI models for generative art and style transfer using multi-GPU training to accelerate iterative design processes; (2) simulating complex particle systems and fluid dynamics for immersive installations through distributed computing frameworks; and (3) enabling real-time interactivity in 4K/8K virtual reality (VR) environments via GPU-accelerated ray tracing and memory-optimized rendering pipelines. Computational methods will include CUDA-optimized algorithms, PyTorch-based neural networks, and MPI-parallelized simulations, validated against benchmarks in rendering efficiency and user experience metrics. The project’s outcomes aim to reduce rendering times by 60–80% for high-fidelity scenes, enable novel artistic workflows through scalable AI tools, and establish best practices for integrating HPC into digital arts pedagogy. By democratizing access to supercomputing resources, this work will empower artists and researchers to explore computationally prohibitive techniques—such as hyperrealistic real-time visuals or billion-parameter generative models—while contributing to interdisciplinary dialogues at the intersection of art, technology, and computational science. Results will directly support faculty-student collaborations, public digital exhibitions, and industry partnerships in game development and immersive media.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A general, undifferentiated program that focuses on the use of computerized digital images as the primary medium of expression in the visual and performing arts, and that may prepare individuals for a wide variety of careers using new media, including graphic design, digital animation, motion graphics, 3D visualization, game and interactive media design, music and sound design, video production, web design, photography, and other fields.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of the neurocomputational mechanisms underlying stress-related behavioral adaptation by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model large-scale neural circuits. Stress responses are governed by dynamic interactions across the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, limbic structures (e.g., amygdala, hippocampus), and prefrontal cortical regions. However, existing models lack the granularity to simulate real-time neurotransmitter dynamics across these distributed networks or to integrate multi-modal data (e.g., fMRI, electrophysiology, cortisol assays) at biologically relevant spatiotemporal scales. To address this gap, we propose developing a spiking neural network (SNN) framework that incorporates biophysically detailed models of glucocorticoid receptor modulation, noradrenergic signaling, and synaptic plasticity across 10^5–10^6 neurons. The SNN will be trained and validated using rodent electrophysiological datasets (in vivo single-unit recordings during acute/chronic stress paradigms) and human fMRI-derived functional connectivity maps. HPC resources are critical for parallelizing simulations across GPU nodes, optimizing parameters via evolutionary algorithms, and performing Bayesian model comparison to identify circuit-level predictors of maladaptive behavioral outcomes. Expected outcomes include (1) a publicly available computational toolkit for simulating stress-induced neuroendocrine-immune interactions, (2) predictive biomarkers of resilience/vulnerability derived from network stability metrics, and (3) mechanistic insights into how chronic stress reshapes cortico-limbic communication. By bridging molecular, systems-level, and behavioral domains, this work will establish a computational foundation for testable hypotheses about stress-related disorders while advancing methods for multi-scale modeling in behavioral neuroscience. The proposed simulations require ~2.5M core-hours annually to achieve millisecond-resolution dynamics over 24-hour circadian cycles, exceeding the capacity of local institutional clusters.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of the biological bases of behavior.

abstract: Hematologic and coagulation disorders present complex diagnostic and therapeutic challenges due to heterogeneous molecular mechanisms, variable clinical presentations, and dynamic interactions between cellular, genetic, and environmental factors. Current approaches to analyzing hematologic data—including high-throughput genomic, proteomic, and clinical datasets—are constrained by computational limitations in processing speed, memory, and integration of multimodal datasets. This project proposes to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop predictive models of disease progression, treatment response, and thrombotic risk in hematologic malignancies and inherited coagulopathies. The research will integrate whole-genome sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, and longitudinal clinical data from patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and rare bleeding disorders to identify biomarkers and signaling networks associated with clinical outcomes. Computational methods will include Bayesian network inference, deep learning for spatial-temporal pattern recognition in coagulation assays, and agent-based modeling of clot formation dynamics under varying physiologic conditions. These analyses require parallelized processing of terabyte-scale datasets and iterative simulations that exceed the capacity of local institutional servers. Expected outcomes include (1) validated algorithms for risk stratification in AML based on clonal architecture and microenvironment interactions, (2) predictive models linking platelet proteomic signatures to bleeding/thrombosis phenotypes, and (3) open-source computational workflows optimized for hematology laboratory data. By enabling large-scale integration of experimental and clinical data, this work will advance precision diagnostics and inform targeted therapeutic strategies while establishing scalable frameworks for computational pathology in resource-constrained clinical settings. The requested HPC allocation is critical to achieving statistically robust results within clinically relevant timelines.
cip_definition: Research focused on the laboratory and analytical procedures for studying all facets of hematologic and coagulation disorders. May included related research in the management of hematology laboratories.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance precision nutrition research by modeling complex interactions between dietary patterns, metabolic responses, and individualized health outcomes. Current dietary recommendations often rely on population-level data, which fail to account for interindividual variability in genetics, microbiome composition, and metabolic dynamics. To address this gap, we propose developing a computational framework integrating multi-omic data (metabolomic, genomic, and microbiome sequencing) with real-time physiological monitoring datasets from clinical nutrition studies. The research problem centers on identifying predictive signatures of glycemic variability and lipid metabolism dysregulation in response to heterogeneous diets, with a focus on populations at risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Computational methods will include machine learning ensemble models to analyze high-dimensional datasets and agent-based simulations of nutrient absorption processes at cellular resolution. The HPC environment is critical for training deep neural networks on multimodal data (>10 TB across 5,000 patient records) and running parallelized simulations of intestinal nutrient transport under varying dietary conditions. Expected outcomes include (1) a validated predictive algorithm for personalized meal planning, (2) mechanistic insights into microbiome-diet interactions affecting metabolic health, and (3) open-source tools for simulating nutrient metabolism across diverse physiological profiles. By enabling rapid analysis of non-linear relationships in nutrition science, this work will directly support the development of targeted clinical interventions, reduce trial-and-error approaches in dietary management, and provide a scalable computational model for future studies in precision dietetics. The requested resources will ensure sufficient capacity for data-intensive model training, reduce runtime for iterative simulation workflows by 70%, and facilitate collaboration with clinical partners through secure, high-throughput data processing.
cip_title: Dietetics and Clinical Nutrition Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in dietetics and clinical nutrition services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The emergence and spread of infectious diseases at the human-animal-environment interface present complex challenges requiring advanced computational tools to model transmission dynamics, evaluate intervention strategies, and inform policy. This project aims to develop a high-resolution, multi-host epidemiological framework to simulate disease spread in livestock populations, with a focus on pathogens of zoonotic potential (e.g., avian influenza, Salmonella spp.). Current models often lack the spatial, demographic, and behavioral granularity needed to capture transmission heterogeneity in diverse agricultural systems, limiting their utility for targeted preventive measures. To address this, we propose an agent-based modeling (ABM) approach integrating livestock movement data, geospatial environmental variables, and genomic surveillance data to simulate pathogen evolution and dissemination across scales. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to parameterize millions of agents (individual animals, farms, transport networks) and execute stochastic simulations across plausible outbreak scenarios. Computational workflows will leverage parallelized Monte Carlo methods to quantify uncertainty in transmission rates, vaccine efficacy, and culling protocol impacts. Machine learning models will further analyze simulation outputs to identify high-risk zones and optimize resource allocation for surveillance. This project will also establish a novel pipeline for real-time integration of field data (e.g., veterinary diagnostic records, climate sensors) into adaptive models, enabled by cloud-HPC hybrid architectures. Expected outcomes include validated predictive tools for state animal health agencies to prioritize testing, design containment perimeters, and mitigate economic losses. By bridging gaps between computational epidemiology and veterinary practice, this work advances preventive strategies for emerging zoonoses while providing a scalable framework for One Health analytics. The requested resources will support GPU-accelerated model training, large-scale parameter sweeps, and public dashboards to disseminate risk forecasts to stakeholders.
cip_definition: Research focused on the investigation of and intervention in health and disease problems of animal and related human communities, comparative medicine, and animal public health. May included related research in biostatistics, epidemiology, environmental control, toxicology and the planning and administration of animal health programs and services.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamics of digital information dissemination in the context of Family and Consumer Sciences (FCS) communication, with a focus on optimizing the reach and efficacy of consumer-oriented content. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how algorithmic curation, platform-specific user behavior, and multimedia content interact to shape the public’s engagement with FCS topics such as nutritional literacy, sustainable consumption, and household financial management. Traditional models of human sciences communication lack the computational rigor to analyze the vast, heterogeneous datasets generated by multi-platform digital ecosystems, limiting the ability to design evidence-based strategies for impactful messaging. To overcome this, the project will employ a hybrid computational approach combining natural language processing (NLP), agent-based modeling, and network analysis. NLP tools will parse textual and visual content from social media, educational platforms, and public forums to identify thematic trends and sentiment patterns. Agent-based simulations will model how diverse user archetypes interact with FCS content under varying algorithmic conditions, while temporal network analysis will map information diffusion pathways across platforms. These methods require HPC capabilities to process terabytes of unstructured data, train machine learning models on high-dimensional feature sets, and execute large-scale simulations iteratively. Expected outcomes include actionable insights into platform-specific content optimization, predictive frameworks for identifying “tipping points” in consumer engagement, and open-source tools for adaptive message tailoring. By bridging computational methodologies with human sciences communication theory, this work aims to enhance the precision and scalability of public-facing FCS initiatives, ultimately supporting informed decision-making in households and communities. The resource request aligns with the interdisciplinary and emerging nature of digital consumer science, advancing a niche that integrates technical innovation with human-centric research imperatives.
cip_title: Family and Consumer Sciences/ Human Sciences Communication
cip_definition: A program that focuses on communication of human sciences subject matter and related consumer information to a variety of audiences through print and non-print media.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational tools to address the growing complexity of high-resolution, dynamic illustration workflows in visual storytelling and client-driven design. Contemporary illustration practices increasingly require the integration of large-scale datasets, real-time rendering of 3D environments, and AI-assisted stylistic adaptations—tasks that exceed the capabilities of standard workstations. The primary research problem lies in optimizing resource-intensive processes such as photorealistic texture synthesis, multi-layered vector animation, and neural network-based style transfer while maintaining artistic intent and client specifications. To achieve this, we propose a hybrid computational approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. GPU-accelerated rendering pipelines will be designed to parallelize frame generation for animated illustrations, reducing processing times for 4K+ resolution sequences. Additionally, distributed computing frameworks will train custom generative adversarial networks (GANs) on curated datasets of historical and contemporary illustration styles, enabling rapid prototyping of client-directed aesthetic outputs. A core innovation involves simulating physically accurate material interactions (e.g., fabric draping in fashion illustration, pigment dispersion in digital painting) through finite element analysis scaled across HPC nodes. The project will validate these methods through case studies in interactive children’s book illustration and architectural visualization, measuring gains in workflow efficiency and creative flexibility. Expected outcomes include open-source toolkits for GPU-optimized illustration pipelines, a database of trained style-transfer models compliant with ethical AI guidelines, and benchmarks for computational resource allocation in creative industries. By bridging advanced computing with human-centered design principles, this work aims to establish new paradigms for computationally augmented artistic practice while informing resource infrastructure needs at the intersection of visual arts and technology.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to use artistic techniques to develop and execute interpretations of the concepts of authors and designers to specifications. Includes instruction in book illustration, fashion illustration, map illustration, rendering, exhibit preparation, textual layout, cartooning, and the use of various artistic techniques as requested by clients.

abstract: The administration of special education programs requires data-driven strategies to optimize resource allocation while addressing the diverse needs of students with disabilities. Current approaches to managing Individualized Education Programs (IEPs), staff workflows, and district-level budgets often rely on fragmented datasets or generalized heuristics, limiting their responsiveness to dynamic student populations and evolving legal standards. This project proposes the development of a computational framework to model the impact of resource distribution on student outcomes and compliance efficiency across heterogeneous school systems. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will analyze multi-year administrative datasets encompassing IEP timelines, service delivery logs, staffing patterns, and student performance metrics from 15 partnering districts. Agent-based modeling will simulate how adjustments to personnel deployment, assistive technology investments, and professional development schedules affect service equity and procedural adherence under varying enrollment scenarios. Natural language processing pipelines will further parse unstructured IEP documentation to identify correlations between plan specificity and longitudinal academic progress. Computational demands include large-scale parameter sweeps to evaluate policy scenarios, parallelized optimization algorithms for budget-strained districts, and training of transformer-based models for text analysis. Expected outcomes include (1) a predictive toolset to guide administrators in balancing individualized student supports with systemic resource constraints, (2) evidence-based thresholds for caseload allocations and intervention frequency, and (3) open-source dashboards visualizing cost-benefit tradeoffs of mainstreaming strategies. By scaling analyses across millions of anonymized records, this work aims to establish computationally tractable methods for advancing equity in special education administration while maintaining compliance with federal mandates. Results will directly inform training modules for district leaders and state-level policy briefs on sustainable special education funding models.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to plan, supervise, and manage programs for exceptional students and their parents. Includes instruction in special education theory and practice, special education program development, evaluation and assessment in special education, state and federal law and regulations, managing individual education plans, problems of low- and high- disability students, mainstreaming, special education curricula, staff management, parent education, communications and community relations, budgeting, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: Athletic training requires precise understanding of biomechanical stresses, physiological responses, and rehabilitation protocols to mitigate sports-related injuries. Current approaches to injury risk assessment and rehabilitation planning often rely on generalized population data or simplified models, limiting their accuracy in predicting individual outcomes. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing patient-specific computational models that integrate multi-modal data—including motion capture, musculoskeletal imaging, and real-time physiological monitoring—to simulate injury mechanisms and optimize recovery strategies. The research problem centers on the computational demands of processing high-resolution biomechanical datasets, running iterative simulations of tissue stress and recovery trajectories, and applying machine learning to personalize interventions. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage the scale and complexity of these tasks, which involve terabyte-level datasets, finite element modeling of musculoskeletal structures, and probabilistic analyses of rehabilitation outcomes. The computational approach will leverage parallelized workflows to (1) model dynamic joint loading during sport-specific movements, (2) predict soft tissue adaptation under therapeutic exercise regimens, and (3) identify biomarkers of overuse injuries through anomaly detection in longitudinal athlete data. Expected outcomes include a validated framework for simulating injury risk at the individual level, data-driven guidelines for tailoring rehabilitation protocols, and open-source tools for athletic trainers to analyze biomechanical efficiency. By enabling precise, computationally intensive analyses of athlete-specific data, this work aims to reduce recovery times, improve return-to-play decision-making, and inform injury prevention strategies across diverse populations. The project aligns with the growing emphasis on translational sports medicine research, bridging gaps between clinical practice and computational innovation in health professions.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to work in consultation with, and under the supervision of physicians to prevent and treat sports injuries and associated conditions. Includes instruction in the identification, evaluation, and treatment of athletic injuries and illnesses; first aid and emergency care; therapeutic exercise; anatomy and physiology; exercise physiology; kinesiology and biomechanics; nutrition; sports psychology; personal and community health; knowledge of various sports and their biomechanical and physiological demands; and applicable professional standards and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to analyze the dynamics of cross-national policy diffusion and compliance in multilateral environmental agreements (MEAs), a critical challenge in international public policy. Despite the proliferation of MEAs aimed at addressing climate change and biodiversity loss, inconsistent national implementation and monitoring gaps hinder global governance effectiveness. Existing research often relies on qualitative case studies or limited quantitative datasets, which struggle to capture the complex, adaptive interactions between governments, non-state actors, and transnational institutions. To address this gap, we propose developing an agent-based model (ABM) simulating negotiation, ratification, and compliance behaviors across 150+ nations over a 30-year timeframe. The ABM will integrate heterogeneous datasets, including treaty accession records, national policy documents, NGO shadow reports, and economic indicators, to parameterize decision-making rules for state and non-state actors. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to run large-scale parameter sweeps testing competing theories of policy diffusion—such as coercion, competition, and learning—while managing stochastic variance across thousands of simulations. Parallelized sensitivity analyses will identify key leverage points for improving treaty adherence, with validation against real-world compliance data from the UN Treaty Body Database. Expected outcomes include a scalable computational framework to predict policy adoption bottlenecks under different globalization scenarios, actionable insights for designing adaptive monitoring mechanisms in future agreements, and open-source tools for simulating transnational governance systems. By quantifying how institutional design choices influence collective policy outcomes, this work directly advances evidence-based strategies for addressing transnational challenges through multilateral cooperation, while avoiding disciplinary overlap with excluded fields through its focus on applied policy systems rather than foundational political or economic theories.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic analysis of public policy issues related to relationships among nations and among governments and non-governmental entities. Includes instruction in international politics, governance, financial policy, and security affairs; globalization; economic and social policies of developing nations; and applications to specific public policy topics such as labor and employment, immigration, and human rights.

abstract: Cybersecurity policy frameworks must rapidly adapt to evolving adversarial tactics, yet existing approaches to strategy development often lack rigorous, data-driven validation of resilience under complex, large-scale attack scenarios. This project seeks to address this gap by developing computational models to simulate multi-stage cyber conflicts across heterogeneous infrastructure networks while evaluating the cascading impacts of policy decisions on systemic security outcomes. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we propose an agent-based modeling environment that integrates geopolitical decision-making algorithms with technical vulnerability landscapes, simulating nation-state and criminal threat actors targeting cross-sector digital ecosystems under varying defense postures. The computational framework will process real-world datasets on critical infrastructure interdependencies, historical incident patterns, and emerging attack vectors to parameterize scenarios ranging from regional ransomware campaigns to coordinated infrastructure disruption. Machine learning techniques will be applied to analyze simulation outputs, identifying policy configurations that optimize tradeoffs between proactive defense investments, incident response agility, and economic constraints. By modeling recursive feedback loops between attacker adaptation and defender policy adjustments at petabyte scale, this research aims to produce quantifiable metrics for policy resilience—a novel contribution to cybersecurity strategy literature. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for stress-testing defense policies under synthetic crisis conditions and evidence-based recommendations for dynamic resource allocation frameworks. This work directly supports policymakers in transitioning from reactive compliance-based paradigms to anticipatory, scenario-hardened strategies while establishing computational social science methodologies for cybersecurity governance research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of strategy, policy, and standards regarding the security of and operations in cyberspace. Includes instruction in incident response, information assurance, recovery policies, vulnerability reduction, deterrence, threat reduction, and resiliency.

abstract: The integration of advanced computational methods with physical science research is critical to overcoming limitations in simulating multi-scale phenomena inherent to next-generation materials and processes. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the dynamic behavior of metastable materials under extreme thermodynamic conditions, a problem currently constrained by the computational intensity of tracking atomic interactions across experimentally relevant timescales. The research will employ hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations, enhanced by machine learning-driven force fields, to model phase transitions and defect propagation in high-entropy alloys and glassy systems. These methods require parallelized computation across thousands of cores to handle the iterative optimization of interatomic potentials and the statistical sampling of rare events. By coupling adaptive sampling algorithms with GPU-accelerated MD frameworks, the project aims to achieve microsecond-scale simulations at near-ab initio accuracy, enabling the prediction of material failure mechanisms and stability thresholds. The outcomes will directly inform the design of alloys with tailored mechanical properties for aerospace and energy applications, reducing reliance on costly trial-and-error experimentation. Furthermore, the development of open-source workflow tools for automated parameter calibration and uncertainty quantification will enhance reproducibility in computational materials science. The scale of data generated—anticipated to exceed 500 TB of trajectory and metadata—necessitates distributed storage and in-situ analysis capabilities provided by HPC infrastructure. This work bridges gaps between atomistic modeling and industrial material testing, advancing the foundational role of computational science in physical technology innovation. Successful execution will establish scalable protocols for simulating non-equilibrium systems, with broader implications for catalysis, nanotechnology, and quantum material discovery.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in physical science technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The complexity of predicting toxicological outcomes arising from mixed chemical exposures, genetic variability, and dynamic physiological conditions presents a critical challenge in medical toxicology. Current experimental models struggle to capture the interplay of these factors at scale, limiting clinical risk assessment and personalized treatment strategies. This project proposes a computational framework to model toxicity mechanisms, predict patient-specific outcomes, and optimize therapeutic interventions using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. We will integrate molecular dynamics simulations, toxicokinetic/toxicodynamic modeling, and machine learning to analyze interactions between xenobiotics (e.g., synthetic opioids, environmental toxins) and biological targets, incorporating genomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data from clinical toxicology registries. HPC resources will enable large-scale virtual screening of antidote candidates, ensemble modeling of exposure scenarios, and real-time simulations of toxin metabolism across diverse patient populations. Key objectives include identifying genetic biomarkers of susceptibility to specific toxicants, predicting dose-response relationships in polydrug exposures, and optimizing protocols for chelation therapies. The computational pipeline will be validated against multicenter clinical data on acute poisonings and chronic occupational exposures. This work addresses critical gaps in toxicological risk prediction, particularly for novel synthetic compounds and mass exposure events. Expected outcomes include an open-access predictive platform for toxicity phenotyping, decision-support tools for bedside management, and mechanistic insights into understudied toxicants. By leveraging HPC capabilities to simulate multifactorial toxicity pathways, this research aims to advance evidence-based practices in overdose treatment, hazard preparedness, and precision toxicology, ultimately improving outcomes for chemically exposed patients.
cip_definition: Research focused on that prepares physicians who specialize in the prevention, evaluation, treatment, and monitoring of injury and illness from exposures to drugs and chemicals, as well as exposures to biological and radiological agents. Important areas include acute drug poisoning; adverse drug events; drug abuse, addiction, and withdrawal; chemicals and hazardous materials; terrorism preparedness; venomous bites and stings; and environmental and workplace exposures.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in crisis communication and image management, a critical subfield of public relations. The research problem centers on modeling the rapid, large-scale dissemination of information—and misinformation—during organizational crises, which challenges traditional manual or small-scale analytical methods. Current approaches often fail to capture the dynamic interplay of social media algorithms, stakeholder networks, and real-time public sentiment, limiting the ability to predict reputational outcomes or optimize response strategies. To address this gap, the project will employ agent-based modeling (ABM) and natural language processing (NLP) to simulate crisis scenarios and evaluate image repair tactics. The ABM framework will integrate heterogeneous agents (e.g., media outlets, social media users, institutional stakeholders) with behavioral rules derived from empirical communication theories, while NLP pipelines will process multilingual social media corpora to parameterize sentiment dynamics. Computational demands arise from simulating millions of agent interactions across diverse crisis archetypes (e.g., product recalls, executive scandals) and iteratively training transformer-based models to detect emerging narrative patterns. HPC resources are essential to parallelize simulations, reduce latency in hyperparameter tuning, and manage memory-intensive tasks such as network graph analysis. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible toolkit for predicting reputational risk trajectories and a decision-support system to guide message framing, timing, and channel selection during crises. By quantifying how specific communication strategies mitigate or amplify reputational damage, this work will provide actionable insights for public relations practitioners while advancing computational social science methodologies. The project directly aligns with institutional strengths in strategic communication research and addresses a growing industry need for data-driven image management in an era of algorithmic media ecosystems.
detailed_field: Applied communication, advertising, and public relations
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theories and methods for managing the media image of a business, organization, or individual and the communication process with stakeholders, constituencies, audiences, and the general public; and that prepares individuals to function as public relations assistants, technicians, and managers. Includes instruction in public relations theory; related principles of advertising, marketing, and journalism; message/image design; image management; special event management; media relations; community relations; public affairs; and internal communications.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in human sciences communication, specifically addressing the challenge of modeling complex, large-scale consumer behavior data in digital ecosystems. The research problem centers on understanding how dynamic, nonlinear interactions between socio-cultural narratives, digital media consumption, and household decision-making influence the adoption of health-related practices (e.g., nutritional literacy, sustainable consumption). Traditional analytical methods struggle to capture the high-dimensional, temporally evolving nature of these interactions across heterogeneous datasets, including social media traces, ethnographic surveys, and longitudinal consumer expenditure records. The proposed computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) and agent-based modeling (ABM) within a unified framework to simulate emergent behavioral patterns at population scales. Custom NLP pipelines will process unstructured text from community forums and multimedia content to extract latent themes and sentiment trajectories, while ABM simulations will parameterize decision-making processes using demographic, economic, and psychosocial variables. HPC resources are critical for managing the combinatorial complexity of scenario testing, particularly when scaling simulations to regional population levels (10^5–10^6 agents) with fine-grained temporal resolution. Expected outcomes include novel metrics for quantifying narrative diffusion efficacy in human sciences contexts and predictive models of intervention effectiveness for public health campaigns. This work bridges computational social science with family resource management theory, creating methodological innovations for a domain where data intensity and system interdependencies have historically limited analytical depth. The requested computing infrastructure will enable unprecedented scalability in simulating socio-technical systems central to modern human sciences communication, directly informing evidence-based strategies for consumer education and community engagement.
cip_title: Family and Consumer Sciences/ Human Sciences Communication
cip_definition: A program that focuses on communication of human sciences subject matter and related consumer information to a variety of audiences through print and non-print media.

abstract: This project seeks to address unresolved questions about turbulence and magnetic field dynamics in molecular clouds, critical drivers of star formation efficiency in galaxies. Despite advances in observational astronomy, the interplay between supersonic turbulence, magnetic pressure, and gravitational collapse remains poorly quantified, limiting predictive models of galactic evolution. We propose a high-resolution numerical study using magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) simulations to resolve multiphase gas interactions at scales from 0.1 pc to 100 pc, capturing both cloud-scale dynamics and localized collapse thresholds. The simulations will utilize the FLASH code, augmented with custom modules for radiative transfer and non-equilibrium chemistry, to model turbulence injection by supernova remnants and feedback from young stellar populations. A parameter space of magnetic field strengths (1–50 μG), metallicities, and cloud densities will be explored to assess their roles in regulating star formation rates under varying galactic environments. The computational workload necessitates high-performance computing resources due to the simulations’ scale: adaptive mesh refinement will require up to 10^6 core-hours to achieve the necessary resolution for tracking density fluctuations and magnetic field topology. Data outputs will be analyzed using machine learning-based feature detection to identify statistical correlations between initial conditions and star formation outcomes. This work will directly inform interpretation of JWST and ALMA observations of nearby galaxies while providing open-source turbulence metrics for the astrophysics community. Results will constrain key parameters in next-generation semi-analytic galaxy evolution models, reducing uncertainties in predictions of stellar mass assembly across cosmic time. The derived datasets will be made publicly available through a dedicated portal, enabling cross-disciplinary studies in interstellar medium physics and computational fluid dynamics.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the planetary, galactic, and stellar phenomena occurring in outer space. Includes instruction in celestial mechanics, cosmology, stellar physics, galactic evolution, quasars, stellar distribution and motion, interstellar medium, atomic and molecular constituents of astronomical phenomena, planetary science, solar system evolution, and specific methodologies such as optical astronomy, radioastronomy, and theoretical astronomy.

abstract: The proposed research investigates the molecular mechanisms underlying plant circadian rhythm plasticity in response to non-canonical environmental stressors, specifically nanoparticulate pollutants and polarized light regimes. While plant circadian systems are well-studied under typical abiotic stresses, emerging anthropogenic factors create unique spatiotemporal signaling challenges that existing models cannot resolve. This project employs a novel computational framework integrating live-cell imaging data of organelle dynamics with hyperspectral fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) datasets to map real-time protein-cofactor interactions in Arabidopsis thaliana under controlled stress matrices. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process terabytes of light sheet microscopy videos (captured at 30 fps over 72-hour cycles) using convolutional neural networks trained to detect phase-shift patterns in chloroplast-nucleus signaling. Molecular dynamics simulations will parameterize newly discovered cryptochrome-phytochrome heterodimers observed in preliminary studies, requiring GPU-accelerated sampling of 10+ microsecond trajectories to characterize allosteric regulation under quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) constraints. Expected outcomes include 1) a predictive model of circadian entrainment thresholds for engineered nanoparticle exposure, 2) identification of plasticity-mediating phosphorylation motifs in clock-associated proteins through comparative kinome network analysis, and 3) open-source tools for correlative 4D organelle tracking across heterogeneous cell populations. This work bridges plant molecular biology with environmental nanotoxicology and quantum biology, addressing critical gaps in understanding how non-linear stressors disrupt temporal coordination of photosynthesis and stress adaptation. The computational infrastructure will enable unprecedented resolution of plant circadian systems at multiple scales, directly informing biotechnological strategies to enhance crop resilience in rapidly changing light pollution and nanomaterial-impacted ecosystems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of molecular biology, biochemistry, and biophysics to the study of biomolecular structures, functions, and processes specific to plants and plant substances. Includes instruction in the biochemistry of plant cells, nuclear-cytoplasmic interactions, molecular cytostructures, photosynthesis, plant molecular genetics, and the molecular biology of plant diseases.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize emergency response protocols and cabin crew coordination during in-flight crises, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate dynamic, high-stakes scenarios. Airline flight attendants must rapidly assess and mitigate risks—such as medical emergencies, cabin depressurization, or evacuation events—under variable conditions, including passenger demographics, crew availability, and aircraft configurations. Current training protocols rely on static scenarios and manual drills, which lack the adaptability to account for real-world complexity. To address this gap, we propose agent-based modeling (ABM) combined with machine learning (ML) to simulate thousands of emergent scenarios, each parameterized by stochastic inputs (e.g., passenger behavior, equipment failures, environmental stressors). HPC resources will enable parallel execution of these simulations, generating datasets to train ML models that predict optimal crew responses. The ABM will integrate real-world data from incident reports, cabin layouts, and biometric feedback to model interactions between crew, passengers, and physical systems. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations will further analyze air circulation patterns during smoke or contamination events to refine evacuation strategies. Outcomes include predictive decision-support tools for crew training and dynamically adjustable emergency checklists optimized via reinforcement learning. This work will advance safety protocols in aviation by quantifying previously unmodeled variables, such as crew fatigue metrics and passenger compliance rates, under crisis conditions. The resulting open-source framework will serve as a scalable resource for airlines and regulatory agencies to validate and iteratively improve safety standards, directly aligning with the program’s focus on applying technical solutions to enhance in-flight passenger care.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to the performance of a variety of personal services conducive to the safety and comfort of airline passengers during flight, including verifying tickets, explaining the use of safety equipment, providing passenger services, and responding to in-flight emergencies.

abstract: Chronic respiratory diseases represent a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet their molecular and biomechanical complexity remains incompletely resolved. This project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding the interplay between genetic, epigenetic, and biomechanical factors in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), with a focus on identifying shared pathways of disease progression. We propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data, spatially resolved proteomics, and patient-derived biomechanical models of airway remodeling. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage the scale and dimensionality of these datasets, which include over 10,000 patient samples from international cohorts and 3D micro-CT lung reconstructions with submicron resolution. Machine learning models will be trained to classify disease subtypes using graph neural networks that capture cell-cell interaction networks, while finite element simulations will map stress-strain distributions in fibrotic lung tissue under varying mechanical ventilation scenarios. These analyses require parallelized processing of multi-terabyte datasets, stochastic optimization for parameter inference in nonlinear biomechanical models, and GPU-accelerated deep learning workflows. Anticipated outcomes include predictive biomarkers of rapid progression in IPF/COPD, computational signatures of treatment-resistant vascular remodeling, and mechanistic insights into matrix stiffness-driven immune dysregulation. By linking molecular features to tissue-scale pathophysiology, this work aims to enable precision therapeutic strategies and inform the design of novel antifibrotic agents. The requested allocation of 500,000 CPU core-hours and 20,000 GPU hours on a tier-3 HPC cluster will support data integration, model training, and large-scale validation against independent clinical datasets. Findings will be disseminated through open-source computational pipelines to accelerate translational research in pulmonary medicine.
cip_definition: Research focused on pulmonary physiology and the treatment of lung diseases, pulmonary malignancies, related vascular diseases, respiratory disorders, diagnostic and therapeutic procedures, and pulmonary pathology.

abstract: The prevention and management of athletic injuries require a nuanced understanding of the complex interactions between biomechanical forces, tissue adaptation, and rehabilitation protocols. Current clinical strategies for injury risk prediction and post-injury care are often limited by reliance on generalized population data and static biomechanical models, which inadequately capture the dynamic, individualized nature of musculoskeletal stress during sports participation. This project seeks to address these limitations by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop multiscale computational models that integrate real-world biomechanical, imaging, and physiological data. These models will simulate the cumulative effects of repetitive loading on musculoskeletal tissues, predict injury risk under varying athletic workloads, and optimize personalized rehabilitation pathways. The computational framework will employ finite element analysis to model tissue-level stress distributions, coupled with machine learning algorithms trained on multivariate datasets—including wearable sensor data, 3D motion capture, MRI-derived tissue properties, and longitudinal patient outcomes. HPC resources are critical to handle the high-dimensional data processing, parallelize simulations across diverse loading scenarios, and enable real-time parameter optimization for patient-specific recommendations. Expected outcomes include validated predictive tools for identifying athletes at high risk of ligament, tendon, or cartilage injuries, as well as dynamic rehabilitation protocols tailored to individual biomechanical profiles. The project will further quantify the efficacy of preventive interventions, such as neuromuscular training programs, through computational scenario testing. By bridging gaps between biomechanical theory and clinical practice, this work aims to advance evidence-based guidelines for injury prevention, reduce recovery times, and improve long-term musculoskeletal health in athletes. The scalable computational pipelines developed will also provide a foundation for future studies on injury mechanisms and precision rehabilitation in sports medicine.
cip_definition: Research on how to prevent and manage athletic injuries and to provide appropriate care for all structures of the musculoskeletal system directly affected by participation in sporting activity.

abstract: Environmental toxicants such as industrial chemicals and heavy metals pose significant risks to ecosystem and human health, yet predicting their transport, bioaccumulation, and molecular toxicity across heterogeneous environments remains challenging. This project seeks to develop an integrated computational framework to model the fate of priority toxins—including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and mercury species—from environmental dispersal to cellular uptake. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to characterize toxin interactions with biological membranes and proteins, coupled with geospatial models of contaminant dispersion in watersheds. Quantum chemistry calculations will predict degradation pathways under varying environmental conditions, while physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models will assess interspecies toxicity thresholds. By leveraging parallelized processing for multi-scale simulations spanning angstroms to kilometers, this approach addresses critical gaps in cross-system toxicity prediction. Expected outcomes include mechanistic insights into dermal absorption rates of PFAS, probabilistic risk maps for mercury bioaccumulation in aquatic food webs, and optimized parameters for in situ toxin remediation strategies. The computational workflows developed will provide a scalable platform for evaluating emerging contaminants, directly supporting regulatory decision-making and advancing protective interventions for environmental health.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the health effects associated with exposure to toxic chemicals and systems occurring in the natural, work, and living environments; the management of environmental toxins and toxicity; and the development of protections for humans, animals, and plants. Includes instruction in applied ecology; microbiology; toxin transport, fate, and degradation; dermal toxicology; reproductive and genetic toxicology; atmospheric and environmental chemistry; metals toxicology; environmental mutagens and biotransformation; nutrient interaction; chemical sensitivity, disorders, and disease; risk assessment; animal waste management; environmental health; and hazardous materials management.

abstract: The increasing complexity of engineering design challenges demands advanced computational tools to optimize performance, reduce iterative prototyping costs, and accelerate innovation in computer-aided design (CAD) workflows. Current CAD software often struggles with large-scale parametric modeling, multi-physics simulations, and generative design optimization due to hardware limitations, leading to prolonged computation times and restricted design exploration. This project seeks to address these bottlenecks by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable high-fidelity simulations, machine learning-driven design automation, and real-time collaborative engineering workflows. The research will focus on developing and benchmarking scalable algorithms for finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and topology optimization within an integrated CAD environment. By parallelizing computationally intensive tasks—such as meshing, solver operations, and design space exploration—we aim to reduce simulation times for complex assemblies by an order of magnitude compared to single-workstation processing. Additionally, the project will implement GPU-accelerated rendering pipelines to support interactive visualization of large 3D models (>10 million polygons) and virtual reality (VR)-based design validation. A secondary objective involves training neural networks on HPC clusters to predict mechanical behaviors from parametric inputs, enabling rapid design iteration for additive manufacturing applications. Expected outcomes include a validated framework for distributed computing in CAD workflows, open-source optimization modules for auto-CAD systems, and performance benchmarks comparing cloud-based HPC configurations to traditional local hardware. This work will directly benefit engineering education by providing case studies and scalable templates for teaching computationally demanding CADD techniques, while its applications extend to industries reliant on precision design, including aerospace, renewable energy systems, and biomedical device development. The requested computing resources will support containerized workloads using OpenFOAM and ANSYS solvers, Python-based machine learning pipelines, and distributed rendering tasks through SLURM job scheduling.
cip_title: CAD/ CADD Drafting and/ or Design Technology
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical skills and advanced computer software and hardware to the creation of graphic representations and simulations in support of engineering projects. Includes instruction in engineering graphics, two-dimensional and three-dimensional engineering design, solids modeling, engineering animation, computer-aided drafting (CAD), computer-aided design (CADD), and auto-CAD techniques.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational methods for modeling and simulating multiscale systems in complex fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems, with applications to biomedical and renewable energy systems. A critical challenge in such systems is the interplay between disparate spatial and temporal scales—from microscale turbulent vortices to macroscale structural deformations—which traditional solvers struggle to resolve efficiently due to prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we propose a hybrid approach combining adaptive finite element methods, reduced-order modeling (ROM), and machine learning (ML)-accelerated surrogate models. The core innovation lies in a dynamically adaptive mesh refinement framework that integrates ROM-based predictions of dominant flow modes with ML-driven error estimation to optimize computational resource allocation. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to parallelize the multiscale simulations, train surrogate models on high-dimensional parameter spaces, and validate the framework against experimental data from collaborative partners. Expected outcomes include a scalable open-source solver capable of resolving FSI systems with 50% faster convergence than existing tools, as well as new insights into energy transfer mechanisms in cardiovascular flows and wind-turbine blade dynamics. The computational tools developed will be disseminated to applied mathematics and engineering communities, enabling broader research into nonlinear, multiscale systems. This work directly advances the algorithmic foundations of applied mathematics by bridging numerical analysis with data-driven modeling, while its applications support the design of more efficient medical devices and sustainable energy infrastructure. The requested resources—including GPU nodes for ML training and high-memory nodes for large-scale eigenvalue computations—are critical to achieving the project’s goals within the proposed timeline.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in applied mathematics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of predictive models for optimizing mineral extraction and processing in complex geological environments. A critical challenge in mining engineering lies in accurately simulating the dynamic interactions between engineered systems (e.g., drill-and-blast operations, comminution circuits) and heterogeneous ore bodies, which exhibit spatially variable mechanical, chemical, and mineralogical properties. Current models often oversimplify these interactions, leading to inefficiencies in resource recovery, energy use, and waste management. To address this, we propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating discrete element modeling (DEM) for granular flow in crushing/grinding processes, finite element analysis (FEA) for rock fracture mechanics, and machine learning (ML) to assimilate real-time sensor data from mining operations. These coupled simulations will resolve microscale particle interactions, mesoscale equipment performance, and macroscale ore body behavior, enabling holistic optimization of extraction parameters. The HPC environment is essential to manage the computational demands of 3D granular flow simulations with >10^8 particles, parallelized FEA for fracture propagation across kilometer-scale domains, and training of physics-informed neural networks on terabyte-scale datasets. Expected outcomes include validated models for predicting optimal blast fragmentation sizes, crusher/grinder configurations, and tailings stabilization strategies under variable ore grades. This work will directly inform sustainable practices by reducing energy consumption per ton of processed ore by an estimated 15–20% and minimizing environmental risks through predictive tailings management. The resulting open-source codebase will provide the mining engineering community with scalable tools to integrate HPC-driven simulations into operational decision-making frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of mineral extraction, processing and refining systems, including open pit and shaft mines, prospecting and site analysis equipment and instruments, environmental and safety systems, mine equipment and facilities, mineral processing and refining methods and systems, and logistics and communications systems.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of predictive models for early-stage neurodegenerative disease detection using multimodal oculomotor and pupillometric data. Neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease and Parkinson’s disease are frequently diagnosed only after irreversible neurological damage has occurred, highlighting a critical need for non-invasive, pre-symptomatic biomarkers. Recent studies suggest that subtle alterations in eye movement patterns, pupil dynamics, and gaze fixation—captured via high-resolution oculography—may correlate with incipient neuropathology. However, analyzing these complex, time-series datasets at scale requires computational workflows capable of integrating heterogeneous data types (e.g., infrared eye-tracking, cognitive task performance metrics, and structural MRI correlations) while accounting for individual variability. We propose a hybrid deep learning framework combining temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) and graph neural networks (GNNs) to model spatiotemporal dependencies in oculomotor behavior and link these to latent neuroanatomical changes. The HPC environment is essential for training these architectures on multi-terabyte datasets, optimizing hyperparameters via Bayesian methods, and conducting permutation-based significance testing across large cohorts. Expected outcomes include validated computational pipelines for identifying high-risk individuals based on oculomotor signatures and open-source tools for granular feature extraction from raw eye-tracking data. This interdisciplinary work bridges clinical neurology, cognitive neuroscience, and computational biomedicine, offering a novel pathway for scalable, low-cost population screening. Successful implementation could inform personalized intervention strategies and accelerate therapeutic trials by enriching participant cohorts with early-stage cases. The requested resources will directly support GPU-accelerated model training, large-scale data storage, and reproducible workflow orchestration, enabling translational insights at the intersection of neurotechnology and precision medicine.
cip_title: Medical Clinical Sciences/ Graduate Medical Studies, Other
cip_definition: Any program in medical clinical sciences or graduate medical studies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The development of efficient and scalable food processing technologies is critical to addressing global challenges in food safety, waste reduction, and nutritional quality. Current thermal processing methods, such as pasteurization and sterilization, rely on empirical models that inadequately predict heat transfer dynamics in heterogeneous food matrices, leading to energy inefficiencies and nutrient degradation. This project seeks to develop high-fidelity computational models to optimize thermal processing parameters for diverse food products, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to overcome limitations in existing simulation frameworks. The research will focus on multiphysics modeling of heat and mass transfer in complex food systems, integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with reaction kinetics to predict microbial inactivation, nutrient retention, and structural changes. HPC-enabled simulations will resolve spatial and temporal heterogeneities in food microstructure, processing equipment geometry, and variable boundary conditions—factors that are computationally prohibitive for conventional systems. Machine learning algorithms will be applied to surrogate models, accelerating parameter optimization for industrial-scale processes. Experimental validation will utilize pilot-scale thermal processing trials with instrumented food analogs, correlating simulation outputs with empirical data on microbial load, vitamin retention, and texture profiles. The outcomes will advance predictive capabilities for food processing design, enabling tailored protocols that minimize energy consumption while maximizing safety and quality. This work will directly support the development of sustainable food manufacturing practices, with implications for reducing spoilage, extending shelf life, and meeting regulatory standards.
