To overcome these limitations, this research proposes the development of adaptive algorithms leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate and model large-scale communication networks under variable conditions. The computational approach will integrate parallelized network simulations with machine learning techniques to predict traffic patterns, optimize content routing, and allocate computational resources dynamically. Key tasks include building a modular simulation environment using distributed computing frameworks (e.g., Apache Spark) to emulate multi-node networks, training deep reinforcement learning models on synthetic and real-world datasets to improve decision-making in resource allocation, and validating outcomes against industry-standard performance metrics. The project will also analyze the energy efficiency of proposed strategies to align with sustainability goals. Expected outcomes include actionable insights for reducing buffering times in streaming services, improving scalability for emerging 5G/6G applications, and informing infrastructure upgrades for telecommunications providers. By combining computational modeling with communication technology principles, this work aims to advance adaptive systems that enhance user experiences while minimizing operational costs—a critical step for next-generation media ecosystems.
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to function as workers and managers within communications industries. Includes instruction in business economics; basic management; principles of interpersonal and mediated communications; radio, television, and digital media production; and related aspects of technology and communications systems.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to predict slope instability and subsurface deformation in geologically complex terrains, a critical challenge in civil and geotechnical engineering. Current analytical methods struggle to integrate high-resolution geophysical data with dynamic hydrological and mechanical processes, limiting their predictive accuracy for infrastructure projects. To address this gap, we propose a multi-scale, coupled hydro-mechanical modeling framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The framework will integrate 3D finite element analysis with machine learning techniques to simulate fluid flow, stress redistribution, and fracture propagation in heterogeneous rock masses. Key computational challenges include resolving centimeter-scale discontinuities across kilometer-scale domains and managing nonlinear interactions between groundwater fluctuations and rock deformation. HPC resources will enable parallelized simulations using GPU-optimized solvers, reducing computation times from weeks to days while maintaining high spatial resolution. The project will validate models against field data from active landslide zones and underground construction sites, incorporating LiDAR, seismic tomography, and borehole sensor inputs. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible simulation toolkit for geotechnical risk assessment and novel guidelines for optimizing excavation and stabilization strategies in tectonically active regions. This work will directly support safer infrastructure development in landslide-prone areas and improve the sustainability of resource extraction projects by minimizing environmental disruption. The requested computing resources are essential to achieving the necessary scale and resolution for these simulations, which cannot be feasibly conducted on local clusters due to memory and processing constraints.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and geological principles to the analysis and evaluation of engineering problems, including the geological evaluation of construction sites, the analysis of geological forces acting on structures and systems, the analysis of potential natural resource recovery sites, and applied research on geological phenomena.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing complex, large-scale organizational decision-making under uncertainty in dynamic market environments. Traditional analytical models in business operations often fail to capture the interdependencies, nonlinear relationships, and real-time data streams inherent in modern supply chains, workforce management systems, and strategic resource allocation. To overcome these limitations, we propose developing a computational framework integrating agent-based modeling, stochastic optimization, and machine learning to simulate enterprise-scale decision scenarios. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to execute parallelized Monte Carlo simulations assessing millions of strategic permutations across multi-echelon supply networks, while concurrently training deep reinforcement learning agents on historical operational data. Key computational challenges include managing heterogeneous datasets spanning procurement logs, IoT sensor outputs, and market intelligence feeds; solving mixed-integer nonlinear programming problems with time-dependent constraints; and validating emergent system behaviors through sensitivity analyses. The HPC infrastructure will enable rapid iteration of hyperparameters in neural network architectures and distributed computation of risk-adjusted performance metrics across diverse economic scenarios. Expected outcomes include a novel decision-support toolkit capable of prescriptive recommendations for inventory allocation, capacity planning, and crisis response strategies under volatility. This work will advance computational management science by demonstrating scalable methods for simulating enterprise resilience, with direct applications to Fortune 500 partner firms facing global supply chain disruptions. The resource-intensive nature of simultaneously optimizing thousands of interacting variables across temporal and organizational hierarchies necessitates dedicated GPU-accelerated nodes and large-memory systems, which cannot be supported through conventional computing infrastructure.
cip_title: Business Administration, Management and Operations, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in business and administration, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of intergenerational cultural transmission and adaptation among Indigenous and diasporic communities across the Pacific Rim, with a focus on how digital and oral narratives reflect evolving identities in response to colonial and post-colonial migration. Existing scholarship lacks large-scale, comparative analyses of these narratives due to the fragmented nature of archival records, multilingual sources, and the technical challenges of processing non-linear oral histories. To address this gap, we propose a computational humanities approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multimodal datasets spanning digitized oral recordings, colonial administrative texts, community-generated digital media, and ethnographic field notes from the 19th century to the present. Natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will be developed to handle under-resourced Pacific languages, employing transformer-based models for cross-lingual semantic alignment and sentiment analysis. Temporal network analysis will map shifts in kinship terminologies and ritual references, while geospatial modeling will correlate narrative themes with migration pathways derived from archival voyage logs and contemporary diaspora surveys. The computational workflow requires parallelized processing of terabyte-scale audiovisual data and heterogeneous text corpora, necessitating GPU-accelerated nodes for deep learning tasks and high-memory nodes for network inference. Expected outcomes include 1) an open-access repository of annotated narratives with culturally sensitive metadata protocols, 2) quantitative frameworks for assessing cultural resilience in migration studies, and 3) visual analytics tools to support Indigenous communities in curating digitized heritage materials. By centering computational methods within Pacific epistemologies, this work aims to redefine area studies scholarship through scalable, community-engaged models of cultural analysis while preserving the nonlinearity and situated knowledge inherent to oral traditions.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of one or more of the peoples of Australasia and the Pacific Ocean, related island groups and bordering coastal regions, and including pre- and post-colonial migration patterns.

abstract: This research project investigates the interplay between cross-border cyber incidents and evolving norms of diplomatic communication in understudied geopolitical contexts. As cyber operations increasingly shape international interactions, existing frameworks struggle to characterize how state and non-state actors interpret and respond to digitally mediated provocations that fall below traditional thresholds of armed conflict. The study employs computational text analysis and agent-based modeling to examine patterns in diplomatic discourse, media narratives, and strategic decision-making across three contested regions where cyber operations have intensified but systematic data remains scarce. Using natural language processing techniques on multilingual corpora of official statements, leaked communications, and social media exchanges, we will identify semantic shifts in conflict-related terminology and correlate these with historical cyber incident timelines. Concurrently, agent-based models will simulate decision pathways under varying information conditions and normative constraints, incorporating empirical data from regional experts through participatory modeling workshops. The computational architecture requires high-performance resources to handle 1) large-scale multilingual text processing with custom transformer models trained on diplomatic lexicon, 2) parallelized Monte Carlo simulations testing thousands of normative evolution scenarios, and 3) integration of heterogeneous data streams through adaptive network graphs. Expected outcomes include a novel taxonomy of cyber-enabled signaling strategies, probabilistic models of normative tipping points in digital statecraft, and an open-source toolkit for tracking escalation dynamics in emergent cyber conflict zones. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational social science with security studies, offering methodological innovations for analyzing asymmetric digital diplomacy while providing actionable insights for conflict prevention mechanisms in technically complex, politically sensitive environments.
detailed_field: International relations and national security studies
cip_title: International Relations and National Security Studies, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in international relations and national security studies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in data-driven decision-making for social service delivery by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model complex, large-scale social systems. Social work interventions often operate within resource-constrained environments where optimizing service allocation and predicting community needs are paramount. Traditional analytical tools struggle to integrate multidimensional data—such as demographic trends, service utilization patterns, and real-time crisis indicators—while accounting for dynamic interactions between individuals, institutions, and policies. To overcome these limitations, this research proposes the development of an agent-based modeling (ABM) framework enhanced by machine learning (ML) techniques. The ABM will simulate population-level outcomes under varying intervention scenarios, incorporating anonymized administrative data from public agencies, nonprofit service providers, and community health surveys. HPC resources are essential to execute parallelized simulations at scale, enabling rapid iteration over thousands of parameter combinations to identify optimal resource distribution strategies. Additionally, natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will analyze unstructured caseworker notes and crisis hotline transcripts to detect emergent vulnerabilities and refine predictive models. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible computational toolkit for social service agencies to forecast demand, evaluate policy trade-offs, and prioritize interventions for high-risk populations. By quantifying the cascading effects of systemic inequities and programmatic changes, this work aims to advance equity-centered practices in public administration while establishing a methodological bridge between computational social science and applied social work. The project’s scalability—capable of adapting to diverse regional contexts—positions it as a template for evidence-based resource allocation in nonclinical social services nationwide.
cip_definition: Any program providing instruction in social work and related services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a next-generation decision-support framework for cyber-electronic warfare (CEW) operations by leveraging advanced computational modeling to simulate adversarial dynamics in contested digital environments. Modern military cyber operations face a critical challenge: existing threat models and defense protocols struggle to account for the rapidly evolving, AI-enhanced capabilities of adversarial actors, particularly in hybrid conflict scenarios where cyber, electronic, and informational attacks converge. Current tools often rely on static vulnerability assessments or historical attack patterns, leaving gaps in proactive adaptation to novel, multi-vector assaults. To address this, we propose a multi-scale simulation environment that integrates agent-based modeling, game-theoretic adversarial interaction frameworks, and machine learning-driven anomaly detection. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to execute parallelized simulations of large-scale network topologies, emulate adaptive adversarial tactics through deep reinforcement learning agents, and analyze real-time sensor data streams from distributed electronic warfare systems. The computational workflow will combine graph neural networks to model infrastructure interdependencies, Monte Carlo methods to assess cascading failure risks, and evolutionary algorithms to optimize defensive countermeasure sequences. Anticipated outcomes include a validated predictive model for identifying high-probability attack surfaces in tactical-edge networks, a library of simulated adversarial behavior profiles for training autonomous cyber defense systems, and a quantitative risk assessment toolkit for mission-critical infrastructure hardening. By enabling dynamic, scenario-driven analysis of emergent threats—such as AI-generated malware polymorphing or coordinated electromagnetic-spectrum/cyber-physical attacks—this research will directly inform doctrinal updates, cyber maneuver strategies, and resilient CEW architecture design for defense networks. The project’s computational demands stem from the need to process petabyte-scale network telemetry datasets, simulate 10,000+ node infrastructure models with <10ms latency constraints, and train ensemble ML models on adversarial interaction histories across classified and open-source threat intelligence repositories.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the technological and operation aspects of information warfare, including cyber attack and cyber defense. Includes instruction in computer and network security, cryptography, computer forensics, systems security engineering, software applications, threat and vulnerability assessment, wireless networks and satellite communications, tactical and strategic planning, legal and ethical issues, and cyber warfare systems development and acquisition.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable, high-performance computing (HPC) infrastructure to address challenges in processing and analyzing large-scale disease registry datasets, which are critical for advancing public health surveillance and precision medicine. Disease registries aggregate heterogeneous data—including demographic records, clinical histories, and treatment outcomes—across millions of individuals, but current systems struggle with computational bottlenecks in real-time analytics, integration of unstructured data (e.g., clinician notes), and predictive modeling of disease trajectories. The proposed research will leverage HPC resources to design parallelized algorithms for cleaning, harmonizing, and querying registry data at scale, with a focus on reducing latency in federated data environments. Machine learning models, including graph neural networks and transformer-based architectures, will be trained to identify underdiagnosed disease patterns, forecast regional outbreak risks, and automate quality assurance in coding and staging workflows. A key innovation involves optimizing natural language processing (NLP) pipelines to extract temporal features from unstructured text, enabling longitudinal analysis of comorbidities and treatment efficacy. Computational experiments will validate models against historical registry data spanning 10+ years from multiple institutions, assessing performance in scenarios with missing data and demographic biases. The outcomes will include open-source tools for distributed disease registry analytics, validated predictive frameworks for early intervention targeting, and benchmarks for ethical AI use in health data governance. By enabling faster, more accurate insights from registry data, this work will directly support public health agencies in resource allocation, policy design, and personalized care strategies, while advancing computational methods for equitable, privacy-preserving healthcare analytics. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing memory-intensive workflows, hyperparameter optimization at scale, and simulating population-level health outcomes under varying intervention scenarios.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to find, interpret, and record demographic and medical information on individuals for healthcare agencies and disease registries. Includes instruction in anatomy, data management, disease registry organization and operations, epidemiology, ethics, fundamentals of disease coding and staging, medical terminology, pathophysiology, pharmacology, physiology, quality management, and statistics.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize energy-efficient building designs and construction workflows through advanced simulations and data-driven modeling. The construction industry faces critical challenges in balancing structural integrity, material efficiency, and energy performance, particularly as sustainability standards become more rigorous. Current manual and siloed approaches to design iteration, thermal analysis, and resource allocation limit the ability to holistically evaluate trade-offs between cost, durability, and environmental impact. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to run multi-physics simulations integrating finite element analysis (FEA) for structural stress modeling, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for HVAC and thermal performance, and machine learning algorithms to identify Pareto-optimal material and design configurations. The project will utilize open-source tools like EnergyPlus and OpenFOAM, coupled with custom Python-based optimization pipelines, to model residential and commercial structures under diverse environmental and load conditions. Key objectives include automating the exploration of non-traditional materials (e.g., bio-composites, recycled aggregates) in digital twins, quantifying lifecycle energy savings, and generating region-specific construction guidelines to minimize embodied carbon. HPC resources are essential to parallelize thousands of design permutations, process LiDAR-based site data, and train neural networks on historical project performance metrics. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of optimized building templates, predictive models for construction waste reduction, and a decision-support toolkit for contractors to evaluate real-time trade-offs during planning. By bridging computational engineering with practical construction workflows, this work aims to advance data-informed practices in the trades, reduce reliance on trial-and-error methods, and accelerate the adoption of high-performance, low-carbon building systems.
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills in the building, inspecting, and maintaining of structures and related properties. May include instruction in masonry, carpentry, electrical and power transmission installation, building/construction finishing, management, inspection and other construction-related applications.

abstract: This project seeks to analyze the evolution of partisan polarization and legislative decision-making in Canadian federal politics through computational modeling of parliamentary speech, voting records, and electoral data. Despite extensive qualitative research on Canadian political institutions, quantitative gaps persist in understanding how intra-party cohesion, inter-regional representation, and ideological alignment shape legislative efficiency and policy outcomes. To address this, the project will employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process and analyze structured and unstructured datasets spanning 40 years of parliamentary debates (1980–2020), voting logs from the House of Commons, and constituency-level election results. Natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based models fine-tuned on Canadian political text, will classify speech content by policy domain, sentiment, and rhetorical strategy. These outputs will be integrated with voting cohesion metrics and demographic data using network analysis and multilevel regression models to identify patterns in party discipline, cross-bench collaboration, and regional representation. The computational demands of processing over 1.5 million speech transcripts, coupled with the need for parallelized model training and large-scale graph computations, necessitate HPC infrastructure. Expected outcomes include a novel framework for mapping ideological shifts within Canadian parties, quantifying the impact of regional interests on federal policymaking, and evaluating how institutional designs—such as electoral systems and committee structures—mediate partisan conflict. Results will contribute to comparative legislative studies and provide evidence-based insights for debates on parliamentary reform, democratic accountability, and the role of regionalism in national governance. All models and processed datasets will be made publicly available to support future research in Canadian political science.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of Canadian political institutions and behavior. Includes instruction in British and North American political theory, political parties and interest groups, provincial and local governments, Constitutional law, federalism and national institutions, executive and legislative politics, judicial politics, popular attitudes and media influences, political research methods, and applications to the study of specific issues and institutions.

abstract: Plant hydraulic systems are critical for maintaining water transport efficiency under environmental stress, yet the integration of structural adaptation, fluid dynamics, and mechanical feedback during drought remains poorly resolved. This project seeks to develop a multiscale computational model of plant vascular networks to predict how dynamic xylem embolism repair and tissue biomechanics interact to stabilize water transport in fluctuating arid conditions. Current models treat embolism formation as irreversible or oversimplify tissue-level hydraulic capacitance, limiting predictive power for species with active repair mechanisms. Using high-performance computing (HPC), we will parameterize a 3D lattice Boltzmann framework to simulate water transport in anatomically accurate xylem networks derived from micro-CT scans of drought-stressed woody plants, integrating real-time feedback between hydraulic resistance, osmotic adjustments, and cell wall mechanics. A parallelized multiscale solver will couple this microvascular model with whole-plant hydraulic architecture data to quantify emergent behaviors under stochastic rainfall regimes. Computational experiments will test hypotheses regarding the role of parenchyma-mediated refilling versus passive capillary recovery in maintaining hydraulic resilience. Sensitivity analyses will identify key anatomical and physiological traits conferring drought adaptation in arid-adapted species. The resulting framework will generate testable predictions for plant mortality thresholds under climate variability while providing a novel platform for simulating trait trade-offs in crop engineering. This work requires HPC resources to manage large parameter spaces, high-resolution fluid-structure interaction simulations, and ensemble modeling across ecological scenarios. Outcomes will advance mechanistic understanding of plant drought responses and inform breeding programs targeting hydraulic resilience, directly addressing food security challenges in water-limited ecosystems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of plant internal dynamics and systems, plant-environment interaction, and plant life cycles and processes. Includes instruction in cell and molecular biology; plant nutrition; plant respiration; plant growth, behavior, and reproduction; photosynthesis; plant systemics; and ecology.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in heterogeneous computing architectures through the development of adaptive resource allocation algorithms optimized for emerging edge computing and AI-driven workloads. As heterogeneous systems integrating CPUs, GPUs, FPGAs, and specialized accelerators become ubiquitous, traditional static allocation strategies fail to account for dynamic workload variability, leading to suboptimal energy efficiency and latency. To bridge this gap, we propose a computational framework combining real-time system telemetry with machine learning-driven optimization models to predict and allocate resources across hybrid hardware platforms. The research will employ distributed simulations of edge computing environments using parameterized workload generators and hardware performance models. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for scaling these simulations to realistic node counts (1,000+ devices) and for training deep reinforcement learning models on the resulting multi-terabyte telemetry datasets. Parallel computing frameworks, including MPI and CUDA, will be used to simulate concurrent device interactions, while PyTorch and TensorFlow will enable iterative model training. Expected outcomes include (1) open-source algorithms for dynamic resource partitioning in heterogeneous systems, (2) quantitative benchmarks comparing energy efficiency and throughput against static allocation baselines, and (3) a scalable simulation toolkit for edge computing environments. This work directly supports the Computer Engineering Technologies field by providing methodologies to optimize next-generation computing infrastructures for AI/ML, IoT, and real-time applications. The requested HPC allocation will enable large-scale validation of our approach, which would be computationally infeasible on local clusters due to memory constraints (>4 TB working datasets) and the need for simultaneous multi-node simulation. Results will be disseminated through academic publications and industry partnerships to advance both theoretical and applied research in adaptive computing systems.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in computer engineering technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address critical challenges in physics teacher education by developing advanced computational tools to model and optimize instructional strategies for complex physics concepts. A persistent issue in physics education is the difficulty students face in mastering abstract topics such as quantum mechanics, electromagnetism, and thermodynamics, which often leads to disengagement. Traditional teaching methods struggle to dynamically adapt to diverse student misconceptions and learning pathways. To bridge this gap, we propose a computational framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate classroom learning environments, analyze student interaction data, and generate evidence-based pedagogical recommendations. The research will employ agent-based modeling to replicate student cohorts, incorporating cognitive and behavioral variables derived from empirical studies. Machine learning algorithms will process historical performance data to identify patterns in misconception formation, while physics-based simulations (e.g., finite-difference time-domain solvers for electromagnetism) will generate adaptive visualizations tailored to address specific learning gaps. HPC resources are essential to handle the high-dimensional parameter space of instructional scenarios, real-time data processing from simulated classrooms, and the optimization of multi-variable teaching strategies. Expected outcomes include a suite of open-access computational tools that enable physics educators to prototype lesson plans, predict student responses, and refine interventions using simulated feedback. These tools will be integrated into teacher training modules, tested in partner high schools and undergraduate programs, and validated against learning outcome metrics. The project aims to advance physics teacher education by providing data-driven methods to personalize instruction, reduce preparation time for new educators, and improve conceptual retention across diverse student populations.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach physics programs at various educational levels.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the understanding of quantum many-body dynamics in ultracold molecular systems, a critical challenge in atomic and molecular physics. Current experimental advances in trapping and cooling diatomic molecules have opened pathways to probe quantum-state-resolved chemical reactions and long-range intermolecular interactions. However, theoretical models struggle to accurately predict collisional and reactive cross-sections due to the computational complexity of solving high-dimensional nuclear-electronic Schrödinger equations under strong coupling regimes. The proposed research will address this gap by developing scalable ab initio methods to simulate molecular collisions and photoassociation processes at microkelvin temperatures. Key computational approaches include time-dependent variational quantum wavepacket propagation on GPU-accelerated architectures and coupled-channel calculations incorporating non-adiabatic couplings and hyperfine interactions. The HPC implementation will optimize tensor network algorithms to reduce memory bottlenecks in handling large rotational-vibrational basis sets. Expected outcomes include predictive models for spin-forbidden reaction pathways in alkali-metal dimer systems and quantitative benchmarks for experimental studies of quantum interference in ultracold chemistry. These results will directly inform ongoing efforts to design molecular qubits and engineer controlled reactive platforms for quantum simulation. The computational framework developed will also enable systematic studies of magnetic dipole transitions in metastable molecular states, with implications for precision measurements of fundamental symmetry violations. By combining advanced numerical techniques with cutting-edge HPC capabilities, this project aims to bridge critical gaps between quantum molecular dynamics theory and emerging experimental capabilities in atomic-molecular physics.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the behavior of matter-energy phenomena at the level of atoms and molecules. Includes instruction in chemical physics, atomic forces and structure, molecular orbital theory, magnetic resonance, molecular bonding, phase equilibria, quantum theory of solids, and applications to the study of specific elements and higher compounds.

abstract: Integrative medicine seeks to optimize health outcomes by addressing the complex interplay of biological, psychological, social, and environmental factors influencing patient health. A critical challenge in advancing this field lies in analyzing large-scale, heterogeneous datasets—including clinical records, multi-omics profiles, lifestyle metrics, and patient-reported outcomes—to identify personalized therapeutic strategies while preserving the centrality of practitioner-patient relationships. This project proposes the development of a computational framework to model patient-specific health trajectories, predict responses to integrative interventions, and simulate practitioner decision-making processes in diverse clinical scenarios. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will integrate machine learning (e.g., ensemble models for treatment outcome prediction) with agent-based simulations of patient-practitioner interactions, incorporating dynamic feedback loops between biomedical data and relational factors. Multi-modal data from electronic health records (EHRs), genomic repositories, and prospective observational studies will be processed using distributed computing pipelines to enable real-time feature extraction and dimensionality reduction. Graph neural networks will map temporal relationships in patient histories, while natural language processing will analyze unstructured clinical notes for contextual insights into practitioner reasoning. The computational demands of training these models on terabyte-scale datasets, coupled with the need for high-throughput simulation of intervention scenarios, necessitate GPU-accelerated nodes and parallelized workflows. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive algorithms for optimizing combination therapies (e.g., pharmacologic and mind-body interventions), (2) quantitative frameworks to assess how relational dynamics influence treatment adherence and efficacy, and (3) open-source tools for simulating integrative care protocols under resource constraints. By bridging data-driven discovery with the humanistic tenets of integrative medicine, this work aims to advance evidence-based strategies for whole-person care while preserving the irreplaceable role of therapeutic relationships in clinical practice.
cip_definition: Research on how to practice medicine in a way that reaffirms the importance of the relationship between practitioner and patient; focuses on the whole person; is informed by evidence; and makes use of all appropriate therapeutic approaches, healthcare professionals, and disciplines to achieve optimal health and healing.

abstract: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is a critical intervention for conditions such as decompression sickness, non-healing wounds, and carbon monoxide poisoning. However, optimizing treatment protocols—including pressure levels, session duration, and oxygen concentration—remains challenging due to complex interactions between physiological responses and hyperbaric environments. This project seeks to develop computational models to simulate tissue oxygenation dynamics, microbubble formation/resolution, and systemic inflammatory responses under varying hyperbaric conditions. A key research problem is the lack of predictive frameworks that integrate real-time patient-specific data with multi-scale physiological processes to guide personalized HBOT regimens. To address this, we propose a hybrid computational approach combining computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for gas transport modeling in hyperbaric chambers, finite element analysis (FEA) for tissue-level oxygen diffusion, and agent-based modeling (ABM) for cellular responses to hyperoxia. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve these coupled models at clinically relevant spatiotemporal scales, particularly for simulating transient pressure changes during compression/decompression phases and their impact on microbubble kinetics. Machine learning techniques will be applied to clinical datasets (including electronic health records and chamber sensor data) to identify predictive biomarkers for treatment efficacy and adverse events. The expected outcomes include an open-source simulation platform for virtual HBOT protocol testing, data-driven dosing guidelines to minimize oxidative stress risks, and a decision support tool for optimizing chamber operation parameters. By elucidating the mechanistic links between hyperbaric exposures and physiological outcomes, this work aims to advance precision medicine in hyperbaric care while improving the safety and efficiency of clinical operations. The requested computing resources will enable large-scale parameter sweeps, sensitivity analyses, and validation against experimental data from collaborating hyperbaric facilities.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of physicians, to operate hyperbaric (recompression) chambers for the treatment of disease. Includes instruction in patient assessment and management, hyperbaric safety, physics of hyperbaric and hypobaric exposures, physiology, hyperbaric chamber operation, and air decompression procedures.

abstract: Cardiopulmonary diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and heart failure, remain leading causes of morbidity globally. Current diagnostic and therapeutic protocols often rely on static, isolated datasets, limiting the ability to model dynamic cardiopulmonary interactions or personalize interventions. This project seeks to address these gaps by developing a computational framework to integrate multi-modal clinical data—such as echocardiography, pulmonary function tests, blood gas analyses, and patient histories—into predictive models of cardiopulmonary function. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process large-scale datasets, simulate physiological interactions, and train machine learning algorithms for real-time clinical decision support. The primary research objectives are threefold: (1) to create patient-specific digital twins simulating cardiopulmonary responses to therapies, (2) to identify predictive biomarkers of acute decompensation using longitudinal data, and (3) to optimize ventilator and hemodynamic support protocols through in silico experimentation. Computational methods will include finite element modeling of cardiac and pulmonary mechanics, computational fluid dynamics for airway and vascular flow analysis, and ensemble machine learning algorithms to correlate heterogeneous clinical parameters. The HPC environment will enable parallel processing of high-resolution imaging data, reduce runtime for iterative model calibration, and support scalable data integration across institutional databases. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for early intervention in critical care scenarios, open-source tools for cardiopulmonary simulation, and protocols for personalized therapeutic titration. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this project aims to advance translational cardiopulmonary research, directly aligning with clinical training priorities in diagnostic accuracy, emergency response, and evidence-based patient management. Results will be disseminated through peer-reviewed platforms and integrated into educational modules for cardiopulmonary technologists, fostering innovation in both clinical practice and training.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of physicians and nurses, to perform both cardiovascular and pulmonary diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Includes instruction in cardiopulmonary pharmacology; anatomy and physiology of the heart, peripheral vascular system, and lungs; pulmonary and cardiovascular disease and dysfunction; peripheral vascular Doppler procedures; invasive and non-invasive cardiology; pulmonary function tests; blood gas analysis; echocardiograph procedures; bronchoscopy; patient management; patient history taking and record-keeping; applications to clinical research; and emergency procedures.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the emergent dynamics of informal communication networks within hybrid work environments and their impact on organizational resilience, using agent-based computational modeling. Traditional studies of organizational behavior often rely on static survey data or ethnographic methods, which struggle to capture the nonlinear, real-time interactions that shape adaptive behaviors during disruptions. The research problem centers on identifying how self-organizing communication patterns—driven by asymmetrical information access, varying risk perceptions, and hierarchical constraints—affect decision-making latency and error propagation in crisis scenarios. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will develop a scalable agent-based model simulating 10,000+ heterogeneous organizational actors with multi-layered network affiliations (professional, social, situational). The computational framework integrates behavioral parameters derived from empirical studies of technology-mediated collaboration, including temporal communication decay rates and context-switching thresholds. Machine learning techniques will be applied to pattern recognition in simulated crisis response outcomes, enabling the identification of critical network topology features that correlate with successful adaptation. Expected outcomes include 1) a novel computational taxonomy of informal network architectures that buffer against systemic failure, 2) quantitative evidence for optimal intervention points in dynamic organizational systems, and 3) open-source tools for simulating hybrid work policy impacts on collective intelligence. By bridging computational social science with complexity theory, this work aims to advance predictive capabilities in organizational behavior while providing actionable insights for designing adaptive governance structures in volatile operational environments. The requested resources are essential for handling the combinatorial complexity of multi-agent interactions and enabling parameter space exploration at sufficient scale to capture rare but high-impact emergence phenomena.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the behavior and motivations of individuals functioning in organized groups, and its application to business and industrial settings. Includes instruction in organization theory, industrial and organizational psychology, social psychology, sociology of organizations, reinforcement and incentive theory, employee relations strategies, organizational power and influence, organization stratification and hierarchy, leadership styles, and applications of operations research and other methodologies to organizational analysis.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in the computational analysis of Baltic languages, with a focus on Latvian, Lithuanian, and the extinct Curonian language. The research problem centers on the scarcity of digitized linguistic resources and the computational complexity of modeling morphologically rich, low-resource languages, which limits advancements in philological studies, historical linguistics, and applications such as machine translation. Current tools optimized for high-resource languages (e.g., English) perform poorly on Baltic languages due to their intricate inflectional systems, dialectal variations, and fragmented historical corpora. This project proposes the development of scalable computational pipelines to automate the analysis of Baltic texts across multiple historical periods and genres. Methods include training transformer-based language models on newly digitized corpora of Old Lithuanian manuscripts and Curonian substrate texts, employing parallelized algorithms for morphological segmentation, and applying phylogenetic modeling to trace diachronic sound shifts. HPC resources are essential for processing terabytes of digitized archival material, running large-scale comparative simulations of language evolution, and optimizing neural architectures for real-time dialect classification. Expected outcomes include (1) open-access digital lexicons and annotated corpora for understudied Baltic variants, (2) computational models quantifying the influence of Curonian on regional Latvian dialects, and (3) a framework for adapting NLP tools to morphologically complex languages. The results will advance scholarly understanding of Baltic language development, support preservation initiatives for endangered linguistic heritage, and enable practical applications in cross-lingual information retrieval for Baltic-speaking communities. By integrating computational linguistics with traditional philological expertise, this project bridges a critical gap in resources for Baltic studies while demonstrating methodologies transferable to other low-resource language families.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the languages of the Baltic peoples, including, but not limited to, the modern languages of Latvian and Lithuanian, and extinct languages such as Old Prussian and Curionian. Includes instruction in philology; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: The study addresses critical gaps in computational resources for Khmer language research, which currently lacks robust tools for large-scale textual analysis despite the language’s rich literary heritage and complex morphology. Existing digital corpora are limited in scope and fail to represent historical texts, regional dialects, and non-literary materials, hindering advancements in philological studies, lexicography, and comparative literature. This project proposes the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to process and analyze diverse Khmer textual sources, including palm-leaf manuscripts, printed literature, and modern digital publications. Computational methods will integrate adaptive optical character recognition (OCR) models for digitizing pre-modern scripts, deep learning architectures for semantic and syntactic annotation, and distributed computing techniques to map lexical and stylistic evolution across six centuries of Khmer writing. The OCR component will address unique challenges posed by Khmer’s conjunct consonants and vowel diacritics in historical orthography, employing convolutional neural networks trained on a newly curated dataset of annotated manuscript images. Parallelized text processing pipelines will extract phonological, morphological, and discourse features at scale, enabling quantitative analysis of linguistic change and intertextual relationships. Expected outcomes include the first multidialectal, diachronic Khmer corpus with machine-readable metadata, an open-source toolkit for Khmer NLP tasks, and empirical insights into the influence of Sanskrit-Pali borrowings on literary registers. By overcoming current computational barriers to handling Khmer’s linguistic complexity and fragmented textual record, this research will empower scholars to investigate previously intractable questions about language standardization, literary canon formation, and cultural identity. The infrastructure developed will serve as a template for computational humanities research on other low-resource languages with non-Latin scripts, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration between linguists, historians, and computer scientists.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Khmer language as spoken in Cambodia. Includes instruction in philology; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: Grapevine health and productivity are challenged by dynamic biotic and abiotic stressors, necessitating advanced predictive tools to optimize vineyard management. Current approaches lack the computational capacity to integrate multi-scale data, from genomic markers to regional climate patterns. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a predictive framework combining large-scale genomic analysis, machine learning, and multi-environment simulation models. By analyzing tera-scale genomic datasets from *Vitis vinifera* cultivars, alongside high-resolution environmental data, we aim to identify genetic loci associated with resilience to pathogens such as powdery mildew and abiotic stressors like drought. Concurrently, deep learning algorithms will be trained on historical pest incidence records and microclimate data to forecast disease outbreaks at subregional scales. HPC-enabled agent-based models will simulate vineyard management strategies under varying climate scenarios, evaluating their impact on yield, fruit quality, and input costs. The integration of these computational approaches will enable the development of precision viticulture tools that recommend cultivar selection, treatment timing, and resource allocation tailored to specific terroirs. Expected outcomes include open-source predictive models for grower decision support, novel insights into grapevine stress response mechanisms, and optimized protocols for sustainable winegrape production. This research directly addresses critical challenges in viticultural sustainability and economic viability, providing computational resources to bridge the gap between genomic potential and field-scale agricultural practices.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of scientific and agribusiness principles to the production of grapes, the making of wine, and the wine business. Includes instruction in grapes and wines of the world; grape production; winemaking technology; plant biology; chemistry; food science, safety, and packaging; soil science; pest management; and marketing and business management.

abstract: The perioperative environment presents complex challenges in patient safety, surgical efficiency, and postoperative outcomes, with variability in clinical decision-making and resource utilization contributing to preventable complications. This project seeks to develop predictive computational models to optimize perioperative workflows, intraoperative risk stratification, and postoperative recovery pathways using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. We will analyze multi-modal datasets, including electronic health records, intraoperative physiological monitoring streams, surgical team communication logs, and postoperative recovery metrics, to identify patterns associated with adverse events such as surgical site infections, hypothermia, and hemodynamic instability. Machine learning models (e.g., transformer-based architectures for temporal data, graph neural networks for team interaction analysis) will be trained on retrospective data from 15,000+ surgical cases to predict intraoperative risks in real time. Agent-based simulations will model OR workflows under varying staffing ratios, emergency scenarios, and equipment availability to stress-test resource allocation strategies. The computational demands of processing high-frequency physiological signals (1kHz sampling rates), natural language processing of surgical team communications, and parallel simulation of 10,000+ workflow permutations necessitate HPC infrastructure for GPU-accelerated training and large-memory nodes for in-memory data processing. Expected outcomes include (1) a risk prediction dashboard integrating real-time analytics for perioperative nurses, (2) evidence-based protocols for dynamic resource reallocation during surgical emergencies, and (3) synthetic data generation pipelines to enhance nursing education through simulated crisis scenarios. This work directly addresses critical gaps in surgical nursing practice by enabling data-driven decisions at the point of care while advancing computational methods for clinical team dynamics research. Results will be disseminated through open-source toolkits tailored for perioperative nursing informatics applications.
cip_title: Perioperative/ Operating Room and Surgical Nurse/ Nursing
cip_definition: A program that prepares registered nurses to provide care to patients before and during surgery, and provide tableside assistance to surgeons. Includes instruction in operating room safety and preparation, aseptic technique, anesthesia, patient preparation, surgical instruments and procedures, sterilization and disinfecting, surgical drugs and solutions, hemostasis, emergency procedures, and patient/family education.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in industrial process optimization by developing a computational framework to model complex interactions between human operators, equipment, and workflow dynamics in manufacturing environments. Current simulation tools struggle to integrate real-time human behavioral data with stochastic production variables at scale, limiting their utility for adaptive resource allocation. To overcome this, we propose a multi-agent simulation approach leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to parallelize discrete-event simulations across thousands of scenarios. The model will incorporate empirical data from motion capture systems and IoT-enabled machinery to represent operator ergonomic constraints, machine reliability patterns, and workflow interdependencies. Machine learning techniques will be applied to optimize task scheduling under dynamic constraints, including fatigue thresholds and maintenance events. By utilizing GPU-accelerated computing clusters, the team will reduce simulation wall times from weeks to hours, enabling rapid sensitivity analyses of layout designs and staffing policies. Expected outcomes include predictive metrics for bottleneck reduction in assembly systems, validated against case studies from automotive component manufacturing. The computational toolkit produced will empower industrial technologists to quantitatively assess trade-offs between automation investments, workforce training, and process redesigns. This work directly supports the program’s mission to bridge engineering principles with operational decision-making, with potential applications in lean manufacturing training modules and digital twin implementations for small-to-medium enterprises. Resource allocation will specifically enable scaling to plant-wide simulations with >10,000 interacting agents, a capability critical for advancing data-driven industrial management beyond current small-scale analytical models.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of industrial engineers and managers. Includes instruction in optimization theory, human factors, organizational behavior, industrial processes, industrial planning procedures, computer applications, and report and presentation preparation.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolving legal and regulatory frameworks governing artificial intelligence (AI) integration in clinical decision support systems (CDSS). As AI tools become pervasive in healthcare, their deployment raises novel legal questions related to liability, algorithmic bias, compliance with privacy statutes (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR), and the interpretation of "standard of care" in malpractice litigation. Traditional legal research methods struggle to systematically evaluate the vast, heterogeneous datasets required to model these interactions, including court opinions, regulatory guidance, insurance claims, and simulated patient outcomes. This project proposes a computational legal analytics framework combining natural language processing (NLP), agent-based modeling, and probabilistic graph networks to map how emerging case law and regulatory actions intersect with technical system performance. Legal texts and healthcare incident reports will be processed using transformer-based models fine-tuned for semantic extraction of legal predicates and causal reasoning patterns. Concurrently, stochastic simulations of CDSS-patient interactions will generate synthetic datasets to quantify how variations in algorithmic transparency and regulatory constraints correlate with litigation risk profiles. By integrating these pipelines on HPC infrastructure, the project aims to identify critical thresholds in system accuracy, explainability, and compliance that influence judicial outcomes and policy reform. Expected outcomes include a scalable toolkit for predicting legal exposure in AI-driven healthcare innovation and a policy optimization model to balance liability frameworks with equitable technology adoption. This interdisciplinary approach bridges computational law, health policy, and ethical AI, offering a paradigm to proactively address legal uncertainties in rapidly evolving medical technologies.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law, policies and regulations affecting the health care industry, health professions, health services and insurance industries, and patients.

abstract: This project investigates the resilience of decentralized information ecosystems under cascading disruptions caused by climate-driven environmental stressors. As global infrastructural and ecological systems become increasingly interdependent, understanding how localized failures propagate through information networks—particularly those reliant on hybrid human-machine decision-making—is critical. The research integrates computational social science, network theory, and environmental informatics to model multi-layer networks that couple physical sensor arrays, community reporting platforms, and institutional data-sharing protocols. Using agent-based modeling and temporal graph neural networks, we will simulate how distributed information systems adapt (or collapse) when facing compound events such as simultaneous power grid failures, communication outages, and population displacement. The computational approach requires high-performance resources to handle three core challenges: 1) scaling discrete-event simulations across heterogeneous network topologies with >10^6 dynamic nodes, 2) training attention-based models on sparse, multi-modal data streams (satellite imagery, crowdsourced text, IoT sensor logs), and 3) optimizing parameter space exploration for resilience metrics under uncertainty bounds derived from climate projection ensembles. Expected outcomes include a framework for quantifying information criticality thresholds in coupled human-technical systems, novel protocols for dynamic network rerouting in resource-constrained environments, and open-source tools enabling communities to stress-test local information infrastructures against climate scenarios. By bridging gaps between disaster informatics, participatory sensing, and adaptive systems theory, this work advances predictive capabilities for information continuity in crisis contexts while informing policy on equitable resource allocation for climate-resilient communication architectures.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory, organization, and process of information collection, transmission, and utilization in traditional and electronic forms. Includes instruction in information classification and organization; information storage and processing; transmission, transfer, and signaling; communications and networking; systems planning and design; human interfacing and use analysis; database development; information policy analysis; and related aspects of hardware, software, economics, social factors, and capacity.

abstract: Clinical laboratory medicine faces growing challenges in integrating heterogeneous, high-dimensional datasets—including genomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and clinical data—to improve diagnostic accuracy and enable personalized treatment strategies. Current analytical methods are often insufficient for handling the scale, complexity, and temporal dynamics of these datasets, particularly when modeling multi-omic interactions or optimizing laboratory workflows. This project proposes to address these limitations by developing scalable computational frameworks to analyze large-scale biomedical datasets using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. The research will focus on two interconnected aims: (1) creating machine learning models to identify predictive biomarkers for sepsis progression by integrating real-time clinical laboratory data with longitudinal multi-omics profiles, and (2) simulating laboratory testing workflows to optimize resource allocation and diagnostic turnaround times in high-volume hospital settings. Computational methods will include parallelized implementations of ensemble learning algorithms for feature selection, graph-based neural networks to model pathogen-host interaction networks, and discrete-event simulations of laboratory operational workflows. The HPC environment will enable rapid iteration of complex models, including Monte Carlo simulations for uncertainty quantification and hyperparameter optimization at scale. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for early sepsis detection, actionable recommendations for laboratory process improvements, and open-source tools for adaptive integration of multi-omics data in clinical research. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this work aims to bridge the gap between translational research and clinical practice, directly supporting precision medicine initiatives while advancing computational methodologies tailored to laboratory medicine’s unique data challenges. The resulting resources will be disseminated to the clinical research community to foster reproducible, data-driven innovation in diagnostic and therapeutic development.
cip_definition: Research focused on the principles and practices of applied medical research and related techniques, equipment, data systems, and research design. Includes instruction in the management of medical laboratories in research and healthcare facilities.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address unresolved questions in the evolution of polyphonic musical practices across Europe from the 12th to 16th centuries. While historical musicology has long studied this transformative period, traditional analytical methods struggle to systematically evaluate the stylistic relationships and transmission pathways among thousands of surviving manuscripts. The research problem centers on mapping large-scale patterns in melodic contour, harmonic progression, and rhythmic organization across digitized corpora of early vocal polyphony, including works by Pérotin, Machaut, and Josquin des Prez. To achieve this, we propose developing machine learning models trained on symbolic musical data (MIDI and MEI encodings) to detect latent structural features and stylistic affinities. Computational challenges include processing over 20,000 score excerpts with variable notation practices, requiring parallelized feature extraction and dimensionality reduction techniques. A second phase will employ agent-based modeling to simulate hypotheses about how theoretical treatises and institutional networks influenced compositional innovation. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing the heterogeneous datasets, training deep learning architectures on pitch/time-series data, and running iterative cultural transmission simulations. Expected outcomes include a quantitative framework for periodizing stylistic change, identification of previously unrecognized regional schools, and publicly accessible tools for computational music analysis. By bridging music theory, paleography, and digital humanities, this work aims to transform scholarly understanding of how musical complexity emerged through intercultural exchange while establishing replicable computational workflows for the broader field.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of the historical evolution of music as a social and intellectual phenomenon, the development of musical instruments and techniques, and the analysis and criticism of musical literature. Includes instruction in music history research methods, aesthetic analysis of musical compositions, history of musical writing and notation, the development of musical instruments, the development of music theory, and the study of specific periods, cultural traditions, styles, and themes.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven decision-support system to optimize credentialing workflows for medical staff in large healthcare systems, addressing inefficiencies in current manual and semi-automated processes. The credentialing of physicians, allied health professionals, and advanced practice providers involves complex validation of licenses, certifications, and training histories—a process prone to bottlenecks that delay clinical staffing and introduce compliance risks. While existing software platforms manage basic document tracking, they lack predictive capabilities to prioritize high-risk applications or detect subtle patterns indicative of fraudulent credentials. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we propose training graph neural networks (GNNs) on multi-modal datasets spanning historical credentialing records, malpractice litigation data, and international medical education registries. The computational approach will integrate natural language processing (NLP) for parsing unstructured training documentation, anomaly detection algorithms to flag discrepancies in career timelines, and federated learning techniques to preserve privacy across collaborating healthcare institutions. Initial benchmarks on a pilot dataset of 50,000 credentialing cases revealed a 22% error rate in manual verification processes, with an estimated 14% of delays attributable to undetected documentation inconsistencies. The HPC infrastructure will enable scaling to analyze over 5 million cross-referenced data points while maintaining sub-second latency for real-time decision support. Expected outcomes include a predictive risk stratification model to prioritize applications requiring manual audit and an open-source toolkit for adaptive credentialing policy simulation. This work bridges gaps between healthcare administration technology and computational trust analytics, with potential to reduce credentialing cycle times by 30-40% in large hospital networks while improving compliance with evolving accreditation standards.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform credentialing, privileging, personnel management, and accreditation compliance services for hospitals and other health care facilities and organizations. Includes instruction in medical staff organization and management, medical terminology, credentialing and re-credentialing, health care accreditation and regulatory standards, health care law, meeting and negotiation management, and office information systems management.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and optimize predictive models for identifying inefficiencies and systemic errors in medical insurance claim processing. Medical billing systems face persistent challenges, including claim denials, coding inaccuracies, and fraud, which impose financial burdens on healthcare providers and insurers while delaying patient care. Current methods for analyzing billing data rely on rule-based algorithms and manual audits, which struggle to scale with the growing volume and complexity of claims data. This research proposes a computational approach using machine learning (ML) to analyze historical claims datasets—spanning millions of records—to detect patterns predictive of denials, coding mismatches, or fraudulent activity. HPC resources will enable the training of ensemble models combining natural language processing (for clinical notes and policy documents) and graph neural networks (to map relationships between providers, patients, and payers). Simulations will also model the downstream effects of policy changes or reimbursement rate adjustments on billing workflows. The project will utilize anonymized claims data from partner healthcare organizations, processed in compliance with HIPAA standards via secure virtual environments. Anticipated outcomes include (1) a scalable framework for real-time claim risk scoring, (2) actionable insights into root causes of billing inefficiencies, and (3) synthetic datasets to simulate insurance policy impacts without exposing sensitive information. By reducing administrative overhead and denial rates, this work aims to enhance revenue cycle management for medical practices while informing equitable policy design. The computational demands of training large-scale ML models on heterogeneous data (structured claims, unstructured text, temporal sequences) necessitate parallelized GPU clusters and high-memory nodes, underscoring the need for HPC support.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to perform and manage the medical and health insurance operations in a medical office, health care facility, health maintenance organization, or insurance provider. Includes instruction in health and medical insurance processes; health insurance law, policy, and regulations; insurance records and paperwork administration; insurance office administration; health/medical insurance software applications; personnel supervision; business mathematics; billing and collection procedures; medical terminology; and communications skills.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the design of functional polymer fibers through multiscale computational modeling. The synthesis and processing of high-performance fibers—such as those with tailored mechanical strength, thermal stability, or dye affinity—remain limited by empirical approaches to optimizing polymer chain alignment, crystallinity, and interfacial interactions. A critical gap exists in understanding how dynamic processing conditions (e.g., extrusion rates, thermal gradients, solvent interactions) govern the mesoscale morphology of fibers, which directly impacts their macroscopic properties. To address this, we propose a computational framework integrating coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG-MD) and finite element modeling (FEM) to simulate polymer behavior across scales, from molecular rearrangements during fiber spinning to stress-strain responses under mechanical loading. The CG-MD simulations will parameterize polymer-polymer and polymer-solvent interactions using atomistic data, while FEM models will predict fiber deformation and failure modes. A key focus will be modeling the diffusion and binding of dye molecules within fibrillar networks to elucidate how surface chemistry and pore architecture influence colorfastness. These simulations demand significant parallel computing resources due to the large system sizes (1M+ particles) and microsecond-scale sampling required to capture phase transitions and solvent dynamics. The outcomes will establish processing-structure-property relationships for acrylate-based and bio-derived polymer fibers, guiding experimental workflows to minimize trial-and-error synthesis. By correlating simulated mesostructures with experimental fiber characterization data, this work will accelerate the development of sustainable, high-performance textiles and composite materials. Access to HPC infrastructure is essential to achieve the resolution and throughput necessary for actionable insights, enabling predictive design in fiber science beyond conventional analytical methods.
detailed_field: Materials chemistry and materials sciences nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the synthesis, structure and properties of polymers with an emphasis on fibers. Includes instruction in polymer chemistry and synthesis, fiber and polymer physics and physical chemistry, the production, processing and properties of fibrous materials, and chemistry of dyes, finishes, and their processes.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model and analyze the complex dynamics of intergenerational caregiving responsibilities within modern families, a critical yet understudied aspect of Work and Family Studies. The research addresses the growing challenge of balancing caregiving demands—such as childcare, eldercare, and support for family members with disabilities—with workforce participation, particularly in contexts shaped by shifting demographic trends, remote work practices, and uneven policy landscapes. Existing studies often rely on small-scale qualitative data or simplified quantitative surveys, limiting their ability to capture nonlinear interactions between socioeconomic variables, temporal constraints, and cultural norms. To overcome these limitations, the project employs agent-based modeling (ABM) and machine learning (ML) techniques to simulate household decision-making processes across diverse demographic scenarios. The ABM framework will integrate real-world datasets, including time-use surveys, employment statistics, and regional caregiving policy records, to parameterize agents representing family members with varying roles, resources, and constraints. Computational experiments will test how interventions such as flexible work policies, subsidized care programs, or community support networks affect caregiving equity and economic resilience at scale. ML algorithms will further identify latent patterns in longitudinal caregiving stress metrics derived from anonymized public health databases. By utilizing parallelized simulations across HPC nodes, the project aims to generate predictive insights into how families adapt to cascading caregiving demands over time, with particular attention to marginalized populations. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible computational toolkit for policymakers and educators to evaluate the systemic impacts of proposed family-support initiatives, as well as evidence-based frameworks for curriculum development in career pathways related to family resource management. This work bridges gaps between computational social science and applied family studies, advancing methodological innovation in a field traditionally underserved by high-performance computational approaches.
cip_definition: An introductory program that focuses on family and consumer science concepts and principles at the basic and vocational levels, and the various potential career paths open to interested students. Includes instruction in career, community, and family connections; family and family/consumer resources; human development; interpersonal relationships; nutrition and wellness; parenting; and career possibilities in various related areas.

abstract: This project seeks to advance pedagogy in Communication Arts and Literature education by investigating how large-scale computational analysis of multimodal classroom interactions can inform the design of equitable, adaptive teaching strategies. A critical challenge in teacher education lies in systematically evaluating how instructional techniques—such as discourse scaffolding, feedback methods, or culturally responsive dialogue—impact student engagement and competency development across diverse learning contexts. Traditional qualitative analyses of classroom data (e.g., discussion transcripts, writing portfolios, or speech recordings) are labor-intensive and limited in scale, hindering generalizable insights. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to process and analyze multimodal educational datasets from K-12 and postsecondary classrooms. Natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will be developed to quantify patterns in student-teacher interactions, including syntactic complexity in written feedback, pragmatic features of oral communication, and semantic shifts in literary analysis tasks. Deep learning models will further examine nonverbal cues in video-recorded teaching simulations to correlate pedagogical gestures with learner outcomes. By parallelizing these workflows across GPU nodes, we aim to process over 10,000 hours of classroom data from statewide partnerships, enabling longitudinal comparisons of instructional efficacy. Outcomes will include (1) evidence-based frameworks for optimizing communication pedagogy across literacy, public speaking, and digital media domains; (2) open-source tools to help educators visualize interaction patterns and personalize instruction; and (3) scalable benchmarks for assessing equitable participation in discourse-heavy disciplines. This computational approach directly supports teacher candidates in refining practice through data-driven reflection, while advancing interdisciplinary innovation at the intersection of educational linguistics and computational social science.
cip_title: Communication Arts and Literature Teacher Education
cip_definition: A program of study that prepares individuals to teach oral expression, literature, and writing to students at various education levels. Includes instruction in interpersonal communication, intercultural communication, language learning, listening instructional techniques, public speaking, reading instructional techniques, writing instructional techniques, and practical teaching experience.

abstract: The increasing complexity of drug discovery and development necessitates advanced computational tools to address challenges in pharmacokinetics, drug-target interactions, and formulation optimization. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to accelerate the design of novel small-molecule therapeutics with enhanced efficacy and reduced off-target effects. A central focus is the development of multi-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to model drug binding kinetics across diverse biological targets, including membrane-bound receptors and intracellular enzymes. These simulations will integrate structural data from cryo-EM and X-ray crystallography with machine learning-driven pharmacophore models to predict binding affinities and residence times under physiological conditions. Concurrently, we will employ quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations to analyze enzymatic degradation pathways of drug candidates in cytochrome P450 systems, addressing critical stability challenges in oral dosage forms.
