The project aims to address the critical gap in systematic, data-driven analysis of how emergent DeFi architectures interact with existing legal doctrines, focusing on case law, regulatory enforcement patterns, and transactional data spanning multiple jurisdictions. Computational methods will include large-scale natural language processing (NLP) of judicial opinions, regulatory filings, and smart contract codebases to identify latent legal risk factors, coupled with agent-based modeling to simulate the systemic impacts of proposed regulatory interventions on decentralized networks. Graph analytics will map cross-jurisdictional regulatory arbitrage pathways, while cryptographic techniques will anonymize sensitive transactional datasets for ethical analysis. The HPC environment is essential for processing multi-terabyte legal corpora, training domain-specific large language models (LLMs) to detect regulatory signal in unstructured text, and running parallelized simulations of market behaviors under varying legal constraints. Expected outcomes include a predictive framework for assessing compliance exposure in DeFi projects, quantitative metrics for evaluating regulatory fragmentation across jurisdictions, and open-source tools for automated audit trail reconstruction in blockchain transactions. By integrating computational social science methodologies with doctrinal legal analysis, this interdisciplinary project aims to establish new paradigms for proactive regulatory design in algorithmically governed financial systems while advancing methodological innovation at the intersection of legal scholarship and high-performance computing.
cip_title: Banking, Corporate, Finance, and Securities Law
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of the law and process related to the regulation of businesses and the financial services industry. Includes instruction in corporate law, antitrust law, securities law and regulation, negotiation, incorporation, partnerships, trusts, and related topics

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to optimize the design and reliability of next-generation electrical power transmission systems, with a focus on addressing challenges posed by increasing energy demand and renewable energy integration. Current installation practices and grid management strategies often rely on static, simplified models that inadequately capture dynamic load behaviors, transient fault conditions, or the stochastic nature of distributed renewable energy sources. This limitation hinders the deployment of resilient, efficient infrastructure capable of supporting modern energy transitions. To bridge this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework integrating multi-physics simulations, machine learning, and real-time data assimilation. Large-scale finite element analysis (FEA) will model electromagnetic and thermal interactions in transmission lines under variable environmental and operational conditions, while graph-based network simulations will assess cascading failure risks in complex grid topologies. Machine learning algorithms, trained on historical grid performance data and synthetic scenarios generated via HPC, will predict fault propagation patterns and optimize maintenance scheduling. The computational demands of these tasks—particularly the parallel processing of terabyte-scale datasets and the execution of millions of transient simulation instances—necessitate access to HPC resources with GPU-accelerated nodes and high-memory capacity. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for identifying vulnerability hotspots in existing infrastructure, adaptive control protocols for mitigating voltage instability, and design guidelines for high-efficiency transmission installations compatible with hybrid renewable energy systems. By leveraging HPC to resolve previously intractable multi-scale interactions, this work aims to provide actionable insights for utility operators and installation professionals, ultimately enhancing grid resilience and reducing energy losses in rapidly evolving power networks.
cip_title: Electrical and Power Transmission Installers, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in electrical and power transmission installation, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a digital humanities study focused on mapping the evolution of multilingual textual production across the Iberian Peninsula from the medieval period to the early modern era. The research problem centers on understanding how linguistic diversity—particularly the coexistence and interaction of Castilian, Catalan, Galician-Portuguese, Arabic, and Hebrew—shaped cultural identity and cross-regional communication in Iberia. Traditional archival methods struggle to analyze the scale and complexity of surviving manuscripts, printed texts, and ephemera, necessitating computational approaches. The project will employ natural language processing (NLP) techniques to analyze syntactic patterns, lexical borrowing, and script adaptation in a corpus of digitized texts, supplemented by network analysis to trace the circulation of multilingual documents across geographic and temporal boundaries. Computational workflows will be designed to handle non-Latin scripts, fragmentary sources, and orthographic variability inherent to premodern Iberian materials. HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based models on historical language variants and running large-scale simulations of textual dissemination pathways. Expected outcomes include a public database of annotated texts, visualizations of linguistic contact zones, and quantitative frameworks for assessing the cultural impact of translation practices during periods of interreligious exchange, such as the Toledo School of Translators. By integrating computational rigor with humanistic inquiry, this work aims to redefine scholarly understanding of Iberia’s pluralistic heritage while developing open-source tools adaptable to other multilingual contexts. The project aligns with the program’s mission to interrogate the intersections of culture, identity, and historical memory in the Iberian world, offering methodological innovations for digital scholarship in area studies.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of the peoples of the Iberian Peninsula and related island groups and border regions from earliest times to the present, with particular emphasis on the development of Spain and Portugal but including other historical and current cultures.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance genomic and systems-level investigations into plant stress adaptation mechanisms critical for crop resilience. Climate variability and emerging pathogens increasingly threaten global food security, yet the molecular networks governing plant responses to combined abiotic and biotic stressors remain poorly resolved. Traditional experimental approaches struggle to disentangle the nonlinear interactions between genetic, metabolic, and environmental variables underlying these complex phenotypes. We propose a computational framework integrating multi-omics datasets—including whole-genome resequencing, time-series transcriptomics, and targeted metabolomics—from stress-treated cultivars of Solanum lycopersicum (tomato) and Triticum aestivum (wheat). Machine learning models will identify predictive signatures of stress tolerance by analyzing terabyte-scale data from controlled-environment experiments and field trials. Concurrently, molecular dynamics simulations will characterize structural changes in key stress-responsive proteins under varying thermodynamic conditions. The scale of these analyses necessitates HPC capabilities for parallelized genome-wide association studies (GWAS), phylogenetic inference of gene family expansions, and ensemble modeling of metabolic pathways. Anticipated outcomes include: (1) predictive models linking genetic variants to stress-resilience traits, (2) candidate regulatory hubs for precision breeding, and (3) open-access computational workflows optimized for plant systems biology. By elucidating conserved adaptation strategies across divergent crops, this work will accelerate the development of climate-resilient varieties while establishing scalable analytical pipelines for the plant science community. The requested resources will enable processing of ~500 TB of genomic data and >1 million CPU-hours for iterative model training and molecular simulations, overcoming current bottlenecks in local computing infrastructure.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: Any instructional program in plant sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to advance precision and efficiency in Computer Numerically Controlled (CNC) machining processes through the development of high-fidelity computational models to optimize toolpath planning, material removal dynamics, and machine-tool interactions. Despite advancements in CAD/CAM systems, modern CNC workflows remain constrained by suboptimal toolpath strategies that lead to excessive machining time, tool wear, and energy consumption, particularly for complex geometries in high-performance alloys. Current industry-standard software relies on heuristic algorithms that do not fully account for real-time thermal-mechanical stresses or material-specific cutting dynamics. To address this gap, we propose a multi-scale simulation framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to model machining processes at unprecedented resolution. Finite element analysis (FEA) will be coupled with machine learning to predict tool deflection, heat generation, and surface finish outcomes across variable spindle speeds, feed rates, and cutting depths. GPU-accelerated simulations will analyze chip formation mechanics in titanium and Inconel alloys, while graph-based optimization algorithms will iteratively refine toolpaths to minimize non-productive movements. The computational workflow integrates open-source CNC kernel systems with custom numerical solvers to enable direct translation of simulation results to G-code adjustments. By harnessing parallel computing to evaluate millions of parameter combinations, this research aims to establish predictive models that reduce machining time by 15-25% and extend tool life by 30-40% compared to conventional methods. Outcomes will be validated through physical experiments on 5-axis CNC platforms, with resulting datasets informing both industrial best practices and educational modules for CNC operator training. The requested HPC resources are critical for overcoming current limitations in single-node computation, enabling parametric studies at process timescales inaccessible to local workstations. This work bridges the gap between theoretical machining mechanics and practical CNC operations, offering a template for data-driven manufacturing optimization applicable to aerospace, medical device production, and other high-precision industries.
cip_title: Computer Numerically Controlled (CNC) Machinist Technology/ CNC Machinist
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to operate computer numerically controlled (CNC) machine tools, such as lathes, mills, precision measuring tools, and related attachments and accessories, to perform machining functions, such as cutting, drilling, shaping, and finishing products and component parts. Includes instruction in CNC terminology, setup, programming, operations, and troubleshooting; blueprint reading; machining; lathe and mill operations; technical mathematics; computer literacy; CAD/CAM systems; shop and safety practices; equipment capabilities; and regulations and laws.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the modeling of infectious disease transmission dynamics and intervention efficacy in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with a focus on integrating sociobehavioral, environmental, and health systems data. A critical challenge in global health is predicting how disease spread—particularly for pathogens like malaria, cholera, and measles—interacts with factors such as vaccine hesitancy, climate variability, and fragmented health infrastructure. Existing models often oversimplify these interdependencies, limiting their utility for real-world policymaking. To address this, we propose developing an agent-based modeling (ABM) framework that incorporates high-resolution demographic, geospatial, and behavioral datasets from LMIC settings. The ABM will simulate disease transmission under varying scenarios, including vaccination campaigns, nutrition supplementation programs, and emergency responses to climate shocks. Computational demands arise from scaling the model to regional populations (10⁶–10⁷ agents), integrating real-time climate and mobility data streams, and conducting sensitivity analyses across thousands of parameter combinations. Machine learning components will further optimize resource allocation strategies by identifying high-risk subpopulations and forecasting outbreak trajectories. Expected outcomes include actionable insights into cost-effective intervention designs for maternal and child health initiatives, crisis-prone regions, and settings with overlapping infectious disease burdens. By quantifying trade-offs between equity, scalability, and sustainability in LMIC health systems, this work will directly inform international health policy agendas. The requested HPC resources are essential to overcome memory and processing bottlenecks inherent in granular, multi-scale simulations, enabling rapid iteration for stakeholder-driven scenarios. Results will be disseminated through open-access modeling tools and partnerships with NGOs and ministries of health, strengthening capacity for data-driven decision-making in resource-constrained contexts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of public health specializations, the social and behavioral sciences, and policy and communications methods to the study of health problems in low- and middle-income countries and regions, and prepares individuals to function as professional international health specialists. Includes instruction in health education and promotion, research design and evaluation, infectious disease epidemiology, international health policy and management, public nutrition and food security, information systems, program evaluation, medical anthropology, international communication, behavioral sciences, maternal and child health, demography and population policy, and health care finance and economics.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of identity formation and resistance within digital spaces used by marginalized cultural and gender groups, with a focus on multilingual, non-Western online communities. Despite growing scholarship on digital activism, there remains a critical gap in large-scale, intersectional analyses of how marginalized groups negotiate systemic inequities and co-create counter-narratives across linguistic and cultural boundaries. The research will employ computational text analysis and network science methods to process terabytes of social media data, including non-Latin script texts from platforms popular in Global South contexts. Key computational challenges include implementing transformer-based language models fine-tuned for low-resource languages, conducting multilevel network analysis of cross-community solidarity patterns, and running agent-based simulations of discourse diffusion under different moderation policies. These tasks require high-performance computing resources due to the scale of data (estimated 10^7 posts across 15 languages), need for parallel processing of multimodal content, and complexity of simulating intersectional identity interactions in evolving digital ecosystems. Expected outcomes include 1) new computational frameworks for analyzing power asymmetries in multilingual digital spaces, 2) identification of cross-cultural patterns in community-led resistance strategies, and 3) open-source tools for ethically monitoring platform governance impacts on marginalized users. By leveraging GPU-accelerated natural language processing and distributed computing for large graph analyses, this work aims to advance both computational social science methodologies and substantive theories of digital cultural resilience. The resource request supports critical infrastructure for handling sensitive data through secure, on-premise clusters while maintaining community partnership protocols essential for decolonial computing approaches in cultural studies.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies

cip_title: Ethnic, Cultural Minority, Gender, and Group Studies, Other

abstract: This project seeks to address the growing complexity of modern electrical power transmission systems, which face challenges such as aging infrastructure, increasing renewable energy integration, and dynamic load demands. Traditional methods for designing and validating electrical installations often rely on static models or simplified simulations, limiting their ability to predict cascading failures, optimize grid resilience, or evaluate the long-term impacts of distributed energy resources. To overcome these limitations, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a scalable, multiphysics simulation framework tailored for power transmission networks. The computational approach integrates finite element analysis (FEA) for thermal and mechanical stress modeling in transmission lines, agent-based simulations for fault propagation under varying environmental conditions, and machine learning algorithms to optimize real-time load balancing. By coupling these methods, the framework will simulate interactions between physical components (e.g., transformers, insulators) and grid-wide operational dynamics at unprecedented spatial and temporal resolutions. Key objectives include identifying failure-prone configurations in high-renewable penetration scenarios, validating code-compliant installation practices under extreme weather patterns, and generating adaptive maintenance schedules to minimize downtime. The HPC environment is critical for handling the computational intensity of modeling large-scale networks with millions of nodes, as well as for training neural networks on historical grid performance data. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for risk assessment in power transmission design, data-driven recommendations for updating installation standards, and a publicly accessible database of simulated failure modes correlated with National Electrical Code (NEC) compliance metrics. This work will directly support vocational training programs by providing empirically validated case studies and enhancing the precision of safety protocols taught in electrical installation curricula.
cip_title: Electrical and Power Transmission Installation/ Installer, General
cip_definition: A program that generally prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to install indoor and outdoor residential, commercial, and industrial electrical systems, and associated power transmission lines. Includes instruction in electricity, safety procedures, wiring, insulation and grounding, schematic blueprint interpretation, equipment operation and maintenance, and applicable codes and standards.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of correlated electron dynamics in molecular systems under intense ultrafast laser fields, a fundamental challenge in atomic and molecular physics. Strong-field ionization, recollision processes, and subsequent multielectron interactions govern phenomena such as high-harmonic generation and laser-induced electron diffraction, yet the quantum many-body nature of these processes resists analytical treatment and demands large-scale numerical modeling. Current limitations in simulating molecular systems with more than three atoms arise from the exponential scaling of exact quantum methods and the inadequate treatment of correlated electronic motion in approximate approaches. We propose to develop hybrid time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) coupled with machine-learned exchange-correlation potentials to address these challenges, enabling simulations of molecules with 5-10 atoms at experimental field intensities (10¹³–10¹⁴ W/cm²). The computational approach combines real-space grid propagation of electronic wavefunctions with tensor network representations of multi-configurational states, optimized for GPU-accelerated architectures. Key objectives include modeling non-adiabatic electron-nuclear coupling in polyatomic molecules during sub-femtosecond laser pulses and characterizing the role of d-orbital participation in transition metal complexes’ strong-field responses. The requested high-performance computing resources will support 1) wavefunction propagation on 3D grids with <0.1 Å resolution across 50+ electronic states, 2) Monte Carlo sampling of initial vibrational/rotational states, and 3) time-dependent electronic current calculations for predicting experimental observables. Expected outcomes include predictive models of attosecond charge migration pathways in biologically relevant molecules and quantitative benchmarks for ultrafast electron diffraction imaging techniques. This work will establish computational protocols for strong-field molecular physics that bridge quantum dynamics across multiple timescales (femtoseconds to attoseconds), with potential impacts on coherent control strategies and the interpretation of emerging ultrafast X-ray probe experiments.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the behavior of matter-energy phenomena at the level of atoms and molecules. Includes instruction in chemical physics, atomic forces and structure, molecular orbital theory, magnetic resonance, molecular bonding, phase equilibria, quantum theory of solids, and applications to the study of specific elements and higher compounds.

abstract: This project seeks to enhance drama and dance pedagogy by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze complex movement and instructional dynamics in teacher-student interactions. Current methods for evaluating teaching effectiveness in performing arts education rely heavily on subjective observation, limiting the scalability and granularity of feedback. To address this, we propose a computational approach integrating motion-capture data, machine learning (ML), and agent-based modeling to quantitatively assess how instructional strategies influence student engagement and skill development. Motion-capture systems will record classroom interactions across diverse dance and drama scenarios, generating high-dimensional datasets of spatial, temporal, and kinematic variables. These datasets will be processed using ML algorithms to identify patterns in teacher gestures, vocal modulation, and spatial positioning that correlate with student performance metrics, such as improvisation quality or technical precision. Concurrently, agent-based models will simulate virtual classroom environments to test hypothetical teaching strategies under varied demographic and resource conditions. HPC resources are critical for handling the computational demands of training deep neural networks on multimodal data (e.g., video, audio, biomechanical signals) and running large-scale simulations with dynamic student avatars. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models linking specific pedagogical techniques to student outcomes, (2) a framework for real-time feedback tools to support teacher training, and (3) open-source simulation templates for drama and dance educators. By bridging computational analysis with performing arts pedagogy, this work aims to establish evidence-based practices for fostering creativity and technical mastery in K–12 and higher education settings, while demonstrating the transformative potential of HPC in arts-focused teacher preparation.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach drama and/or dance programs at various educational levels.

abstract: Chronic liver diseases, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), are driven by complex interactions between genetic, metabolic, and microenvironmental factors. Current clinical paradigms lack robust tools to predict disease trajectories or optimize therapies for heterogeneous patient populations. This project seeks to address these gaps by developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to integrate multi-modal clinical, imaging, and multi-omics data. We will employ machine learning models to identify molecular signatures of disease progression from whole-genome sequencing, single-cell RNA-seq, and proteomic datasets derived from longitudinal hepatology cohorts. Agent-based models will simulate liver tissue dynamics, incorporating patient-specific parameters such as immune cell infiltration, fibrotic remodeling, and metabolic stress. These simulations will be coupled with pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models to predict therapeutic responses to existing and novel drug candidates. The scale of data processing—terabytes of imaging and sequencing data—and the computational intensity of simulating millions of interacting cellular agents across diverse virtual patient cohorts necessitate HPC resources for parallelized workflows, GPU-accelerated model training, and large-scale parameter sweeps. Expected outcomes include predictive algorithms for early detection of cirrhosis-to-carcinoma transition, validated against multicenter clinical datasets, and a computational platform for in silico testing of combination therapies. This work will provide clinically actionable tools for risk stratification and personalized treatment, directly addressing the urgent need for precision medicine approaches in hepatology. By elucidating mechanisms of treatment resistance and disease recurrence, the project aims to reduce trial-and-error prescribing and improve survival rates in advanced liver disease, with broader implications for computational methods in organ-specific pathophysiology research.
cip_definition: Research focused on Hepatology

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a public history initiative focused on reconstructing and analyzing historical urban landscapes through large-scale geospatial and archival data integration. The research addresses the challenge of synthesizing fragmented historical records—including municipal maps, census data, property ledgers, and photographic archives—to model urban development patterns and their socio-economic impacts in early 20th-century American cities. Traditional methods of manual data aggregation and analysis are insufficient for processing the scale and complexity of these heterogeneous datasets, which span multiple decades and jurisdictions. To overcome these limitations, the project proposes a computational workflow combining geospatial machine learning, optical character recognition (OCR) for digitized documents, and network analysis to map relationships between land use, demographic shifts, and policy decisions. HPC resources are critical for training convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to classify and georeference historical maps, as well as for running parallelized simulations of urban growth under varying policy scenarios. Expected outcomes include an open-access digital repository of annotated historical datasets, interactive visualizations of urban change, and a framework for evaluating the long-term effects of public policies on community displacement and infrastructure development. By integrating computational methods with historical inquiry, this work aims to provide actionable insights for policymakers and preservationists addressing contemporary urban equity issues while demonstrating the transformative potential of HPC in applied historical research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of history and administrative skills to the recording of public events and the management of related historical resources. Includes instruction in historical research methods, the planning and administration of public history projects, and applications to specific problems in public organizations, government agencies, foundations, and other facilities.

abstract: The increasing complexity of healthcare data, including electronic health records (EHRs), genomic datasets, and real-time clinical monitoring streams, presents a critical challenge in deriving actionable insights for patient care and system efficiency. Traditional analytical tools are often inadequate for processing these multi-modal, high-dimensional datasets, limiting the ability to predict patient outcomes, optimize treatment protocols, or allocate resources effectively. This project seeks to address these gaps by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop scalable computational models that integrate heterogeneous health data, enabling precision health strategies and evidence-based clinical decision-making. The research will focus on two interconnected aims: (1) creating machine learning frameworks to predict patient-specific risks for adverse outcomes (e.g., hospital readmissions, treatment complications) by synthesizing EHRs, imaging data, and genomic profiles, and (2) simulating large-scale healthcare delivery networks to identify bottlenecks and test intervention strategies for resource optimization. Computational methods will include deep neural networks for feature extraction from unstructured clinical notes, parallelized Monte Carlo simulations for probabilistic risk modeling, and graph-based algorithms to map care pathways across populations. HPC capabilities are essential for training models on terabyte-scale datasets, conducting millions of parameter iterations in simulated environments, and ensuring real-time processing of streaming ICU sensor data. Expected outcomes include open-source predictive tools for clinicians, validated models for personalized intervention timing, and policy-relevant insights into capacity planning for allied health services. By advancing the integration of computational science into health services research, this project aims to establish a replicable framework for data-driven healthcare optimization, directly supporting the program’s mission to bridge foundational health sciences with translational applications. The requested resources will enable processing efficiencies unattainable with local computing infrastructure, reducing model training times from weeks to days and supporting concurrent analyses across diverse patient cohorts.
cip_title: Health Services/ Allied Health/ Health Sciences, General
cip_definition: A general, introductory, undifferentiated, or joint program in health services occupations that prepares individuals for either entry into specialized training programs or for a variety of concentrations in the allied health area. Includes instruction in the basic sciences, research and clinical procedures, and aspects of the subject matter related to various health occupations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational workflows to optimize the design and analysis of civil infrastructure systems using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Civil drafting and engineering workflows increasingly rely on high-fidelity simulations to address complex challenges such as geological variability, dynamic load distributions, and environmental constraints. However, traditional CAD/CADD tools often lack the scalability to process large-scale datasets or perform real-time simulations of multi-physics systems, particularly for infrastructure projects in seismically active or environmentally sensitive regions. To address this gap, we propose a hybrid computational approach combining finite element analysis (FEA), machine learning (ML)-driven design optimization, and parametric modeling to enhance the precision and efficiency of civil engineering simulations. The project will leverage HPC resources to parallelize finite element meshing for geological stability assessments, automate topology optimization of structural components, and simulate fluid-structure interactions in drainage and flood mitigation systems. A key innovation involves integrating AI-assisted generative design algorithms with CADD workflows to iteratively refine blueprints under multi-objective constraints (e.g., material costs, carbon footprint, and seismic resilience). By deploying containerized computational environments on HPC clusters, we aim to reduce simulation runtime for large-scale urban planning scenarios by 60–75% compared to current workstation-based methods. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for GPU-accelerated civil infrastructure simulations, validated against physical scale models and field data from ongoing highway and wastewater management projects. This work will directly support curriculum development in computational civil engineering, providing students with hands-on experience in HPC-aided design while advancing industry adoption of resource-efficient, data-driven drafting methodologies. The resource allocation will enable critical benchmarks of distributed memory architectures for processing LiDAR-derived terrain models and automating compliance checks against evolving building codes.
cip_title: Civil Drafting and Civil Engineering CAD/ CADD
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to develop working drawing and electronic simulations in support of civil engineers, geological engineers, and related professionals. Includes instruction in basic civil engineering principles, geological and seismographic mapping, machine drafting, computer-aided drafting (CAD), pipe drafting, survey interpretation, and blueprint reading.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance computational methodologies in interior design, focusing on optimizing spatial planning, environmental systems integration, and material performance in complex architectural environments. Current design workflows rely on static simulations and simplified approximations of lighting, acoustics, and thermal dynamics, limiting the accuracy of predictions for occupant comfort and sustainability outcomes. The research problem centers on developing dynamic, multi-physics simulations that integrate real-world sensor data, parametric design variables, and machine learning models to iteratively refine design solutions under diverse operational conditions. Key computational approaches include finite element analysis (FEA) for structural-acoustic coupling, ray-tracing algorithms enhanced by neural networks for real-time lighting optimization, and agent-based modeling to simulate human interaction with adaptive interiors. These methods require parallel processing capabilities to manage large-scale datasets, including 3D LiDAR scans of existing spaces, high-resolution material texture maps, and time-varying occupancy patterns. By deploying GPU-accelerated workflows on HPC infrastructure, the project aims to reduce simulation times for multi-objective design scenarios from days to hours, enabling rapid prototyping of energy-efficient layouts, adaptive furniture systems, and biophilic design elements. Anticipated outcomes include open-source tools for scalable interior design simulation, validated against physical prototypes in commercial and residential case studies, and a framework for embedding computational fluid dynamics (CFD) into augmented reality (AR) visualization platforms. This work will bridge gaps between theoretical design principles and data-driven practice, offering novel strategies to address challenges in post-pandemic workspace redesign, aging-in-place housing, and carbon-neutral material selection. The requested resources will directly support interdisciplinary collaboration between interior design, computational engineering, and human-computer interaction researchers, fostering innovation in a field traditionally constrained by software limitations and computational bottlenecks.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program in the applied visual arts that prepares individuals to apply artistic principles and techniques to the professional planning, designing, equipping, and furnishing of residential and commercial interior spaces. Includes instruction in computer applications, drafting, and graphic techniques; principles of interior lighting, acoustics, systems integration, and color coordination; furniture and furnishings; textiles and their finishing; the history of interior design and period styles; basic structural design; building codes and inspection regulations; and applications to office, hotel, factory, restaurant and housing design.

abstract: Urban environments face escalating challenges from rising temperatures, exacerbated by heat island effects and climate change, yet traditional planning tools often lack the resolution to model microclimatic interactions with built infrastructure and human behavior at scale. This project seeks to develop a high-resolution computational framework to simulate urban microclimates and evaluate adaptive planning strategies for heat mitigation. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC), we propose an agent-based modeling approach integrated with fluid dynamics simulations to capture interactions between urban morphology, material properties, vegetation systems, and pedestrian activity. The computational model will synthesize geospatial data, real-time sensor inputs, and socioeconomic datasets to simulate heat distribution and public mobility patterns across diverse urban typologies. Key objectives include quantifying the efficacy of interventions such as reflective pavements, green corridors, and shade structures under varying climate scenarios, as well as identifying equity gaps in thermal comfort access. The HPC environment is critical to process large-scale 3D urban datasets, run parallelized simulations across multiple climate projections, and apply machine learning techniques to optimize mitigation strategies. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible toolkit for planners to visualize heat risk and prioritize interventions at the neighborhood scale, alongside policy recommendations for integrating microclimatic resilience into zoning codes and capital improvement plans. This work bridges computational modeling and participatory planning, advancing the capacity of cities to address climate justice through data-driven design while establishing a methodological precedent for interdisciplinary urban analytics. By situating computational rigor within community-centered planning frameworks, the project aims to redefine how emerging technologies can address systemic vulnerabilities in non-STEM domains.
detailed_field: City/ urban, community, and regional planning
cip_title: City/ Urban, Community, and Regional Planning
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply principles of planning, analysis, and architecture to the development and improvement of urban areas and surrounding regions, and to function as professional planners. Includes instruction in principles of architecture; master plan development; service, communications, and transportation systems design; community and commercial development; zoning; land use planning; applied economics; policy analysis; applicable laws and regulations; and professional responsibilities and managerial duties.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to model and simulate complex human-technology interactions at scale, with a focus on adaptive interface systems that dynamically respond to user behavior and cognitive states. The research addresses a critical gap in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI): current models often oversimplify the interplay between individual cognitive processes, social context, and real-time system adaptation, limiting their applicability to diverse populations and dynamic environments. To overcome this, we propose an interdisciplinary approach combining machine learning, agent-based modeling, and neurocognitive simulation. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to train multimodal deep learning architectures on heterogeneous datasets (eye-tracking, EEG, user logs, and social network data) while maintaining the temporal resolution required for real-time interaction analysis. Agent-based simulations will model population-level outcomes of interface designs, incorporating cognitive psychology principles and sociological variables. The computational pipeline will integrate transformer-based models for natural interaction processing, graph neural networks for social influence modeling, and reinforcement learning for adaptive system optimization. Expected outcomes include a scalable open-source toolkit for HCI researchers, validated through case studies on accessible educational interfaces and ethical AI collaboration systems. By enabling simultaneous analysis of micro-scale cognitive processes and macro-scale societal impacts, this work aims to advance the design of equitable, context-aware technologies. The requested resources will support large-scale parameter sweeps, hyperparameter optimization, and validation across synthetic and real-world datasets, which are computationally prohibitive on local clusters. This project bridges computational innovation with behavioral science rigor, directly aligning with the program’s mission to address societal challenges through interdisciplinary HCI research.
cip_definition: An interdisciplinary program that focuses on the study of the interaction between people and technology and how that technology impacts society, and combines disciplines within the fields of computing and information science (information systems, software engineering, artificial intelligence and design), engineering, and the behavior sciences (cognitive science, cognitive psychology, sociology, organizational psychology, and social psychology). Includes instruction in information technology, cognitive and behavioral sciences, and systems design.

abstract: This project seeks to optimize radiopharmaceutical imaging protocols for rare oncologic and neurodegenerative conditions using advanced computational modeling, addressing critical limitations in spatial resolution and quantitative accuracy of positron emission tomography (PET) and single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). Current clinical workflows rely on generalized protocols that inadequately account for patient-specific anatomical variability, tracer kinetics, or detector physics, leading to suboptimal diagnostic sensitivity for small lesions or early-stage disease. We propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework to simulate and iteratively refine imaging parameters across diverse virtual patient phantoms. Monte Carlo simulations (GATE/Geant4) will model photon transport and detector response at unprecedented scale, incorporating individualized CT-derived anatomical data, radiopharmaceutical biodistribution models, and noise characteristics. Machine learning architectures (3D convolutional neural networks) will then analyze simulated datasets to identify protocol adjustments that maximize lesion detectability while minimizing radiation exposure. The computational workflow will be validated against physical phantom experiments and retrospective clinical data. By leveraging GPU-accelerated nodes for parallelized simulation batches and distributed training of deep learning models, this approach aims to establish patient-adaptive imaging protocols that improve diagnostic confidence in complex cases. Anticipated outcomes include open-source tools for protocol optimization, quantitative benchmarks for novel tracer applications, and a computational pipeline adaptable to emerging detector technologies. This work bridges nuclear medicine physics with computational oncology, offering a paradigm shift toward precision nuclear imaging that enhances diagnostic accuracy while maintaining ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) safety principles—a critical advancement for managing rare diseases with limited therapeutic windows.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of physicians, to employ radioactive and stable nuclides in diagnostic evaluations and therapeutic applications while monitoring for patient health and safety. Includes instruction in nuclear physics, health physics, instrumentation and statistics, biochemistry, immunology, radiopharmacology, radiation biology, clinical nuclear medicine, radionuclide therapy, computer applications, safety regulations, equipment operation, quality control, laboratory procedures, taking patient histories, patient evaluation and monitoring, emergency first aid, administration and record-keeping, and personnel supervision.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a public health research initiative focused on modeling the spread of infectious diseases in heterogeneous urban populations. Traditional epidemiological models often oversimplify human mobility patterns, social determinants of health, and infrastructure disparities, limiting their utility for targeted intervention planning. Our work addresses this gap by developing a multi-scale, agent-based simulation framework that integrates high-resolution demographic data, real-time mobility traces, and spatially explicit healthcare access metrics. The computational challenge lies in simulating millions of individual agents with unique behavioral profiles across city-scale geographies while maintaining temporal granularity sufficient to capture transmission dynamics. We propose parallelizing the model using a hybrid MPI-OpenMP architecture to distribute agent interactions across nodes while optimizing intra-node memory usage for large-scale parameter sweeps. The HPC environment will enable sensitivity analyses across 50+ socioeconomic and biological variables, including vaccination rates, public transit usage, and variant-specific viral loads. Validation will occur through retrospective comparison with historical outbreak data from three major U.S. metropolitan regions. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of neighborhood-level vulnerability hotspots disproportionately affected by healthcare inequities, (2) quantification of threshold effects for targeted vaccine distribution strategies, and (3) open-source release of optimized simulation code for public health agencies. This work directly supports pandemic preparedness goals by creating decision-support tools that account for real-world complexity in urban health systems. Successful implementation requires sustained access to HPC resources capable of managing 10,000+ core-hour jobs with 2TB memory nodes, as smaller clusters cannot accommodate the concurrent simulation of >5 million agents with daily activity patterns over six-month horizons. Results will inform a NIH R01 proposal and collaborative interventions with municipal health departments.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in public health, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the computational analysis of under-documented Semitic and Middle/Near Eastern languages, with a focus on automating the reconstruction and comparative study of historical linguistic features. The research addresses a critical gap in computational linguistics: existing tools for morphological parsing, syntactic annotation, and dialectal variation modeling remain underdeveloped for many Semitic languages, particularly those with limited digital corpora or non-standard orthographies. By integrating rule-based morphological analyzers with neural sequence-to-sequence models, the project aims to develop scalable pipelines for parsing and annotating Classical Ethiopic (Ge’ez) and Neo-Aramaic textual corpora, which exhibit complex templatic morphology and dialectal diversity. HPC resources will enable the training of transformer-based models on augmented datasets combining extant digitized texts with synthetically generated linguistic variants, simulating phonological and morphological shifts across historical periods. Additionally, graph-based algorithms will be applied to model lexical borrowing networks across Arabic, Aramaic, and Akkadian, leveraging distributed computing to process cross-lingual phonological and semantic similarity metrics at scale. The computational workflows will be validated against manually annotated gold-standard texts and historical linguistic reconstructions from secondary literature. Outcomes will include open-source tools for low-resource Semitic language processing, a publicly accessible database of annotated texts with diachronic linguistic features, and quantitative models of language contact phenomena in the ancient Near East. This work will provide novel methodologies for resource-scarce linguistic research while contributing to interdisciplinary studies of cultural exchange, textual transmission, and language evolution in the region. The requested HPC allocation is essential to manage memory-intensive corpus preprocessing, parallelize model training across multiple GPU nodes, and optimize hyperparameter searches for domain-specific language tasks.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: Middle/ Near Eastern and Semitic Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in Middle/Near Eastern and Semitic languages, literatures, and linguistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Large-scale graph analysis is fundamental to advancing computational solutions in social network dynamics, infrastructure resilience, and genomic interactions, yet remains hindered by the inherent complexity of billion-edge datasets. Current algorithms for critical tasks such as community detection, dynamic shortest-path computation, and temporal anomaly detection exhibit prohibitive time complexity when applied to real-world graphs, limiting their utility in time-sensitive applications. This project proposes the development of adaptive parallel algorithms optimized for heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) architectures to address these scalability barriers. We will implement a multi-tiered computational strategy combining distributed-memory parallelism (via MPI) for coarse-grained graph partitioning, shared-memory multicore optimization (using OpenMP) for local subgraph analysis, and GPU acceleration for regular subroutines like similarity scoring. Key innovations include a dynamic load-balancing framework that adjusts work distribution based on real-time vertex centrality metrics and a communication-reduction protocol leveraging probabilistic data structures. The research will validate these methods on web-scale crawls (Common Crawl), urban mobility networks (OpenStreetMap), and biomedical interaction graphs (STRING DB), requiring access to HPC resources with multi-terabyte memory capacity and support for hybrid CPU-GPU workflows. Anticipated outcomes include (1) open-source implementations demonstrating ≥50% speedup over state-of-the-art frameworks (Dask, CuGraph) on 10^9-edge graphs, (2) theoretical advances in complexity analysis of asynchronous graph traversal models, and (3) applied breakthroughs in pandemic spread prediction through mobility graph analysis. By establishing scalable computational patterns for massive graph processing, this work will enable new research capabilities across computational social science, infrastructure planning, and systems biology while advancing foundational knowledge in parallel algorithm design.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on computer theory, computing problems and solutions, and the design of computer systems and user interfaces from a scientific perspective. Includes instruction in the principles of computational science, computer development and programming, and applications to a variety of end-use situations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop scalable statistical methodologies for analyzing high-dimensional, complex datasets using Bayesian hierarchical models, with a focus on addressing computational bottlenecks in inference tasks. Modern applications in epidemiology, environmental monitoring, and social sciences increasingly involve datasets with millions of observations, intricate dependency structures, and latent processes, rendering conventional Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods computationally infeasible. To overcome these limitations, we propose a hybrid computational framework combining parallelized Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) samplers, variational inference techniques, and distributed computing strategies. The core innovation lies in partitioning high-dimensional parameter spaces into conditionally independent subsets, enabling asynchronous gradient calculations across multi-node high-performance computing (HPC) clusters. This approach will be implemented through a custom integration of Stan and PyTorch, optimized for GPU-accelerated architectures, with adaptive load-balancing mechanisms to handle heterogeneous data structures. Key challenges include ensuring numerical stability in large-scale sparse matrix operations, minimizing communication overhead in distributed memory systems, and validating approximation fidelity through theoretical error bounds. The requested HPC resources—specifically, access to GPU nodes with high memory bandwidth and multi-terabyte distributed storage—are critical for benchmarking against existing methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, including a 10-million-record climate sensor network dataset and genomic variant-phenotype association data. Expected outcomes include (1) open-source software for scalable Bayesian inference, (2) novel convergence criteria for partitioned MCMC workflows, and (3) applications to real-time pandemic risk modeling with spatially varying transmission parameters. This work will advance statistical computing by bridging theoretical rigor with practical scalability, directly supporting reproducible research in public health and environmental statistics. The computational infrastructure will also facilitate training graduate students in cutting-edge statistical computing techniques, strengthening institutional capacity in data-intensive statistics.
cip_definition: A program with a general synthesis of mathematics and statistics or a specialization which draws from mathematics and statistics. Includes instruction in calculus, linear algebra, numerical analysis and partial differential equations, discrete mathematics, probability theory, statistics, computing, and other related topics.

abstract: Dental biofilm dysbiosis is a critical yet understudied driver of oral-systemic health interactions, with microbial community dynamics influencing conditions from periodontal disease to cardiovascular outcomes. Current clinical dental hygiene practices rely on generalized preventive strategies, lacking tools to model patient-specific biofilm evolution or predict dysbiosis triggers. This project seeks to develop a computational framework for simulating oral microbiome ecological networks and their response to mechanical/chemical interventions. Leveraging high-performance computing resources, we will construct agent-based models integrating species-level metabolic data from the Human Oral Microbiome Database with physicochemical parameters of the oral environment (pH, salivary flow, nutrient availability). The simulations will incorporate clinical data from longitudinal biofilm samples collected during routine dental hygiene visits, including 16S rRNA sequencing and mass spectrometry metabolomics. Machine learning techniques will be applied to identify tipping points in microbial community stability and test virtual interventions targeting putative keystone pathogens. Validation will occur through parallel microfluidic lab models replicating interproximal and subgingival niches. By establishing computational workflows for personalized dysbiosis risk prediction, this research aims to transform preventive care paradigms in dental hygiene practice. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source simulation platform for clinical decision support, evidence-based guidelines for optimized interdental cleaning regimens, and novel biomarkers for early caries/periodontitis detection. The resource-intensive nature of multi-scale modeling – spanning molecular interactions to community ecology – necessitates parallelized computing architectures to achieve clinically relevant temporal resolutions. Successful implementation will position computational dental hygiene as a frontier discipline in precision oral health, bridging microbial ecology theory with preventive clinical practice.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to clean teeth and apply preventive materials, provide oral health education and treatment counseling to patients, identify oral pathologies and injuries, and manage dental hygiene practices. Includes instruction in dental anatomy, microbiology, and pathology; dental hygiene theory and techniques; cleaning equipment operation and maintenance; dental materials; radiology; patient education and counseling; office management; supervised clinical training; and professional standards.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of cultural narratives and identity formation in Ukraine through large-scale textual and visual data. The research addresses a critical gap in Ukraine Studies: the lack of systematic, computationally driven investigations into how regional, linguistic, and historical factors have shaped collective memory and cultural expression across Ukraine’s diverse communities. While existing scholarship has relied on qualitative or localized case studies, this project will process multilingual corpora spanning pre-modern chronicles, 19th-20th century literature, and contemporary digital media (e.g., social media, news archives) to identify patterns of cultural continuity and divergence at an unprecedented scale. Computational methods will include natural language processing (NLP) for sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and semantic network mapping across Ukrainian, Russian, Crimean Tatar, and other regional languages, alongside image recognition tools to analyze iconography in historical art and public monuments. Custom algorithms will trace diachronic shifts in narrative themes tied to sovereignty, ethnicity, and territorial belonging, with attention to underrepresented voices, including gender and minority perspectives. The HPC infrastructure is essential for handling terabyte-scale datasets, training transformer-based language models on low-resource languages, and running iterative simulations to test hypotheses about cultural diffusion. Expected outcomes include an open-access digital atlas of Ukrainian cultural narratives, methodological frameworks for computational cultural studies in contested historical regions, and policy-relevant insights into the interplay between heritage preservation and contemporary identity politics. By integrating computational rigor with area studies expertise, this project aims to establish new interdisciplinary paradigms for understanding Ukraine’s cultural dynamics, with applications to post-conflict reconciliation and heritage digitization efforts.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of the Ukraine and its inhabitants, and related border regions, from earliest times to the present.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing preservation strategies for historic urban landscapes through advanced computational modeling, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze complex interactions between conservation priorities, material degradation, and socioeconomic factors. Historic preservation planning requires balancing structural integrity, cultural significance, and contemporary land-use demands, yet current methods often rely on siloed data or simplified simulations that fail to capture dynamic environmental and human variables. Our research proposes a multidisciplinary framework integrating 3D spectral imaging of building materials, geospatial analysis of urban microclimates, and agent-based modeling of stakeholder decision-making. HPC resources will enable large-scale simulations of material decay under projected climate scenarios, machine learning-driven pattern recognition in archival records to identify vulnerable structures, and probabilistic models evaluating preservation outcomes across policy interventions. Key computational tasks include finite element analysis of stress distributions in aging masonry, parallel processing of LiDAR datasets to map erosion patterns, and Monte Carlo simulations testing zoning code adaptations. Expected outcomes include an open-access predictive toolset for prioritizing conservation efforts, evidence-based recommendations for adaptive reuse policies, and a replicable model for quantifying the long-term economic value of preservation investments. By synthesizing architectural history, materials science, and computational social science, this work aims to transform how cities safeguard cultural heritage amid climate change and urban development pressures while maintaining compliance with ethical preservation standards. The requested HPC allocation is critical for handling petabyte-scale cultural asset inventories and running iterative simulations that traditional computing infrastructure cannot support within practical timeframes.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the design and implementation of plans to restore and maintain historic buildings, districts, and landscapes in a way that balances conservation and preservation with commercial and development interests. Includes instruction in architectural history, building conservation, cultural resource management, economics, historical documentation and preservation, land-use and zoning codes, public policy, public relations, real estate law, and taxation.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for analyzing emergent collective behaviors in decentralized information systems, with a focus on ethically aligned decision-making in multi-agent networks. The research addresses the challenge of modeling how large-scale, heterogeneous systems—such as distributed sensor networks or crowdsourced data platforms—achieve coherence without centralized control, particularly when ethical constraints (e.g., fairness, privacy, transparency) dynamically influence agent interactions. Current models often oversimplify ethical parameters as static inputs, neglecting their adaptive interplay with system-wide goals. To bridge this gap, we propose a hybrid approach combining graph neural networks (GNNs) with mechanism design theory, implemented via high-performance computing (HPC) to simulate systems at unprecedented scale. Agent behaviors will be encoded using message-passing GNN architectures, while optimization processes will integrate game-theoretic principles to balance global efficiency with local ethical compliance. The computational workload involves iterative simulations across parameter spaces spanning network topologies, agent rationality models, and constraint violation penalties, necessitating GPU-accelerated parallel processing and distributed memory management. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable library for simulating ethical decision-making in decentralized systems, (2) quantitative metrics for trade-offs between ethical adherence and operational efficiency, and (3) identification of critical thresholds where system-wide ethical alignment emerges from local interactions. This work will provide foundational tools for designing responsible distributed AI systems in domains such as community-driven disaster response networks and privacy-preserving federated learning architectures, where traditional optimization frameworks fail to capture complex sociotechnical dynamics. The requested HPC resources are essential for achieving statistical significance in results given the high dimensionality of modeled systems and stochastic nature of agent interactions.
cip_title: Computer and Information Sciences and Support Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in computer and information sciences and support services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in computational research on Bengali (Bangla) linguistics, with a focus on dialectal variation and historical philology. Despite Bengali’s status as the seventh most spoken language globally, large-scale quantitative analyses of its regional dialects and historical text corpora remain underdeveloped due to computational limitations. The research problem centers on mapping phonetic, syntactic, and lexical divergences across Bengali dialects and tracing their evolution through digitized pre-modern texts, tasks requiring intensive processing of unstructured linguistic data. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based models for low-resource languages, to analyze spoken and written corpora spanning six major dialects and texts from the 15th–19th centuries. Key methods involve training dialect classification models using phonetic transcriptions, applying diachronic word embedding algorithms to track semantic shifts, and simulating language change through agent-based models. These workflows demand parallelized processing of terabyte-scale datasets, including audio recordings, annotated manuscripts, and lexical databases, which exceed the capacity of local computing infrastructure. The requested HPC resources will enable efficient execution of distributed training for deep learning models, large-scale text normalization, and phonetic alignment across heterogeneous data types. Expected outcomes include the first comprehensive digital atlas of Bengali dialect boundaries, a diachronic corpus with semantic change annotations, and open-access tools for low-resource NLP applications. This work will advance scholarly understanding of Bengali’s linguistic history, support preservation efforts for endangered dialects, and provide computational frameworks applicable to other under-resourced languages. By bridging gaps between traditional philology and modern NLP, the project aims to establish a foundation for data-driven humanities research in Bengali studies while contributing methodologies to the broader field of computational linguistics.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Bengali language (Bangla) and related dialects. Includes instruction in philology; dialects; and applications in business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: Wildfire behavior prediction remains a critical challenge in fire protection science, with existing models struggling to integrate real-time environmental variables, fuel dynamics, and atmospheric interactions at operational scales. This project proposes to develop a next-generation wildfire spread simulation framework using coupled fire-atmosphere modeling enhanced by machine learning techniques. The research aims to address two key gaps: (1) insufficient resolution of current operational models to capture localized firebrand transport mechanisms, and (2) inadequate computational efficiency for scenario-based risk assessment during active incidents. Our approach combines the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model with a parallelized fire spread algorithm that dynamically incorporates satellite-derived fuel moisture data, LiDAR terrain mapping, and crowd-sourced incident reports. High-performance computing resources are required to execute ensemble simulations across multiple parameter spaces simultaneously, including varying wind field perturbations, fuel heterogeneity scenarios, and suppression strategy effectiveness. The computational workflow will leverage GPU-accelerated atmospheric solvers coupled with agent-based fire front propagation models, requiring access to large-memory nodes for processing 1m-resolution vegetation datasets. Expected outcomes include a validated predictive framework capable of generating probabilistic fire spread forecasts at 15-minute refresh intervals during incidents, with particular attention to wildland-urban interface dynamics. This work will produce open-source tools for fire departments to conduct virtual tabletop exercises using scenario libraries generated through our simulations. The computational results will directly inform national standards for wildfire evacuation zone planning and contribute to the development of AI-assisted decision support systems for incident commanders. By advancing the fidelity and operational utility of fire behavior models, this research addresses critical homeland security needs for resilient community protection against escalating wildfire threats.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in fire protection, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop a computational framework for optimizing individualized training protocols in athletic performance and injury prevention. Current methods for designing sport-specific training regimens rely on generalized physiological thresholds and static biomechanical models, often failing to account for dynamic interactions between an athlete’s neuromuscular adaptation, environmental stressors, and real-time biometric feedback. The proposed work addresses this gap by integrating agent-based modeling (ABM) with machine learning (ML) to simulate multi-scale physiological responses to training loads across diverse populations. Using anonymized datasets from wearable sensors, motion capture systems, and historical injury records, the project will parameterize athlete-specific agents to predict performance outcomes under variable training intensities, recovery intervals, and environmental conditions. HPC resources are critical for scaling simulations to accommodate high-dimensional data streams (e.g., electromyography, heart rate variability, and kinematic sequences) and for training deep reinforcement learning models that iteratively refine protocol recommendations. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source toolkit for coaches and sports scientists to generate adaptive, evidence-based training plans that minimize injury risk while maximizing performance gains. By quantifying the nonlinear relationships between biomechanical stressors and adaptive responses, this work aims to advance precision sports science, offering novel insights into load management strategies for elite athletes and recreational populations alike. The computational framework will also establish a foundation for future studies on aging athletes, rehabilitation protocols, and climate-resilient training practices in extreme environments.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_title: Sports, Kinesiology, and Physical Education/ Fitness, General
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on activities and principles that promote physical fitness, achieve and maintain athletic prowess, and accomplish related research and service goals. Includes instruction in human movement studies, motivation studies, rules and practice of specific sports, exercise and fitness principles and techniques, basic athletic injury prevention and treatment, and organizing and leading fitness and sports programs.

abstract: This project seeks to develop and evaluate computational models to optimize personalized learning strategies for K–12 students with emotional disturbances (ED) by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Students with ED often exhibit complex, dynamic behavioral and academic needs that challenge traditional one-size-fits-all pedagogical approaches. While individualized education programs (IEPs) are mandated, designing effective, adaptable interventions remains resource-intensive and inconsistently implemented due to the heterogeneous nature of emotional disturbances. This research aims to address this gap by creating predictive models that analyze multimodal student data—including behavioral logs, academic performance metrics, and demographic factors—to recommend tailored instructional and behavioral supports. The computational approach integrates machine learning (ML) techniques, such as reinforcement learning and natural language processing, to identify patterns in longitudinal student outcomes and simulate the efficacy of hypothetical interventions. HPC resources are critical for processing large-scale datasets from partnering school districts, training ensemble models that account for contextual variables (e.g., classroom environment, educator experience), and running iterative simulations to refine intervention strategies. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable framework for dynamically updating IEP recommendations based on real-time student data, (2) evidence-based insights into the relationship between specific instructional practices and behavioral outcomes in ED populations, and (3) open-source tools to help educators prioritize interventions without overburdening manual workflows. By bridging computational analytics and special education pedagogy, this work has the potential to improve the precision of resource allocation in classrooms, reduce trial-and-error inefficiencies, and advance equity in educational support for students with emotional disturbances.
cip_title: Education/ Teaching of Individuals with Emotional Disturbances
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the design of educational services for children or adults with emotional conditions which adversely affect their educational performance and that may prepare individuals to teach such students. Includes instruction in identifying students with emotional disturbances, developing individual education plans, teaching and supervising individuals with emotional disturbances, counseling, and applicable laws and policies.

abstract: This project seeks to address the challenge of analyzing complex, multi-level educational data to evaluate heterogeneous treatment effects in large-scale intervention studies. Educational research increasingly relies on longitudinal and hierarchical datasets (e.g., student outcomes nested within classrooms, schools, and districts) that require advanced statistical models to account for variability across levels, missing data, and non-randomized designs. Traditional computing resources often prove inadequate for estimating these models efficiently, particularly when conducting sensitivity analyses, bootstrapping, or Bayesian simulations to validate findings. The proposed research will develop and apply computationally intensive methods, including multilevel causal inference models and machine learning algorithms, to assess how interventions such as personalized learning programs differentially impact student subgroups. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable parallel processing for Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation of Bayesian hierarchical models, cross-validation of predictive algorithms, and large-scale simulations to test the robustness of results under varying conditions. These approaches will be applied to a national dataset comprising 5 million K–12 students’ academic records, demographic variables, and program participation metrics. The project aims to produce scalable, open-source code for educational researchers working with similar datasets, along with methodological insights into optimizing statistical power in quasi-experimental designs. Outcomes will directly inform resource allocation strategies for equity-focused educational policies by identifying intervention components most effective for marginalized student populations. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this work advances the precision and reproducibility of statistical methods in education research while addressing computational bottlenecks that hinder the analysis of high-dimensional, real-world data.
detailed_field: Educational assessment, evaluation, and research methods
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of statistics to the analysis and solution of educational research problems, and the development of technical designs for research studies. Includes instruction in mathematical statistics, research design, computer applications, instrument design, research methodologies, and applications to research problems in specific education subjects.

abstract: The increasing complexity of geospatial data acquisition and processing in surveying engineering demands advanced computational solutions to address accuracy, scalability, and real-time analysis challenges. Modern surveying workflows integrate heterogeneous data streams from terrestrial LiDAR, aerial photogrammetry, satellite remote sensing, and global navigation satellite systems (GNSS), generating multi-dimensional datasets that strain conventional processing systems. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and optimize computational workflows for large-scale geospatial data fusion, error modeling, and deformation analysis in civil and transportation infrastructure applications. The research will focus on three computational objectives: (1) parallelizing point cloud registration algorithms to enable real-time alignment of multi-sensor LiDAR data for construction monitoring, (2) implementing machine learning models to automate anomaly detection in long-term structural health monitoring datasets, and (3) simulating urban-scale GNSS signal propagation to improve positional accuracy in dense built environments. Methods will leverage GPU-accelerated computing for deep learning-based feature extraction from orthophotos and distributed memory architectures for Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis in geodetic networks. Expected outcomes include open-source tools for photogrammetric bundle adjustment optimization and a computational framework for predictive modeling of ground subsidence risks in transportation corridors. By enabling faster processing of TB-scale surveying datasets with rigorous precision validation, this work will directly support infrastructure resilience planning and advance the integration of HPC capabilities into geospatial education curricula.
