Results will be disseminated through open-access platforms and collaborations with Lao academic institutions to ensure sustainable impact.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Lao language. Includes instruction in philology; dialects; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in understanding spatial and temporal population dynamics affecting public health infrastructure planning in aging populations. While demographic shifts are well-documented at macro scales, localized projections integrating real-time migration, mortality, and fertility data remain computationally constrained, limiting actionable insights for policymakers. We propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to model subnational population changes at unprecedented granularity (census tract level) across a 20-year horizon, combining agent-based microsimulation with Bayesian hierarchical spatial-temporal models. The research will integrate multi-source data, including U.S. Census microdata, Medicare utilization records, and georeferenced vital statistics, to simulate individual life-course trajectories while accounting for spatial dependencies and uncertainty propagation. Computational challenges include parallel processing of 100+ million agent interactions per simulation year, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) parameter estimation for high-dimensional spatial models, and real-time visualization of uncertainty metrics through GPU-accelerated geospatial analytics. The HPC environment is essential for scaling ensemble simulations across parameter spaces, reducing runtime from estimated 18 months on local clusters to 6 weeks via distributed memory parallelism and optimized memory handling for terabyte-scale demographic datasets. Expected outcomes include (1) open-source tools for adaptive demographic forecasting under policy scenarios, (2) vulnerability indices identifying regions at risk of healthcare infrastructure mismatches, and (3) validation frameworks comparing model projections against emerging migration patterns observed in the 2020s post-pandemic era. This work directly supports evidence-based decision-making for hospital capacity planning, geriatric service allocation, and regional workforce development strategies, while advancing methodological integration of demographic microsimulation with spatially explicit uncertainty quantification.
detailed_field: Sociology, demography, and population studies nec
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the practical application of demographic methods and materials for decision-making in business, education, health, and government. Includes instruction in statistics, research methods, geographic information systems, and demographic methods and techniques.

abstract: This research project seeks to investigate the structural and conceptual relationships between ethical frameworks across diverse religious and philosophical traditions using advanced computational methods. The core challenge lies in systematically analyzing large-scale textual corpora—spanning foundational scriptures, commentaries, and philosophical treatises from traditions such as Buddhism, Abrahamic faiths, and classical Greek philosophy—to identify latent patterns in moral reasoning, value prioritization, and argumentative logic. Manual comparative analysis of such voluminous and linguistically complex materials remains prohibitively time-intensive and susceptible to human bias. To address this, we propose deploying natural language processing (NLP) techniques, including transformer-based language models and semantic network analysis, to map ethical concepts, trace their contextual evolution, and quantify intertextual influences. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical for training domain-specific language models on our curated multilingual corpus (approximately 10TB of text across 15 languages) and for running iterative simulations of conceptual interaction networks. The computational pipeline will integrate phylogenetic algorithms adapted from biological sciences to model the historical development of ethical ideas, alongside graph neural networks to detect cross-cultural epistemic correlations. Expected outcomes include a novel taxonomy of transreligious ethical paradigms, an open-access toolset for computational hermeneutics, and quantitative evidence addressing longstanding philosophical debates about universalism versus cultural relativism in morality. By bridging humanistic inquiry with scalable computational analysis, this project aims to establish new methodologies for interdisciplinary research in religious and philosophical studies while generating resources for ethically informed AI development.
cip_definition: A general program that combines the study of philosophy and religious studies. Includes instruction in logic; ethics; epistemology; symbolism; phenomenology; the sociology, psychology, philosophy, anthropology, literature, and art of religion; and world religions.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework to optimize predictive maintenance protocols for legacy military hardware systems, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to address challenges unique to aging equipment with limited digital integration. While predictive maintenance is well-studied in modern industrial contexts, military systems—particularly those designed decades ago—present distinct constraints due to heterogeneous data sources (e.g., analog logs, sparse sensor retrofits), security-restricted telemetry, and operational variability across deployment environments. The research problem centers on overcoming data sparsity and uncertainty to build robust machine learning (ML) models capable of forecasting mechanical failures in platforms such as armored vehicles, rotary-wing aircraft, and naval propulsion systems. Computational methods will integrate physics-informed neural networks with Bayesian uncertainty quantification to synthesize incomplete maintenance records, real-time sensor snapshots, and domain-specific degradation models. HPC resources will enable large-scale parameter optimization for ensemble ML architectures and Monte Carlo simulations evaluating maintenance policy trade-offs under stochastic operational conditions. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for adaptive maintenance scheduling, validated against historical failure datasets from three military platforms, and a comparative analysis of computational efficiency gains over conventional reliability-centered maintenance approaches. The project’s significance lies in bridging a critical gap between legacy system constraints and modern data-driven maintenance paradigms, directly supporting sustainment readiness while reducing lifecycle costs. By prioritizing interoperability with low-bandwidth field environments and hardware-agnostic deployment, this work aims to establish a template for modernizing maintenance workflows in resource-constrained defense contexts without requiring costly system overhauls.
cip_title: Military Systems and Maintenance Technology, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in military systems and maintenance technology, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Medical toxicology faces critical challenges in predicting and mitigating complex toxicological interactions, particularly in cases of polydrug exposures, environmental chemical mixtures, and novel synthetic agents. Traditional experimental methods struggle to model the dynamic, multi-scale interactions between toxins, biological systems, and patient-specific variables such as genetic polymorphisms or comorbidities. This project proposes to develop a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework integrating pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) modeling, machine learning, and molecular dynamics simulations to advance predictive toxicology and personalized treatment strategies. The research will focus on three interconnected aims: (1) creating multi-compartment PK/PD models for emerging synthetic opioids and stimulants using parallelized differential equation solvers, (2) training graph neural networks on curated toxicology databases to predict synergistic toxicity risks in polydrug combinations, and (3) simulating toxin-receptor interactions at atomic resolution to guide antidote development. Computational workflows will leverage heterogeneous computing architectures, combining GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics (using AMBER and GROMACS) with CPU-based ensemble modeling for uncertainty quantification. The project will utilize electronic health record data from poison control centers, molecular structure databases, and environmental exposure registries. Expected outcomes include predictive models for acute poisoning outcomes, computational tools for rapid risk assessment of novel psychoactive substances, and open-source frameworks for simulating toxin-biomolecule interactions. These resources will directly address clinical needs in overdose management, chemical threat preparedness, and precision toxicology. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing the computational intensity of ensemble toxicity simulations, large-scale hyperparameter optimization in machine learning models, and population-scale PK/PD analyses requiring >10^5 parallel simulations. This work bridges molecular-scale toxic mechanisms with clinical decision-making, offering transformative potential for evidence-based medical toxicology practice.
cip_definition: Research focused on that prepares physicians who specialize in the prevention, evaluation, treatment, and monitoring of injury and illness from exposures to drugs and chemicals, as well as exposures to biological and radiological agents. Important areas include acute drug poisoning; adverse drug events; drug abuse, addiction, and withdrawal; chemicals and hazardous materials; terrorism preparedness; venomous bites and stings; and environmental and workplace exposures.

abstract: Medical education faces the challenge of optimizing training efficacy while adapting to rapidly evolving clinical practices, diverse learning needs, and variable resource constraints. Traditional approaches to curriculum design and evaluation often rely on retrospective analyses or small-scale trials, limiting their ability to model complex educational interactions or predict longitudinal outcomes. This project proposes a computational approach to address these limitations by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate, analyze, and iteratively refine medical education strategies. Using anonymized datasets from institutional learning management systems, competency assessments, and longitudinal performance records, we will develop agent-based models to simulate learner trajectories under varying curricular conditions. Machine learning algorithms will identify patterns linking instructional methods, learner engagement, and clinical competency outcomes, while natural language processing (NLP) will analyze qualitative feedback from students and faculty. Computational demands arise from the scale of multimodal data (structured assessments, free-text evaluations, and time-series engagement metrics) and the need for parallelized simulations to test hypothetical curriculum designs. The project will deploy graph neural networks to model knowledge integration across disciplines and reinforcement learning to propose adaptive curricular interventions. Expected outcomes include a framework for predicting the impact of pedagogical changes on learner proficiency, tools for personalized curriculum optimization, and scalable metrics for evaluating educational equity. By enabling data-driven, dynamic approaches to medical education, this work aims to reduce gaps in clinical preparedness and foster resilience in training programs, ultimately improving patient care outcomes. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling memory-intensive simulations, training large NLP models on unstructured text, and enabling rapid iteration of complex, multi-layered educational scenarios.
cip_definition: Research on how to teach deliver, design, and evaluate courses and curricula for medical students, residents, and faculty.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the thermodynamic and kinetic controls on silicate melt evolution in magmatic systems under extreme pressure-temperature conditions, with a focus on resolving discrepancies between experimental data and predictive geochemical models. Current models of melt behavior in Earth’s upper mantle and crust often fail to reconcile observed mineral-melt equilibria, particularly for alkali-rich and volatile-bearing systems, limiting their utility in understanding magma genesis and differentiation. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven approach combining ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations and Monte Carlo-based phase equilibria modeling. AIMD simulations will quantify atomic-scale bonding environments, diffusion coefficients, and melt viscosity in multicomponent silicate systems (e.g., Na-K-Al-Si-O-H) at pressures up to 3 GPa and temperatures of 1200–1800°C. These data will parameterize a new thermodynamic database for use in the Gibbs-free-energy minimization software MELTS, enhanced with machine learning algorithms to accelerate convergence in complex compositional spaces. The HPC component is critical due to the computational expense of simulating large (>500-atom) systems over nanosecond trajectories at mantle conditions, requiring parallelized density functional theory calculations across thousands of cores. Expected outcomes include (1) refined activity-composition models for alkali feldspar and amphibole crystallization in hydrous magmas, (2) a mechanistic understanding of how H2O and CO2 modify melt transport properties, and (3) open-source release of simulation-derived forcefields optimized for geochemical applications. This work will directly improve the predictive capacity of magma evolution models, with implications for interpreting volcanic unrest signals, ore-forming processes, and planetary-scale geochemical cycles. Successful implementation depends on access to HPC resources capable of sustaining large-scale molecular dynamics ensembles and iterative thermodynamic modeling.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the chemical properties and behavior of the silicates and other substances forming, and formed by geomorphological processes of the earth and other planets. Includes instruction in chemical thermodynamics, equilibrium in silicate systems, atomic bonding, isotopic fractionation, geochemical modeling, specimen analysis, and studies of specific organic and inorganic substances.

abstract: This research project seeks to investigate the structural and evolutionary mechanisms underlying host-cell manipulation by RNA viruses, with a focus on elucidating how viral protein dynamics and genetic variation influence pathogenesis. A critical gap exists in understanding the real-time conformational changes of viral entry proteins during host receptor binding and the relationship between viral quasispecies diversity and immune evasion. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to perform large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of viral envelope proteins interacting with host membranes, alongside phylogenetic reconstructions of viral populations from longitudinal clinical sequencing data. MD simulations will model key glycoproteins (e.g., influenza hemagglutinin, coronaviral spike) to resolve transient structural states that mediate membrane fusion, using all-atom and coarse-grained approaches. Concurrently, evolutionary analysis of whole-genome viral sequences will identify conserved versus adaptive regions under host immune pressure. These computational workflows demand significant parallel processing for ensemble simulations spanning microsecond timescales and maximum-likelihood phylogenetics on terabyte-scale sequence datasets. The integration of structural and evolutionary data aims to pinpoint conserved functional domains vulnerable to cross-reactive therapeutics and predict antigenic shifts in emerging strains. Expected outcomes include mechanistic insights into viral entry, frameworks for predicting strain fitness, and actionable targets for broad-spectrum antiviral design. This work directly advances virological knowledge by linking molecular-scale protein behavior to population-level evolution, with implications for improving pandemic preparedness and adaptive vaccine platforms. Successful execution requires dedicated HPC allocations for GPU-accelerated simulations, large-memory nodes for phylogenetic inference, and scalable storage for multi-modal data integration.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of subcellular pieces of genetic material, called viruses, that inhabit living cells in parasitical relationships and their role in disease. Includes instruction in virus taxonomy and systematics, viral structures, viral genetics, prions, virus/host cell interaction, viral pathogenesis, and applications to specific topics such as cancer biology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the study of precolonial African social and political networks through large-scale spatial and temporal analysis of fragmented historical data. While Africa’s precolonial history is richly documented in diverse sources—including oral traditions, archaeological findings, traveler accounts, and colonial records—these materials remain dispersed, heterogeneous, and challenging to synthesize at continental scales. Traditional historiographic methods struggle to systematically analyze patterns of state formation, trade dynamics, or cultural diffusion across such vast, interconnected geographies and timeframes. This project addresses this gap by developing computational models to integrate and visualize multi-source data, enabling the identification of macrohistorical trends and localized interactions. Using geospatial analysis, network modeling, and machine learning techniques, we will map shifting political boundaries, trade routes, and cultural exchange networks across West and Central Africa from 1000–1800 CE. Key tasks include processing unstructured textual data (e.g., Arabic manuscripts, Portuguese colonial records) via NLP tools, georeferencing archaeological site data, and simulating trade network resilience under environmental stressors. HPC resources are critical for handling the scale of geospatial datasets, running agent-based simulations of social interactions, and training transformer models to detect linguistic and thematic patterns in multilingual corpora. Expected outcomes include an open-access interactive atlas of precolonial African polities, a repository of computationally enhanced historical datasets, and new insights into the longue durée impacts of trans-Saharan and intra-African exchange systems. By bridging computational methods with African historiographic scholarship, this project aims to reshape understandings of precolonial statecraft, mobility, and connectivity while centering African agency in global historical narratives.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the development of the societies, cultures, and institutions of one or more peoples of the African Continent, usually with an emphasis on Africa south of the Sahara (and including the African diasporas overseas) from their origins to the present. Includes instruction in the historiography of specific cultures and periods; sources and materials; historical research methods; and applications to the study of specific themes, issues, periods, and institutions.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the evolutionary dynamics of digital business ecosystems through large-scale simulations of decentralized, adaptive market networks. As emerging technologies like blockchain, IoT, and AI reshape transactional frameworks, traditional models of business interaction fail to capture the nonlinear feedback loops and self-organizing behaviors inherent in these systems. The research problem centers on identifying critical thresholds in ecosystem resilience when subjected to competitive resource allocation strategies and regulatory shocks. Using a novel combination of multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and game-theoretic network analysis, we will simulate heterogeneous agent populations—business entities, automated contracts, and hybrid human-AI decision systems—operating under dynamically shifting incentive structures. High-performance computing resources are essential to model mesoscale network formation (10^4-10^5 nodes) with real-time adaptation mechanisms, requiring parallelized optimization of multi-objective payoff matrices across distributed memory architectures. The computational framework integrates evolutionary algorithms to test hypotheses about path dependency in ecosystem governance and emergent coordination patterns under resource scarcity. Expected outcomes include predictive metrics for ecosystem collapse/recovery cycles and a taxonomy of stable coordination equilibria in permissionless business networks. Results will inform adaptive regulatory frameworks for decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) and provide empirical benchmarks for resilience engineering in platform-based economies. This work bridges computational social science with next-generation business model design, addressing gaps in understanding how algorithmic intermediation redefines value creation hierarchies in post-platform capitalism.
cip_title: Business, Management, Marketing, and Related Support Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in business, management, marketing and related support services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This research project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing real-time financial risk assessment in complex, multi-stakeholder supply chain networks by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model dynamic interdependencies between accounting data streams and financial market signals. Traditional risk models in accounting and finance often rely on static, siloed datasets, limiting their ability to predict cascading disruptions in globalized supply chains where accounting events (e.g., invoice delays, inventory revaluations) interact with financial market reactions (e.g., commodity price volatility, credit default swaps). The proposed computational framework integrates agent-based modeling with temporal graph neural networks to simulate bidirectional impacts between granular transactional accounting data (accounts payable/receivable ledgers, audit trails) and high-frequency market data across foreign exchange, equity, and derivatives markets. By deploying this model on HPC infrastructure, the project will enable parallel processing of petabyte-scale datasets spanning 10+ years of multinational corporate financial records and synchronized market tick data. Key computational challenges include developing hybrid architectures that maintain accounting transaction integrity during distributed computing operations while achieving sub-second latency for real-time stress testing scenarios. Expected outcomes include a novel metric for supply chain financial contagion risk, validated against historical crisis events, and an open-source toolkit for simulating regulatory interventions. This work bridges a critical gap between operational accounting practices and systemic financial stability analysis, offering enterprises and policymakers predictive capabilities to mitigate compound risks arising from accounting anomalies and market shocks. The HPC implementation will significantly advance methodological capabilities in financial computing by demonstrating scalable integration of heterogeneous temporal data structures central to modern accounting-finance decision support systems.
cip_definition: An integrated or combined program in accounting and finance that prepares individuals to function as accountants and financial managers or analysts.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework for optimizing the design of adaptive urban soundscapes through the integration of acoustic metamaterials, real-time sensor networks, and machine learning. Urban noise pollution, a growing public health concern, remains inadequately addressed by conventional noise mitigation strategies, which are static, material-intensive, and fail to account for dynamic environmental conditions. We propose an engineering solution that combines tunable metamaterial arrays with distributed sensor feedback to actively reshape acoustic environments in response to changing noise sources and urban activity patterns. The research problem centers on overcoming the computational complexity of modeling wave propagation in heterogeneous, time-varying metamaterial systems while optimizing their geometric and material parameters under real-world constraints. High-performance computing (HPC) resources will enable large-scale finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations of 3D acoustic wave interactions with dynamically reconfigurable meta-surfaces, coupled with reinforcement learning algorithms to train adaptive control policies. Key challenges include resolving multiscale physics (kHz-MHz frequency ranges), managing stochastic input from distributed sensor networks, and minimizing latency in control loop simulations. The computational workflow integrates open-source wave solvers (e.g., OpenFOAM-AMR) with custom PyTorch-based neural architecture search tools to co-optimize material configurations and control logic. Expected outcomes include validated design principles for field-deployable adaptive acoustic systems, a publicly available dataset of urban noise-metamaterial interaction scenarios, and generalized methods for engineering reconfigurable material systems in complex wave environments. This interdisciplinary work bridges gaps between mechanical wave theory, computational material science, and urban infrastructure design, offering new pathways for smart city technologies that dynamically mediate human-environment interactions.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in engineering, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The increasing complexity of radioisotopic analyses in clinical pathology demands advanced computational infrastructure to address challenges in data processing, modeling, and validation. Current in vitro studies of radionuclide interactions with biological samples—such as blood, urine, or biopsied tissues—generate high-dimensional datasets from multi-modal instrumentation (e.g., gamma spectrometry, autoradiography, and liquid scintillation counting). These datasets require robust computational frameworks to resolve signal-to-noise limitations, quantify isotope kinetics, and model radiation-dose relationships at subcellular scales. Existing workflows lack the capacity to integrate heterogeneous data streams efficiently, hindering the development of predictive models for diagnostic accuracy, radiation safety protocols, and quality control in laboratory settings. This project proposes the development of a scalable, high-performance computing (HPC) pipeline to address these gaps. Leveraging GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo simulations, we will model radiation transport and energy deposition in biological matrices, informed by experimental data on radionuclide decay spectra and tissue-specific absorption coefficients. Concurrently, machine learning algorithms will be deployed to classify spectral anomalies in large-scale datasets, enabling real-time quality assurance during isotopic analyses. The HPC environment will further support the optimization of laboratory workflows through parallelized pharmacokinetic modeling of isotope retention and clearance in vitro, reducing computational bottlenecks associated with traditional single-threaded approaches. Expected outcomes include a validated open-source toolkit for radioisotopic data analysis, enhanced predictive models for radiation safety in sample handling, and improved protocols for quantifying low-abundance biomarkers in complex biological fluids. By integrating HPC resources with experimental radioisotopic pathology, this work aims to advance precision in diagnostic applications while establishing computational standards for radiation-based in vitro research.
cip_definition: Research focused on the use of radionuclides in the study of body fluids, excreta, or tissues quantified outside the body. May included related research in laboratory management and safety, quality control, instrumentation, isotope storage and in vitro analyses.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of atmospheric gravity wave (GW) dynamics and their multiscale interactions with planetary-scale circulation, a critical gap in current atmospheric modeling. Gravity waves generated by convection, topography, and wind shear play a fundamental role in transferring energy and momentum between the troposphere, stratosphere, and mesosphere. However, global climate models (GCMs) struggle to resolve these subgrid-scale processes, relying on parameterizations that inadequately capture wave generation, propagation, and dissipation, leading to uncertainties in middle atmospheric circulation and climate projections. We propose a high-resolution modeling campaign using the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM) coupled with a novel spectral GW parameterization to investigate wave-mean flow interactions during sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) events. The project requires high-performance computing (HPC) resources to execute global simulations at 0.25° horizontal resolution, explicitly resolving mesoscale GWs while integrating over seasonal timescales. A key innovation involves machine learning-assisted validation against satellite limb-sounding data (AIRS, MLS) to iteratively refine parameterization schemes. Computational demands include 1.8 million core-hours for ensemble simulations across varying GW forcing scenarios, supported by GPU-accelerated data assimilation workflows. Expected outcomes include improved representation of GW drag in SSW predictability and stratosphere-troposphere coupling mechanisms. The resulting open-source parameterization module will directly benefit next-generation GCMs, enhancing fidelity in seasonal forecasts and long-term climate scenarios. By resolving scale interactions between GWs and polar vortex dynamics, this work addresses urgent knowledge gaps in atmospheric energy transfer, with implications for extreme weather prediction and ozone layer variability. The requested HPC allocation will enable unprecedented resolution and computational throughput, bridging critical scales between localized GW sources and their global impacts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the processes governing the interactions, movement, and behavior of atmospheric phenomena and related terrestrial and solar phenomena. Includes instruction in cloud and precipitation physics, solar radiation transfer, active and passive remote sensing, atmospheric electricity and acoustics, atmospheric wave phenomena, turbulence and boundary layers, solar wind, geomagnetic storms, coupling, natural plasma, and energization.

abstract: The design and optimization of orthotic and prosthetic devices remain constrained by challenges in modeling complex biomechanical interactions, material behaviors, and patient-specific anatomical variability. Current approaches often rely on simplified simulations or iterative clinical adjustments, leading to prolonged development timelines, suboptimal device performance, and patient discomfort. This project seeks to address these limitations by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to develop advanced computational frameworks for simulating and predicting the biomechanical efficacy of orthotic/prosthetic devices under real-world conditions. The research will focus on three primary objectives: (1) creating multi-scale finite element models to analyze stress distribution and material fatigue in prosthetic components during dynamic activities, (2) employing machine learning to correlate patient-specific factors (e.g., residual limb morphology, gait patterns, tissue compliance) with device fit and functional outcomes, and (3) simulating neuromuscular responses to novel assistive technologies, such as powered prostheses, using coupled biomechanical and control system models. Computational workflows will integrate clinical datasets, including 3D scans, motion capture, and pressure mapping, to enable patient-specific predictions. The HPC environment is critical for managing large-scale parameter sweeps, high-resolution tissue-device interaction simulations, and training predictive algorithms on heterogeneous clinical data. Expected outcomes include a validated pipeline for rapid virtual prototyping of customized devices, reducing empirical trial-and-error in clinical workflows. This work will advance the understanding of load transfer mechanisms in orthotic interfaces, identify failure-prone design features, and enable data-driven personalization of assistive technologies. By bridging computational engineering and clinical orthotics/prosthetics practice, the project aims to improve functional outcomes for patients with limb loss or musculoskeletal impairments while establishing scalable methodologies for future innovation in rehabilitative device development.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, in consultation with physicians and other therapists, to design and fit orthoses for patients with disabling conditions of the limbs and/or spine, and prostheses for patients who have partial or total absence of a limb or significant superficial deformity. Includes instruction in biomechanics, gait analysis, pathomechanics, kinesiology, pathology, neuroanatomy, materials science, diagnostic imaging, patient analysis and measurement, impression taking, model rectification, assistive/restorative technology and engineering applications, product finishing, diagnostic and definitive fitting and alignment, power devices, postoperative management, and patient counseling and follow-up.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of Polish cultural identity through large-scale textual and visual datasets spanning the medieval period to the 20th century. The research addresses a critical gap in Polish Studies: the lack of systematic, data-driven investigations into how narratives of collective identity, gender roles, and regional belonging were constructed and transformed across different historical contexts. Traditional close-reading methods struggle to process the vast corpus of Polish-language texts, folk art digitizations, and archival materials required to map these dynamics at scale. The proposed computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) for historical Polish texts, computer vision techniques to analyze iconographic patterns in folk art, and network analysis to trace the circulation of cultural motifs. Key challenges include adapting NLP models to premodern orthographic variations, aligning visual motifs with textual references in temporally stratified datasets, and managing multilingual metadata from borderland regions. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of over 250,000 digitized pages from the National Digital Library of Poland, 18,000 ethnographic artifacts, and 19th-century regional press archives. Expected outcomes include 1) a geotemporal visualization platform tracking cultural narrative diffusion, 2) quantitative evidence challenging monolithic interpretations of Polish identity formation, and 3) open-access tools for diachronic analysis of Slavic cultural materials. This work will provide the first computational framework to model Poland’s cultural history as a dynamic, multi-voiced process, with implications for comparative studies of identity in contested borderland regions globally. By bridging digital humanities and area studies methodologies, the project aims to establish new standards for data-intensive cultural analysis while preserving endangered historical perspectives.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of Poland and the current and historical inhabitants of the Polish lands, including borderlands, from earliest times to the present.

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing predictive maintenance frameworks for heterogeneous energy systems, including aging power grids, distributed renewable energy infrastructure, and hybrid generation-storage installations. Current maintenance protocols struggle to account for the complex interdependencies between legacy systems and modern smart grid components, often leading to inefficient resource allocation, unplanned downtime, and accelerated equipment degradation. The research proposes developing a computational decision-support system that integrates multi-physics simulations with machine learning to model failure propagation pathways across coupled electrical, thermal, and mechanical subsystems. High-performance computing resources are essential for running parallelized simulations of component degradation under diverse operational scenarios, processing high-resolution sensor data streams from field deployments, and training neural networks capable of identifying precursor signatures for cascading failures. The computational workflow will combine finite element analysis for stress modeling in physical components, graph neural networks for analyzing system topology vulnerabilities, and reinforcement learning algorithms for optimizing repair prioritization strategies. Expected outcomes include a validated framework for risk-informed maintenance scheduling that accounts for both technical performance metrics and workforce capacity constraints. The resulting models and datasets will be made available through an open-access repository to support workforce training programs in next-generation energy system maintenance. This research directly addresses the urgent need for adaptive maintenance strategies in rapidly evolving energy infrastructures, with potential applications in utility operations, renewable energy integration, and grid resilience planning. The computational intensity of simultaneously modeling physical degradation processes and network-level impacts necessitates access to GPU-accelerated nodes and large-memory systems for handling terabyte-scale operational datasets.
cip_title: Energy Systems Maintenance and Repair Technologies/ Technicians, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in energy systems maintenance and repair technologies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of theological and ethical frameworks within Mormon thought, focusing on doctrinal texts, sermons, and institutional communications produced by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS) from the mid-19th century to the present. The research problem centers on identifying patterns, conceptual shifts, and sociocultural influences in Mormon theology that are difficult to discern through traditional close-reading methods due to the scale and complexity of the textual corpus. Using natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques, the project will process approximately 500,000 pages of digitized sermons, doctrinal commentaries, and official church publications. Computational methods will include topic modeling to trace thematic developments, sentiment analysis to assess rhetorical tone in doctrinal debates, and network analysis to map relationships between theological concepts and sociopolitical contexts. HPC resources are critical for training transformer-based models (e.g., BERT) fine-tuned on LDS-specific terminology and for handling high-dimensional data across temporal and geographic axes. Expected outcomes include a dynamic visualization platform for exploring theological trends, a publicly accessible annotated corpus of Mormon doctrinal texts, and peer-reviewed analyses of how specific doctrines (e.g., free agency, communal responsibility) have been reinterpreted in response to cultural change. This work will advance interdisciplinary methodologies in digital religious studies by demonstrating how computational tools can uncover latent narratives in religious discourse, offering new insights into the interplay between theology, ethics, and institutional authority in Mormonism.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on beliefs, practices, culture, and history of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormon). Includes instruction in Mormon culture, history, literature, philosophy, sociology, and theology.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of algorithmic bias in U.S. constitutional jurisprudence, particularly within Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment case law. As machine learning systems increasingly inform policing, sentencing, and public policy, legal scholarship lacks a systematic, data-driven framework to evaluate how courts interpret algorithmic outputs in light of constitutional principles like due process and equal protection. The research problem centers on identifying patterns in judicial reasoning—spanning federal and state appellate decisions from 2010 to 2023—that reveal inconsistencies in addressing algorithmic fairness, transparency, and accountability under constitutional standards. Using natural language processing (NLP) models fine-tuned on legal corpora, we will process over 500,000 pages of judicial opinions, briefs, and related legal texts to map doctrinal shifts and latent biases in judicial language. Computational methods include transformer-based semantic clustering to classify reasoning archetypes, graph neural networks to model citation dynamics, and counterfactual simulation to assess how variations in algorithmic evidentiary input might alter case outcomes. The scale and complexity of these tasks require HPC resources for distributed training of domain-specific language models, parallelized legal text annotation, and large-scale graph analysis. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible dataset linking algorithmic bias typologies to constitutional doctrine, a computational framework for simulating judicial responses to emerging technologies, and policy recommendations for standardizing algorithmic accountability in legal proceedings. This work bridges computational legal studies and constitutional theory, offering novel methodologies to address gaps in how interdisciplinary scholarship anticipates the jurisprudential challenges posed by AI-driven governance. By quantifying previously qualitative debates about algorithmic fairness, the project aims to inform judicial education programs, legislative reforms, and ethical AI development within constitutional constraints.
cip_title: American/ US Law/ Legal Studies/ Jurisprudence
cip_definition: An advanced, professional program of the U.S. legal system, Constitution law, and jurisprudence. Includes instruction in legal history, legal sociology, philosophy of law, Constitutional law, legal procedure, and related topics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a digital humanities study examining the formation and evolution of cultural narratives within Polish borderland communities from the late 19th to mid-20th century. The research problem centers on identifying patterns of cultural exchange, linguistic hybridity, and collective memory in digitized archival materials—including personal correspondence, regional periodicals, and community records—produced in historically contested regions such as Galicia and Silesia. Traditional qualitative methods struggle to systematically analyze the scale and complexity of these multilingual, multi-script sources (Polish, Ukrainian, German, Yiddish), which contain overlapping cultural references and fragmented historical contexts. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) tools optimized for historical text analysis, including transformer-based language models fine-tuned on diachronic Polish corpora and custom optical character recognition (OCR) pipelines for handwritten and printed Fraktur scripts. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of over 500,000 digitized pages, training cross-lingual embeddings to trace semantic shifts in identity-related terminology, and network analysis of interpersonal connections across ethnic and religious groups. Expected outcomes include a publicly accessible database of annotated texts, visualizations of cultural convergence/divergence in borderland regions, and quantitative frameworks for assessing the impact of geopolitical upheavals on localized identity constructs. This work will contribute new methodologies to intersectional cultural studies by bridging computational scalability with the interpretive demands of regional historiography, while preserving endangered narratives from marginalized communities. The requested resources are critical to handling memory-intensive NLP tasks, reducing processing times for iterative model training, and managing large-scale data storage for collaborative access by international scholars in Polish Studies.
major_field: Area, ethnic, cultural, gender, and group studies
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the history, society, politics, culture, and economics of Poland and the current and historical inhabitants of the Polish lands, including borderlands, from earliest times to the present.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of detecting precancerous and malignant cellular abnormalities in cytopathology, addressing critical challenges in manual screening processes. While cytotechnologists are trained to identify subtle cellular changes through microscopy, increasing sample volumes, diagnostic complexity, and inter-observer variability underscore the need for scalable, AI-driven decision-support tools. The research will focus on creating deep learning models trained on high-resolution whole-slide cytology images—spanning cervical, thyroid, and respiratory specimens—to classify cellular atypia, prioritize high-risk cases, and reduce false negatives. The computational approach involves multi-stage convolutional neural networks (CNNs) optimized for segmenting cellular structures, quantifying nuclear features (e.g., chromatin distribution, nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios), and integrating contextual spatial data across slides. Due to the terabyte-scale imaging data and the need for hyperparameter optimization, high-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage distributed training, validate models against histopathology-confirmed outcomes, and ensure robustness across diverse demographic cohorts. The project will leverage GPU-accelerated nodes for parallel processing of 3D cellular clusters and probabilistic uncertainty estimation to flag low-confidence predictions for expert review. Outcomes include open-source model architectures tailored for cytotechnological applications, benchmarks for AI-assisted screening accuracy, and protocols for human-AI collaboration in diagnostic workflows. By augmenting cytotechnologists’ expertise with computational tools, this work aims to improve early cancer detection rates, reduce diagnostic turnaround times, and establish reproducible standards for integrating machine learning into cytopathology education and practice. The requested HPC allocation will directly support data-intensive tasks, including image preprocessing, model training, and validation against multi-institutional datasets, ensuring clinical relevance and scalability.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to work with pathologists to detect changes in body cells that may indicate, and permit diagnosis of, the early development of cancers and other diseases. Includes instruction in biochemistry, microbiology, applied mathematics, microscopy, slide preparation, identification of cellular structures and abnormalities, and laboratory procedures and safety.

abstract: The proposed research seeks to advance understanding of the dynamics and ecological impacts of concurrent ocean acidification and hypoxia in coastal and open-ocean systems under climate change. These co-occurring stressors threaten marine biodiversity, fisheries, and biogeochemical cycles, yet their interactions and feedbacks remain poorly resolved at regional scales. To address this gap, we propose a high-resolution, three-dimensional modeling framework that integrates physical circulation, biogeochemical cycling, and species-level physiological responses. The project will employ the Regional Ocean Modeling System (ROMS) coupled with a customized biogeochemical module incorporating carbonate chemistry dynamics, oxygen transport, and metabolic responses of key taxa. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve fine-scale processes (1-5 km resolution) across decadal timescales, including upwelling events, mesoscale eddies, and benthic-pelagic coupling. Ensemble simulations will assess uncertainty under multiple climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP3-7.0, SSP5-8.5), requiring ~2 million core-hours to complete. Machine learning techniques will be applied to optimize parameterizations and analyze petabyte-scale output. Expected outcomes include predictive maps of acidification-hypoxia hotspots, thresholds for ecological tipping points in commercially important species, and quantification of feedbacks between deoxygenation and carbon export. Results will directly inform marine spatial planning and adaptive management strategies for climate-resilient fisheries. The computational framework will be openly shared as a community resource for regional climate-impact projections. This work addresses priorities outlined in the UN Decade of Ocean Science and contributes to IPCC assessments, while pushing the limits of marine predictive modeling through innovative coupling of physical, chemical, and biological processes at previously unachievable resolutions.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in the ocean/marine sciences, not elsewhere classified.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the structural and behavioral impacts of complex tax code provisions on compliance strategies and economic decision-making. Contemporary tax systems, particularly in the U.S., are characterized by multilayered statutes, administrative rulings, and judicial interpretations that create dynamic interactions between legal constraints, taxpayer behavior, and macroeconomic outcomes. Traditional legal analysis and econometric modeling often fail to capture the nonlinear feedback loops and scalability challenges inherent in these systems. To address this gap, the research employs agent-based modeling (ABM) frameworks to simulate taxpayer decision-making under varying regulatory scenarios, integrating granular tax code data, historical audit outcomes, and socioeconomic variables. Computational legal parsing tools will preprocess tax statutes and case law into machine-readable rule sets, while HPC resources will enable large-scale parallelized simulations across diverse demographic and economic agent profiles. The project further applies graph-based algorithms to map interdependencies between tax provisions, identifying systemic vulnerabilities to strategic avoidance or unintended fiscal consequences. Expected outcomes include predictive models quantifying how specific code amendments might influence compliance rates, revenue projections, and distributional equity at scale. These insights aim to provide policymakers with evidence-based tools to evaluate trade-offs between tax complexity, enforcement efficiency, and economic growth. By bridging computational modeling and legal analysis, this work establishes a methodological foundation for simulating emergent behaviors in regulatory ecosystems, advancing tax law scholarship beyond doctrinal or case-study approaches into data-driven, systems-oriented inquiry.
cip_definition: An advanced, professional study of tax law and taxation procedures in U.S. or Canadian jurisdictions affecting individuals and corporations.

abstract: Prostate cancer remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in urology, with significant variability in treatment response driven by molecular heterogeneity. Current clinical tools lack the precision to predict individualized outcomes or optimize therapy selection, particularly for advanced or resistant cases. This project seeks to address this gap by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to integrate multi-modal data—including genomic, transcriptomic, radiomic, and longitudinal clinical records—into predictive models of disease progression and therapeutic efficacy. The computational approach will focus on developing machine learning algorithms to identify biomarkers of treatment resistance and simulate tumor-immune interactions under varying therapeutic conditions. Bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data from institutional cohorts and public repositories (e.g., TCGA) will be processed using scalable bioinformatics pipelines to characterize tumor microenvironment dynamics. Concurrently, deep learning architectures will analyze multiparametric MRI and histopathology images to extract spatial features correlating with genomic subtypes. Agent-based modeling, implemented via parallelized simulations, will explore clonal evolution and immune checkpoint inhibitor responses. These computationally intensive tasks require HPC resources for efficient handling of large datasets (>100 TB), hyperparameter optimization of neural networks, and real-time visualization of simulation outputs. Expected outcomes include the identification of novel composite biomarkers for risk stratification, predictive models to guide radiotherapy and systemic therapy choices, and mechanistic insights into resistance pathways. By translating these findings into clinical decision-support tools, this work aims to advance precision urologic oncology, reduce overtreatment, and improve survival rates for high-risk patients. The scalability of the computational framework will also enable future adaptation to other urologic malignancies, such as bladder and kidney cancers.
cip_definition: Research focused on Urology

abstract: This project seeks to address the computational challenges inherent in solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) arising in quantum dynamical systems, where traditional numerical methods fail due to exponential scaling with dimensionality. Current approaches, such as finite element or spectral methods, become intractable beyond moderate dimensions, limiting progress in understanding complex quantum phenomena. To overcome this, we propose a novel hybrid algorithm combining stochastic gradient descent with adaptive sparse grid collocation, designed to exploit low-rank structures in solution manifolds while mitigating the curse of dimensionality. The method integrates deterministic solvers for localized features and probabilistic sampling for global behavior, enabling scalable approximations in phase space. Implementing this framework requires high-performance computing (HPC) resources due to the iterative nature of the algorithm, the need for parallelized linear algebra operations on distributed sparse matrices, and large-scale parameter optimization. Key computational steps include GPU-accelerated tensor decomposition, dynamic load balancing for irregular grid refinements, and ensemble simulations to quantify numerical uncertainty. The project will leverage MPI for inter-node communication and CUDA for fine-grained parallelism, with validation against exact solutions in lower dimensions and benchmark quantum systems. Successful implementation will yield a publicly available software toolkit for high-dimensional PDEs, advancing mathematical tools for quantum mechanics and nonlinear wave propagation. Outcomes will demonstrate the feasibility of resolving 8-10 dimensional quantum systems with sub-exponential computational costs, providing a pathway to study entanglement dynamics and decoherence in scalable settings. This work bridges theoretical numerical analysis and practical HPC innovations, offering broadly applicable strategies for dimensionality reduction in computational mathematics.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of theoretical and applied mathematics to the solution of functional problems. Includes instruction in numerical analysis, numerical statistics, optimization, operational research, signal analysis, wavelets, image processing, fuzzy sets, spline, stochastic analysis, integral equations, differential equations, and partial differential equations.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate dysregulated subcellular communication mechanisms that drive cancer cell adaptation to metabolic stress, with a focus on ion channel-transporter networks and endocrine signaling crosstalk in tumor microenvironments. Despite advances in characterizing molecular physiology of cancer, predictive models of how dynamic ion gradients and hormonal signals jointly regulate malignant cell survival remain underdeveloped due to computational limitations in simulating multi-scale interactions. We propose to develop a high-performance computing (HPC) framework integrating stochastic modeling of calcium-regulated transport proteins with continuum-scale simulations of paracrine/autocrine signaling dynamics. The computational workflow will parameterize models using existing experimental datasets from pancreatic cancer models, including single-channel electrophysiology recordings and spatiotemporal hormone release profiles. Machine learning approaches will optimize parameter space exploration across interdependent timescales (nanosecond ion channel gating to minute-range secretory events). Key deliverables include: 1) A novel multi-algorithm simulation platform coupling Brownian dynamics for membrane proteins with reaction-diffusion models for extracellular signaling molecules; 2) Predictive maps of stress-induced signaling hotspots where ion flux modulates endocrine feedback loops; 3) Identification of targetable network motifs governing cancer cell osmotic regulation. The HPC resources are essential for managing the combinatorial complexity of 10^6 simulated ion channels interacting with 3D diffusible ligand fields across millimeter-scale tumor regions. Expected outcomes include fundamental insights into how subcellular transport systems enable cancer progression through physiological plasticity, with direct implications for disrupting pro-survival signaling architectures. This computational infrastructure will establish a scalable platform for investigating molecular control systems across multiple solid tumor types, advancing precision oncology strategies grounded in physiological network modulation.
detailed_field: Physiology, oncology, and cancer biology nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of dynamic interactive processes and biochemical communications at the subcellular level. Includes instruction in ion channels and transporters, molecular signaling pathways, endocrine control and regulation, genetic information transfer, homeostasis and molecular control systems, electrophysiology and sensory mechanisms, protein synthesis, and applicable research methods and technologies.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the development of real-time, interactive 3D visualization tools for complex cellular and molecular processes, with applications in medical education, surgical planning, and biomedical research. Medical illustrators face significant challenges in accurately modeling dynamic biological systems—such as protein interactions, intracellular signaling cascades, or viral replication cycles—due to the computational intensity of rendering high-resolution, time-dependent datasets. Existing tools often rely on static or oversimplified representations, limiting their utility for conveying nuanced physiological or pathological mechanisms. To address this gap, we propose a computational workflow integrating cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) data, molecular dynamics simulations, and machine learning-driven predictive modeling to generate interactive, multi-scale visualizations. The project will utilize HPC clusters to parallelize three core tasks: (1) processing terabyte-scale cryo-EM datasets to reconstruct time-resolved 3D structures, (2) simulating molecular interactions at physiologically relevant timescales using GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics frameworks, and (3) training generative models to predict and visualize intermediate states not directly captured by experimental data. These components will be unified through a custom visualization engine optimized for real-time rendering of adaptive meshes and particle systems. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible library of dynamic anatomical models and an open-source pipeline for converting heterogeneous biomedical data into interactive educational and research assets. By enabling medical illustrators to create more accurate, data-driven visualizations, this work aims to enhance comprehension of complex biological systems for diverse audiences, from medical students to research scientists. The HPC infrastructure is critical due to the iterative nature of model refinement, the need for rapid parameter space exploration, and the computational demands of coupling simulation outputs with real-time rendering requirements.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply the principles and techniques of art and computer-assisted imaging, graphics, and animation to create visual materials to facilitate the recording and dissemination of biomedical knowledge for educational, research, and clinical purposes. Includes instruction in anatomy, physiology, pathology, histology, embryology, neuroanatomy, medical terminology, artistic media and techniques, illustration techniques, three-dimensional modeling, prosthetics, data display design, exhibit design and production, medical photography, multimedia, computer graphics and animation, digital imaging, business management, production technology, and instructional design.

abstract: This project seeks to address critical gaps in medication-use safety by leveraging advanced computational methods to model and predict adverse drug events (ADEs) and optimize therapeutic decision-making. Despite rigorous clinical testing, ADEs remain a leading cause of hospitalizations and healthcare costs, often arising from complex interactions between patient-specific factors (e.g., genetics, comorbidities, polypharmacy) and drug properties. Traditional pharmacovigilance tools struggle to analyze these multidimensional datasets at scale, limiting proactive risk mitigation. To overcome this, we propose a machine learning framework integrating electronic health records (EHRs), genomic data, and pharmacological databases to identify high-risk medication regimens and patient subgroups. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to process and harmonize heterogeneous datasets spanning millions of patient encounters, model nonlinear drug interaction effects using deep neural networks, and conduct large-scale simulations of drug response variability. Key computational steps include federated learning to preserve patient privacy across institutions, ensemble methods to reduce prediction bias, and graph-based algorithms to map drug-disease-gene networks. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models for ADE risk stratification validated across diverse populations, (2) actionable insights into modifiable risk factors for high-priority drug classes, and (3) an open-source computational toolkit for real-time medication safety monitoring. By enabling rapid analysis of complex interactions at unprecedented scale, this work will advance personalized therapeutic strategies and inform clinical decision support systems, directly aligning with national priorities to reduce preventable medication-related harm. The requested HPC infrastructure will support GPU-accelerated model training, secure data storage, and parallelized simulations, which are computationally infeasible with local resources.
cip_definition: Research focused on Medication-Use Safety

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the historical and contemporary linguistic evolution of regional Spanish and Portuguese dialects across Latin America, with a focus on understudied contact zones between Indigenous, African, and European language traditions. The research addresses a critical gap in Hispanic and Lusophone linguistics: the lack of large-scale, computationally intensive studies examining how syntactic, phonetic, and lexical features develop in multilingual contexts over time. Current methodologies struggle to process the complex interplay of sociolinguistic variables in terabyte-scale corpora spanning four centuries of texts, oral histories, and modern speech recordings. Our team proposes a hybrid computational approach combining neural language models fine-tuned on historical texts, phonetic alignment algorithms optimized for non-European sound systems, and agent-based simulations of language contact scenarios. The HPC infrastructure will enable parallel processing of 19th-century manuscript scans through optical character recognition (OCR) pipelines, acoustic analysis of endangered language recordings from the Amazon and Andes regions, and comparative syntax modeling across 30+ dialectal variants. Expected outcomes include the first diachronic map of grammatical convergence patterns in Ibero-American creoles, a publicly accessible database of annotated speech features linked to sociocultural metadata, and predictive models of language shift in marginalized communities. This work will directly support preservation initiatives for Afro-Bolivian Spanish and Brazilian Vernacular Portuguese while advancing computational methods for low-resource language analysis. The requested resources—particularly GPU nodes for transformer model training and high-memory nodes for corpus linguistics workflows—are essential to handle the project’s unique requirements in processing heterogeneous, multilingual data at unprecedented scale. Results will be disseminated through the open-source LinguaConnect toolkit, designed specifically for Hispanic and Lusophone linguistic research.
detailed_field: Hispanic/ Latin American languages, literatures, and linguistics
cip_title: Hispanic and Latin American Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, General
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the languages and literatures of the Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking areas of the world, including the Iberian, Latin American, and Lusophone worlds. Includes instruction in Spanish and Portuguese language and linguistics; regional and Latin American dialects; and Spanish, Portuguese, Spanish American, Luso-Brazilian, and Chicano literature.

abstract: The fashion industry faces mounting pressure to balance rapid innovation with sustainable practices, yet current computational tools struggle to address the complexity of integrating real-time consumer trends, material science, and ethical production workflows. This project seeks to develop an AI-driven framework for dynamic apparel design that minimizes waste while adapting to evolving market preferences. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) to enable large-scale simulations of biodegradable and recyclable textile behavior under diverse environmental conditions, coupled with generative adversarial networks (GANs) to synthesize region-specific style trends from global social media and e-commerce datasets. Additionally, reinforcement learning algorithms will optimize cutting patterns and supply chain logistics to reduce overproduction. Computational challenges include resolving high-resolution, non-linear fabric deformation models in multi-physics environments and training spatially aware GANs on terabyte-scale visual datasets. By parallelizing finite element analysis across GPU clusters and implementing distributed training protocols for heterogeneous data streams, the project aims to achieve near-real-time feedback loops between design iteration, material testing, and production planning. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for sustainable virtual prototyping, predictive metrics for regional trend forecasting, and a scalable digital twin framework to simulate garment lifecycles from design to disposal. This work will provide apparel designers with data-driven strategies to lower carbon footprints while maintaining creative agility, bridging gaps between aesthetic experimentation, technical constraints, and ecological accountability in fashion education and industry practice.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply artistic principles and techniques to the professional design of commercial fashions, apparel, and accessories, and the management of fashion development projects. Includes instruction in apparel design; accessory design; the design of men's', women's', and children's' wear; flat pattern design; computer-assisted design and manufacturing; concept planning; designing in specific materials; labor and cost analysis; history of fashion; fabric art and printing; and the principles of management and operations in the fashion industry.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance the computational analysis of Punjabi dialects and literary texts, addressing critical gaps in digital scholarship for this linguistically diverse yet under-resourced language. The research problem centers on the lack of large-scale, systematic studies of Punjabi’s regional variations, historical evolution, and syntactic structures, which are essential for preserving endangered dialects, improving language technologies, and informing pedagogical tools. Current limitations stem from fragmented digital corpora, the computational complexity of processing Punjabi’s dual scripts (Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi), and the need for scalable models to analyze morphosyntactic patterns across millions of tokens. To address this, we propose a multi-phase computational approach. First, we will aggregate and preprocess a corpus of digitized Punjabi texts, oral histories, and contemporary media (≈10 TB), employing parallelized workflows to normalize orthographic variations and align cross-dialectal data. Next, we will train transformer-based models for dialect classification and philological annotation, utilizing GPU-accelerated fine-tuning to handle Punjabi’s agglutinative morphology and code-switching tendencies. Finally, network analysis algorithms will map semantic shifts and syntactic innovations across temporal, geographic, and sociolinguistic dimensions. The scale of data and complexity of modeling—particularly for real-time processing of under-documented dialects like Majhi and Malwai—necessitate HPC infrastructure for distributed storage, multi-node training, and high-throughput validation. Anticipated outcomes include the first open-access computational toolkit for Punjabi dialectology, an annotated multilingual corpus with diachronic metadata, and probabilistic models of syntactic change applicable to low-resource language contexts. These resources will directly support endangered language revitalization initiatives, enhance machine translation systems for Punjabi, and provide humanities scholars with quantitative frameworks to interrogate literary trends. By integrating computational linguistics with Punjabi philology, this project aims to establish a replicable paradigm for studying linguistic diversity within high-performance computing environments.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Punjabi language (Punjabi) and related dialects. Includes instruction in philology; dialects; and applications in business, science/technology, and other settings.

abstract: This research project seeks to employ high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the semantic and structural evolution of ethical frameworks within biblical texts, integrating computational linguistics with theological hermeneutics. While traditional biblical scholarship has relied on close reading and comparative analysis, the scale and complexity of textual variants, intertextual references, and ancient Near Eastern contextual parallels necessitate advanced computational methods. The research problem centers on identifying and modeling patterns in moral reasoning across canonical and non-canonical texts, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, Septuagint, and early Christian writings, to trace how ethical concepts (e.g., justice, covenant, mercy) were reinterpreted in response to socio-political shifts. A multi-layered computational approach will be implemented: natural language processing (NLP) pipelines will parse morphosyntactic features and semantic roles in original languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Greek), while graph-based network analysis will map conceptual linkages across texts and temporal layers. Machine learning models, trained on annotated theological corpora, will classify ethical arguments and simulate their hypothetical development under varying historical scenarios. HPC resources are critical for handling the heterogeneous dataset (over 50,000 digitized manuscript fragments and multilingual secondary literature) and running iterative simulations of textual-interpretive trajectories. Expected outcomes include a dynamic, open-access database of ethical concept networks, quantitative models of doctrinal adaptation, and methodological frameworks for computational theological analysis. This project bridges gaps between digital humanities and religious studies, offering scalable tools to address longstanding questions about the interplay between textual transmission and ethical thought while establishing a precedent for HPC-driven research in specialized hermeneutical domains.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Christian and/or Jewish Bible and related literature, with an emphasis on understanding and interpreting the theological, doctrinal, and ethical messages contained therein. May include preparation for applying these studies in various religious vocations.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the sociolinguistic and cultural dynamics of missionary-mediated communication networks across Indigenous communities in the Amazon Basin (1850–1950). Missionary archives from this period contain vast, untapped multilingual corpora—including journals, transcribed oral narratives, lexicons, and educational materials—that reflect complex intercultural exchanges. However, the scale, linguistic diversity, and non-standardized orthographies of these materials pose significant challenges for traditional humanities methodologies. The project addresses this gap by developing computational workflows to 1) process and align digitized texts in Spanish, Portuguese, and 12 Indigenous languages using transformer-based NLP models fine-tuned for low-resource languages; 2) reconstruct semantic networks to trace conceptual shifts in key domains (e.g., kinship, ecology, spirituality); and 3) map spatiotemporal patterns of lexical borrowing and translation strategies through GIS-integrated network analysis. HPC resources are critical for training custom tokenizers, optimizing OCR correction for archival manuscripts, and running large-scale semantic similarity calculations across 15+ language pairs. Expected outcomes include an open-access digital repository of annotated texts, interactive visualizations of contact-induced language change, and computational models quantifying the relationship between missionary literacy practices and Indigenous knowledge preservation. By bridging computational linguistics, anthropology, and mission studies, this work will provide new methodologies for analyzing asymmetrical cultural encounters in colonial contexts while advancing ethical frameworks for applying AI/ML tools to Indigenous language materials. The project’s computational outputs will directly inform contemporary debates in heritage language revitalization initiatives led by descendant communities.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the theory and practice of religious outreach, social service and proselytization, and that prepares individuals for mission vocations. Includes instruction in theology, evangelism, preaching, medical and social mission work, missionary education, missionary aviation, emergency services, legal and political aspects of working in other countries, and preparation for ordination as missionaries.

abstract: Surgical wound healing and reconstruction outcomes are influenced by complex interactions between biomechanical forces, tissue properties, and patient-specific factors such as comorbidities. Current clinical approaches to predicting complications (e.g., dehiscence, infection) or optimizing reconstructive techniques rely on generalized guidelines, which often fail to account for multidimensional variability in patient physiology and surgical scenarios. This project seeks to develop patient-specific computational models to predict biomechanical stress distributions in surgical wounds and reconstructed tissues, enabling data-driven decision support for surgeons. We propose a multi-scale computational framework integrating finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) to simulate tissue response under dynamic physiological loads. High-resolution imaging data from clinical cohorts (CT, MRI, intraoperative 3D scans) will inform anatomically accurate FEA models of wound geometry and layered tissue mechanics. CFD simulations will evaluate perfusion dynamics at incision margins, while ML algorithms trained on retrospective electronic health record data will incorporate patient risk factors into predictive outputs. The computational pipeline requires high-performance computing (HPC) resources to manage iterative simulations across parameter spaces, including hyperelastic material modeling of heterogeneous tissues, transient load conditions, and sensitivity analyses.
