The research will integrate multi-modal datasets, including high-resolution cardiac MRI/CT imaging, electronic health records (EHR), and longitudinal genomic data, to characterize hemodynamic and molecular factors influencing surgical success and cardiac remodeling. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations will model blood flow dynamics in 3D-reconstructed patient cardiac geometries, while machine learning pipelines will analyze heterogeneous clinical and omics data to identify prognostic biomarkers. The HPC environment is critical for handling the computational intensity of large-scale simulations, parallel processing of imaging datasets (>10,000 high-resolution images), and training deep learning models on multi-terabyte EHR repositories. Expected outcomes include the development of a validated computational framework for predicting postoperative complications (e.g., right ventricular failure in tetralogy of Fallot repairs) and optimizing surgical intervention timing in CHDs. This work will also establish open-source tools for pediatric cardiac simulation, enabling reproducible hemodynamic analysis across institutions. By advancing precision medicine in pediatric cardiology, the project aims to reduce reoperation rates, improve long-term functional outcomes, and inform risk-stratified follow-up protocols. The computational infrastructure will additionally support future investigations into population-level trends through integration with public health databases, bridging gaps between individualized care and community health strategies.
cip_definition: Research focused on the diagnosis and management of diseases and disorders of the cardiovascular and cardiopulmonary systems of infants, children, and adolescents. May include related research in public health and community medicine issues.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance data-driven decision-making in sport facility optimization, an emerging interdisciplinary niche within Sport and Fitness Administration. Modern sports organizations face complex challenges in balancing operational efficiency, financial sustainability, and user experience across dynamic, large-scale facilities. Traditional analytical tools often fail to integrate real-time data streams—such as crowd movement, revenue flow, and facility wear-and-tear—into cohesive models for adaptive management. This research proposes the development of a computational framework to simulate multi-variable scenarios, including event scheduling, resource allocation, and emergency egress protocols, under fluctuating conditions (e.g., attendance variability, equipment failures). The framework will employ agent-based modeling to simulate patron behavior, Monte Carlo methods to quantify financial and operational risks, and machine learning to optimize maintenance schedules based on sensor-derived facility usage data. By parallelizing these computationally intensive tasks, HPC resources will enable granular, venue-specific simulations at scale, accounting for interactions between thousands of agents (patrons, staff, equipment) and environmental variables. Expected outcomes include predictive tools to minimize operational costs while maximizing safety and revenue, as well as generalized protocols for adaptive facility management. This work bridges gaps between sports management theory and computational systems engineering, offering novel methodologies for an industry increasingly reliant on real-time data. The resulting models will be validated against datasets from collegiate athletic complexes, with scalability tested for professional arenas. By integrating HPC-driven insights into sport administration practices, this project aims to establish a replicable paradigm for evidence-based facility management in non-STEM domains.
detailed_field: Parks, recreation, leisure, fitness, and sport studies and management
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply business, coaching and physical education principles to the organization, administration and management of athletic programs and teams, fitness/rehabilitation facilities and health clubs, sport recreation services, and related services. Includes instruction in program planning and development; business and financial management principles; sales, marketing and recruitment; event promotion, scheduling and management; facilities management; public relations; legal aspects of sports; and applicable health and safety standards.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance a large-scale textual analysis study examining how writers adapt compositional strategies across genres, media, and cultural contexts. While traditional writing studies rely on manual close reading or small-sample qualitative methods, this research addresses the challenge of systematically analyzing stylistic, rhetorical, and linguistic patterns in heterogeneous digital writing corpora spanning professional, academic, and public domains. The computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning techniques to model compositional features—such as syntactic complexity, multimodal integration, audience adaptation markers, and genre-specific discourse structures—across millions of documents. Key tasks include training transformer-based models on domain-specific writing samples, conducting cross-corpus rhetorical analysis via graph-based representation learning, and simulating audience reception through agent-based modeling. HPC resources are critical for processing terabytes of text and multimedia data, running parallelized feature extraction pipelines, and iteratively refining computational models that account for the dynamic interplay between writerly choices and contextual constraints. Anticipated outcomes include 1) scalable frameworks for mapping writing practices in digitally mediated environments, 2) open-access tools to support adaptive writing pedagogy through data-driven genre analysis, and 3) theoretical contributions to understanding how emerging writing technologies reshape compositional processes. By bridging computational methods with writing studies’ humanistic foundations, this project aims to provide novel insights into the sociotechnical dimensions of contemporary writing while demonstrating how HPC can expand the scale and precision of textual research in the humanities.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on writing for applied and liberal arts purposes. Includes instruction in writing and document design in multiple genres, modes, and media; writing technologies; research, evaluation, and use of information; editing and publishing; theories and processes of composing; rhetorical theories, traditions, and analysis; communication across audiences, contexts, and cultures; and practical applications for professional, technical, organizational, academic, and public settings.

abstract: The increasing complexity of air traffic management systems, driven by rising global air traffic volumes and the integration of autonomous aircraft, demands advanced computational tools to ensure safety, efficiency, and scalability. Current air traffic control (ATC) simulations and decision-support systems often rely on simplified models that fail to capture the dynamic, high-dimensional interactions between aircraft, weather systems, and human operators in real time. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing a high-fidelity, multi-agent simulation framework capable of modeling large-scale air traffic scenarios with unprecedented granularity. The research will leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to simulate thousands of concurrent aircraft trajectories, integrating real-time radar data, stochastic weather models, and machine learning-driven predictions of pilot and controller behavior. Key computational challenges include optimizing parallelized airspace conflict detection algorithms, scaling neural networks for predictive anomaly detection, and validating simulations against historical FAA incident datasets. The proposed framework will employ a hybrid approach, combining agent-based modeling for aircraft interactions, computational fluid dynamics for localized weather impacts, and reinforcement learning to iteratively improve traffic flow management policies. Outcomes will include open-source tools for dynamic airspace reconfiguration, risk-aware controller decision support, and capacity planning under uncertainty. By enabling hyper-realistic scenario testing, this work aims to reduce operational delays, mitigate mid-air collision risks, and inform next-generation ATC training protocols. The computational demands of this project—particularly the need for rapid, large-scale simulations with low-latency data assimilation—necessitate access to HPC infrastructure with GPU-accelerated nodes and high-memory bandwidth. Successful implementation will provide a foundation for scalable, adaptive ATC systems capable of supporting emerging aviation technologies while maintaining stringent safety standards.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to air-traffic management and control, usually with additional training at the FAA Flight Control Center in a cooperative education program. Includes instruction in flight control, the use of radar and electronic scanning devices, plotting of flights, radio communication, interpretation of weather conditions affecting flights, flight instrumentation used by pilots, and maintenance of flight-control center or control-tower log books.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance predictive modeling and simulation capabilities in autobody repair and collision analysis, addressing critical gaps in real-world damage assessment and repair optimization. Current methods for evaluating structural integrity, material behavior under stress, and refinishing outcomes rely heavily on physical testing, which is time-intensive, costly, and limited in scalability. The research problem centers on developing computational models to simulate collision dynamics, composite material responses, and paint adhesion properties under diverse environmental and mechanical conditions. These models will integrate finite element analysis (FEA) for structural deformation, molecular dynamics to study adhesive and plastic polymer interactions, and machine learning algorithms trained on empirical repair data to predict optimal repair pathways. By parallelizing these workflows on HPC clusters, the project aims to resolve multi-scale, multi-physics challenges—such as micro-crack propagation in coatings or heat-affected zones in welded repairs—at resolutions impractical for local computational resources. Anticipated outcomes include a publicly accessible simulation toolkit for educators and technicians, enabling virtual training scenarios and damage diagnostics. Additionally, the project will generate material-specific failure thresholds and refinishing guidelines to improve repair accuracy and reduce resource waste. This work aligns with industry demands for data-driven repair standards and supports curricular modernization in collision repair programs by introducing computational literacy into technical training. The requested HPC allocation will directly enable large parameter sweeps, validation against experimental datasets, and real-time visualization of repair processes, fostering innovation in a field traditionally reliant on manual expertise.
cip_title: Autobody/ Collision and Repair Technology/ Technician
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to repair, reconstruct and finish automobile bodies, fenders, and external features. Includes instruction in structure analysis, damage repair, non-structural analysis, mechanical and electrical components, plastics and adhesives, painting and refinishing techniques, and damage analysis and estimating.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in traditional printing press operations, such as material waste, inconsistent color calibration, and mechanical wear, by developing computational models to simulate and optimize press performance. Despite advances in digital printing, analog press systems remain critical for specialized applications, yet their operation relies heavily on manual adjustments and trial-and-error workflows. This research proposes leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to create high-fidelity simulations of press mechanics, ink dispersion dynamics, and substrate interactions under varying operational conditions. Using finite element analysis (FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and machine learning (ML) techniques, the project will model stress distributions in press components, predict ink transfer efficiency across substrates, and identify optimal pressure-temperature settings for diverse materials. Sensor data from operational presses will be integrated to train ML algorithms for real-time anomaly detection and predictive maintenance. The simulations will account for stochastic variables such as humidity, paper texture, and ink viscosity, enabling probabilistic optimization of press configurations. Expected outcomes include predictive models to minimize waste during setup, a framework for adaptive calibration, and recommendations to extend machinery lifespan. By translating these computational insights into operator-friendly guidelines, the project aims to bridge theoretical models with practical workflows, reducing resource consumption and improving reproducibility in print media production. The use of HPC is critical due to the need for parallel processing of multi-physics simulations and large datasets from high-resolution press sensors. This work will enhance technical training in printing press operations by introducing data-driven decision-making tools, while contributing to sustainability goals in the communication and journalism sectors through optimized resource use.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to set up, operate, and maintain printing presses.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in the analysis of large-scale, multilingual translation corpora within Translation Studies. While the field has traditionally relied on qualitative methods to examine translation practices, the increasing digitization of historical texts, audiovisual media, and institutional archives demands scalable computational tools to analyze patterns across languages, time periods, and cultural contexts. The research problem centers on identifying systemic biases, stylistic shifts, and sociocultural influences in translated works—tasks that require processing terabytes of text, audio, and visual data spanning diverse linguistic systems. The proposed computational approach integrates natural language processing (NLP) models, unsupervised clustering algorithms, and network analysis to map translation norms, track lexical evolution, and model the diffusion of translated content across geopolitical boundaries. Custom pipelines will be developed to preprocess heterogeneous data (e.g., parallel texts, translator metadata, paratextual commentaries) while preserving contextual nuances critical to interdisciplinary analysis. GPU-accelerated transformer models will fine-tune multilingual embeddings to detect subtle pragmatic variations in literary and technical translations. Concurrently, agent-based simulations will model how institutional policies and cultural hierarchies shape translation workflows. Anticipated outcomes include a scalable framework for diachronic and synchronic translation analysis, open-access tools for corpus-based translation studies, and novel insights into how power dynamics manifest in cross-linguistic mediation. By enabling the processing of previously intractable datasets, this project aims to advance empirical methodologies in Translation Studies while fostering interdisciplinary dialogue with computational linguistics and digital humanities. The requested HPC resources are essential to handle memory-intensive tasks, including training domain-specific language models and conducting large-scale comparative analyses across 50+ language pairs, ultimately contributing to a more robust, data-driven understanding of translation as a sociocultural practice.
cip_definition: A multidisciplinary program that prepares individuals to explore the historical, social, institutional and cultural facets of translation. Includes instruction in general and literary translation, business translation, technical translation, and other specific applications of linguistic skills.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance interdisciplinary research on cultural and intellectual exchange across medieval and Renaissance Europe through the computational analysis of fragmented historical datasets. Traditional scholarship in this domain has been constrained by the manual processing of disparate sources—including digitized manuscripts, archival records, art inventories, and archaeological reports—limiting the scale at which patterns of transmission can be identified. The proposed research will integrate natural language processing (NLP), network analysis, and machine learning to systematically analyze multilingual textual corpora, artistic iconography, and material culture data spanning the 12th to 16th centuries. Key objectives include modeling the diffusion of literary motifs, reconstructing trade and pilgrimage routes using geospatial datasets, and identifying socio-cultural hubs through dynamic network simulations. HPC resources are critical to process terabytes of high-resolution manuscript images, optimize OCR accuracy for archaic scripts, and train neural networks to detect stylistic correlations in art and architecture. Expected outcomes include an open-access digital repository of annotated datasets, interactive maps visualizing transnational exchange networks, and computational models that quantify the impact of specific institutions (e.g., monastic scriptoria, merchant guilds) on cultural dissemination. By bridging gaps between textual, artistic, and archaeological evidence, this project aims to reveal previously unrecognized pathways of influence, enriching scholarly debates on regional identity formation and the transmission of knowledge. The tools and methodologies developed will establish a scalable framework for computational humanities research, enabling future studies to interrogate large, heterogeneous datasets with greater precision. This work underscores the transformative potential of HPC in addressing complex historical questions that transcend disciplinary boundaries.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the study of the Medieval and/or Renaissance periods in European and circum-Mediterranean history from the perspective of various disciplines in the humanities and social sciences, including history and archeology, as well as studies of period art and music.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in the evolving publishing industry, specifically the optimization of digital content dissemination and the ethical implications of algorithmic decision-making in publishing workflows. As the industry shifts toward data-driven strategies for audience engagement, publishers face challenges in balancing efficiency, profitability, and ethical standards—particularly when deploying automated tools for content recommendation, rights management, and market analytics. Current methods for analyzing reader behavior, copyright compliance, and cross-platform content performance rely on fragmented datasets and simplistic models, limiting their scalability and accuracy. This research proposes a computational framework to model large-scale publishing ecosystems, integrating heterogeneous data sources (e.g., sales metrics, social media interactions, digital rights registries) with machine learning (ML) and natural language processing (NLP) techniques. Key tasks include training transformer-based models to predict content viability across demographics, simulating the impact of algorithmic bias in recommendation systems, and developing graph-based networks to trace copyright infringement patterns in digital publications. The scale of data—spanning millions of texts, user interactions, and historical publishing records—necessitates HPC resources for distributed processing, GPU-accelerated model training, and real-time simulations. Expected outcomes include (1) a scalable pipeline for ethical auditing of AI-driven publishing tools, (2) predictive models to prioritize culturally inclusive content distribution, and (3) open-access datasets annotated with copyright and ethical risk metrics. By providing actionable insights into the computational governance of publishing workflows, this project aims to bridge gaps between technological innovation and industry accountability, offering tools that align commercial objectives with professional standards in communication and journalism. The results will directly inform curriculum development for digital publishing programs and provide a replicable framework for small-to-midsize publishers lacking in-house technical capacity.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the process of managing the creation, publication, and distribution of print and electronic books and other text products and prepares individuals to manage the editorial, technical, and business aspects of publishing operations. Includes instruction in product planning and design, editing, author relations, business and copyright law, publishing industry operations, contracting and purchasing, product marketing, electronic publishing and commerce, history of publishing, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: Mind-body therapies such as yoga, tai chi, and somatic movement practices are increasingly recognized for their benefits in managing chronic pain, stress, and neurological disorders. However, the underlying neurophysiological and biomechanical mechanisms remain poorly understood, partly due to the complexity of integrating multimodal data streams across temporal and spatial scales. This project seeks to address this gap by developing a computational framework to model the dynamic interactions between neural activity, musculoskeletal kinematics, and autonomic responses during mind-body interventions. The research will leverage high-performance computing resources to process and analyze large datasets, including high-resolution functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), motion capture kinematics, electromyography (EMG), and heart rate variability (HRV) metrics. Computational methods will involve multilevel Bayesian modeling to infer causal pathways between cognitive-affective states and biomechanical outputs, alongside deep learning architectures for pattern recognition in heterogeneous data. Additionally, agent-based simulations will explore how individual differences in movement quality and cognitive engagement modulate therapeutic outcomes. The scale of data integration—combining terabyte-level neuroimaging with real-time biomechanical tracking—necessitates distributed computing infrastructure for parallel processing and memory-intensive tasks. Expected outcomes include the development of predictive models that identify optimal movement parameters and mental focus strategies for targeted health outcomes, as well as a publicly available toolbox for analyzing mind-body therapy datasets. By elucidating the synergies between movement and cognition, this work aims to advance evidence-based practices in mind-body therapies, enabling personalized interventions and informing clinical guidelines. The requested computing resources are critical to overcoming current limitations in data processing capacity, ultimately fostering a deeper understanding of holistic health interventions.
cip_title: Movement and Mind-Body Therapies and Education, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in movement and mind-body therapies, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to address the critical challenge of optimizing resource allocation in early childhood education (ECE) programs through advanced computational modeling. ECE administrators face complex decisions in balancing budgetary constraints, staffing needs, facility utilization, and regulatory compliance while maintaining program quality and accessibility. Traditional decision-making frameworks often lack the capacity to account for dynamic variables such as fluctuating enrollment, evolving policy requirements, and socioeconomic disparities. This research proposes the development of a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled simulation platform to model multi-dimensional resource allocation scenarios across diverse ECE settings. The computational approach will integrate demographic data, funding structures, staff qualifications, and facility capacities into agent-based models that simulate program operations under varying constraints. Machine learning techniques will be applied to historical program outcomes to identify patterns in resource utilization efficiency and predict the impact of administrative decisions on equity metrics. By leveraging parallel processing, the platform will enable rapid scenario testing for large-scale program networks, including sensitivity analyses of policy changes and disaster preparedness planning. Expected outcomes include a decision-support tool for administrators to visualize trade-offs between fiscal responsibility, regulatory adherence, and educational quality, with particular emphasis on underserved communities. The project will also generate scalable frameworks for evaluating state-level funding distribution models and workforce development investments. This work advances the field of education leadership by introducing computational social science methodologies to early childhood administration, offering empirically grounded strategies to enhance program sustainability and equitable access. The requested HPC resources are essential for managing the computational complexity of simulating thousands of interdependent variables across heterogeneous program environments while maintaining the fidelity required for policy-relevant conclusions.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on early childhood educational program administration and prepares individuals to serve as a principal or director of an early childhood educational program. Includes instruction in early childhood education, program and facilities planning, budgeting and administration, public relations, human resources management, early childhood growth and development, counseling skills, applicable law and regulations, school safety, policy studies, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the accuracy of high-resolution numerical weather prediction (NWP) models to improve short-term forecasting of mesoscale convective systems (MCSs) in the context of climate change. Current operational models struggle to resolve the fine-scale dynamics and microphysical processes driving MCS initiation and evolution, particularly in regions prone to extreme precipitation and severe weather. To address this gap, we propose a series of convection-permitting simulations using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model at horizontal resolutions below 3 km, coupled with ensemble-based data assimilation. These simulations will integrate novel stochastic parameterizations to better represent subgrid-scale cloud processes and boundary layer interactions, which are critical for MCS development. The computational demands of such high-resolution, ensemble-based experiments—spanning multiple climate scenarios and requiring frequent data assimilation cycles—necessitate access to high-performance computing (HPC) resources. We request allocation for 500,000 core-hours to execute the simulations, alongside GPU nodes for machine learning-assisted analysis of output data. The project will leverage advanced statistical-dynamical downscaling techniques to quantify uncertainties in precipitation forecasts and assess how warming scenarios modulate MCS intensity and spatial organization. Expected outcomes include improved physical understanding of convective predictability thresholds, optimized parameterization schemes for operational NWP systems, and actionable data for regional climate adaptation planning. By bridging the gap between climate projections and weather-scale extremes, this work will directly support mitigation strategies for flood risks and infrastructure resilience, addressing a critical need in atmospheric science and public safety.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the prediction of atmospheric motion and climate change. Includes instruction in general circulation patterns, weather phenomena, atmospheric predictability, parameterization, numerical and statistical analysis, large- and mesoscale phenomena, kinematic structures, precipitation processes, and forecasting techniques.

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of multi-scale physical and chemical interactions governing nutrient transport and carbon cycling in the global ocean, with a focus on regions of intense vertical mixing and frontal dynamics. Current models struggle to resolve the fine-scale turbulence, eddy-driven advection, and biogeochemical feedbacks that modulate the ocean’s capacity to sequester anthropogenic carbon and sustain marine ecosystems. To address this gap, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled study integrating a coupled physical-biogeochemical model (ROMS-BEC) with machine learning-driven parameterizations of submesoscale processes. The simulations will resolve turbulent kinetic energy dissipation rates, 3D tracer dispersion, and air-sea gas exchange at unprecedented horizontal resolutions (≤1 km) in key regions, including the Southern Ocean and equatorial upwelling zones. Concurrently, a novel neural network framework will assimilate satellite-derived chlorophyll, Argo float data, and shipboard sensor measurements to optimize representations of iron-limitation dynamics and dissolved organic carbon partitioning. The computational workload necessitates access to GPU-accelerated nodes and large-memory resources for ensemble runs under IPCC climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP5-8.5), with petabyte-scale output analysis using parallelized Python workflows. Expected outcomes include quantitative constraints on how subgrid-scale mixing efficiency impacts macronutrient redistribution and carbon export fluxes, reducing uncertainties in projections of ocean deoxygenation and acidification. Results will inform international assessments of marine carbon dioxide removal feasibility and provide open-access datasets to improve Earth system model parameterizations. By elucidating the mechanistic links between ocean physics and biogeochemistry, this work aims to strengthen predictive models critical for climate mitigation and marine resource resilience.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the chemical components, mechanisms, structure, and movement of ocean waters and their interaction with terrestrial and atmospheric phenomena. Includes instruction in material inputs and outputs, chemical and biochemical transformations in marine systems, equilibria studies, inorganic and organic ocean chemistry, oceanographic processes, sediment transport, zone processes, circulation, mixing, tidal movements, wave properties, and seawater properties.

abstract: This research project seeks to investigate the diachronic evolution and synchronic variation of understudied Semitic languages through computational modeling and large-scale textual analysis. The primary challenge lies in analyzing fragmented, multilingual corpora—including historical manuscripts, inscriptions, and modern dialectal recordings—that require advanced processing to identify phonological, morphological, and syntactic patterns across millennia. Current methodologies lack the capacity to efficiently parse non-standardized orthographies or model complex language contact scenarios in the ancient Near East. To address this, we propose deploying high-performance computing (HPC) resources to implement neural machine translation frameworks adapted for low-resource languages, automate grapheme-to-phoneme conversion for epigraphic materials, and run phylogenetic algorithms to reconstruct proto-language features. Key datasets include digitized cuneiform tablets, early Arabic papyri, and contemporary Neo-Aramaic speech corpora, totaling approximately 12 TB of multimodal data. Computational workflows will leverage distributed processing for parallelized text alignment, GPU-accelerated transformer models for semantic role labeling in ancient texts, and Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to quantify uncertainty in linguistic divergence timelines. Expected outcomes include the first probabilistic atlas of Semitic language contact zones (circa 2000 BCE–1000 CE), open-source tools for automated morphological parsing of Akkadian dialects, and a corpus-driven typology of grammatical borrowing between Semitic and non-Semitic Near Eastern languages. These results will advance understanding of language change mechanisms in multilingual historical contexts while providing infrastructure for interdisciplinary studies of cultural exchange. The scale of data processing and model training—particularly for transformer-based architectures applied to epigraphic noise—necessitates dedicated HPC allocation to achieve project milestones within feasible timeframes.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: Middle/ Near Eastern and Semitic Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in Middle/Near Eastern and Semitic languages, literatures, and linguistics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the interplay between environmental change, host-pathogen dynamics, and emerging infectious disease risk in human populations using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Rapid urbanization, climate shifts, and habitat fragmentation are altering ecological networks and evolutionary pressures on zoonotic pathogens, yet scalable models integrating these processes remain underdeveloped. We propose to build spatially explicit, multiscale simulation frameworks to analyze how landscape connectivity, wildlife migration patterns, and anthropogenic stressors jointly influence cross-species transmission hotspots. Agent-based models will incorporate empirical data on reservoir host distributions (e.g., rodents, bats), vector ecology, and human mobility across three regions with accelerating spillover events: Southeast Asia, the Amazon Basin, and East Africa. Phylogenetic comparative methods will be adapted to assess pathogen trait evolution under simulated environmental gradients, avoiding genomic sequence analysis to align with program scope. A novel feature integrates adaptive behavioral responses in human communities—such as changes in land use or healthcare access—as dynamic feedbacks altering transmission pathways. The computational workflow requires parallelized parameter sweeps across >10^5 ecological scenarios, Bayesian inference for model calibration, and real-time visualization of epidemic trajectories. Expected outcomes include 1) identification of high-risk interfaces where land-use change amplifies evolutionary selection for human-adapted pathogens, 2) predictive maps of outbreak vulnerability under multiple climate projection scenarios, and 3) quantitative evaluation of ecological intervention strategies targeting wildlife-livestock-human contact networks. By coupling evolutionary ecology principles with epidemiological modeling at unprecedented spatial granularity, this work will provide actionable insights for preventing spillover events while advancing theoretical frameworks for planetary health. The requested HPC resources are critical for managing memory-intensive landscape layers, optimizing stochastic simulation kernels, and enabling iterative model refinement through ensemble machine learning techniques.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of disease, disability, and trauma patterns within and across populations and the development of health management mechanisms to prevent and control disease outbreaks and injurious behaviors. Includes instruction in biostatistics, biochemistry, molecular biology, immunology, disease and injury determinants, genetic disease and disability factors, behavioral studies, health services research, environmental disease and injury factors, and population studies.

abstract: This project seeks to address the persistent challenge of equitable student success in developmental education by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model and optimize adaptive learning systems for underprepared college learners. Despite advances in instructional technology, scalable frameworks for predicting individual learner trajectories and dynamically tailoring interventions remain underdeveloped, particularly for non-traditional and historically marginalized student populations. The research will utilize anonymized, multimodal datasets from institutional learning management systems (e.g., Moodle, Canvas), including temporal engagement patterns, assessment performance, and discussion forum interactions, to train machine learning models that identify early risk factors and effective support strategies. Computational workflows will integrate natural language processing (NLP) to analyze qualitative feedback, graph neural networks to map peer learning networks, and reinforcement learning to simulate intervention outcomes across diverse virtual student cohorts. HPC resources are essential for processing terabytes of longitudinal behavioral data, training complex multimodal architectures, and running parallelized simulations of instructional design scenarios. Expected outcomes include 1) a predictive framework for identifying at-risk students with higher temporal resolution than current institutional methods, 2) evidence-based recommendations for context-aware adaptive learning pathways in developmental mathematics and writing courses, and 3) open-source tools for simulating the equity impacts of different pedagogical approaches under varying demographic conditions. By combining learning science theory with large-scale computational modeling, this work aims to advance precision support systems that balance scalability with the nuanced needs of underprepared learners, ultimately informing both educational technology design and professional development for developmental educators.
detailed_field: Teacher education, specific levels and methods
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to teach educational strategies for assisting students who are perceived as underprepared for the academic rigor of college-level coursework at a postsecondary institution. Includes instruction in andragogy, assessment, classroom motivation, instructional design and technology, learner-centered teaching, learning science, syllabus construction, and teaching critical thinking.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a novel computational framework to analyze the dynamic interplay between urban infrastructure resilience and socio-environmental vulnerability under climate change stressors. While existing studies often silo engineering, social science, or ecological perspectives, our approach integrates heterogeneous datasets—including high-resolution climate models, real-time sensor networks from transportation/energy grids, and demographic mobility patterns—to quantify cascading failure risks in metropolitan systems. The research addresses a critical gap in predictive modeling by unifying physics-based simulations of infrastructure performance with agent-based models of human adaptation behaviors, which operate at conflicting spatial and temporal scales. Using Houston, Texas, as a testbed, we will process multi-terabyte datasets spanning decade-long weather records, social media sentiment during extreme events, and 3D cityscape geometries. The computational workflow employs graph neural networks to detect latent dependencies between infrastructure nodes, coupled with Bayesian hierarchical models to assess how socioeconomic inequities amplify systemic vulnerabilities. High-performance computing resources are essential for three components: (1) parallelized ensemble simulations of flood propagation under 500+ climate scenarios, (2) training transformer architectures on unstructured text and satellite imagery to predict evacuation behavior, and (3) optimizing reinforcement learning agents for adaptive infrastructure investment policies. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source digital twin platform capable of stress-testing urban systems against compound hazards while accounting for human decision-making feedback loops. This work advances interdisciplinary data science methodologies by bridging computational engineering, climate analytics, and social systems modeling—providing actionable insights for equitable resilience planning in complex, interconnected environments.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the analysis of large scale data sources from the interdisciplinary perspectives of applied statistics, computer science, data storage, data representation, data modeling, mathematics, and statistics. Includes instruction in computer algorithms, computer programming, data management, data mining, information policy, information retrieval, mathematical modeling, quantitative analysis, statistics, trend spotting, and visual analytics.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate how institutional structures and political decision-making processes shape economic policy outcomes in contexts of systemic complexity, such as democratic backsliding or global trade realignments. While existing scholarship acknowledges the interdependence of political and economic systems, methodological limitations hinder granular analysis of their nonlinear interactions across temporal and spatial scales. To address this gap, the research employs a multi-method computational framework integrating agent-based modeling (ABM), natural language processing (NLP), and dynamic network analysis. The ABM component will simulate strategic interactions between legislative bodies, bureaucratic agencies, and market actors under varying constitutional constraints. NLP techniques will process historical legislative texts and economic reports to identify patterns in policy framing and implementation delays. Temporal exponential random graph models (TERGMs) will map coevolutionary relationships between political alliances and sectoral economic performance using longitudinal data from 40 democracies (1990–2020). High-performance computing resources are critical for three components: 1) parallelized Monte Carlo simulations testing 10^6+ policy intervention scenarios, 2) training transformer models on multilingual parliamentary corpora, and 3) maintaining Markov chain Monte Carlo convergence in TERGM estimations with sparse temporal networks. Expected outcomes include a novel taxonomy of institutional configurations that predict economic policy efficacy under political volatility, validated through out-of-sample testing across regime types. The computational toolkit developed will enable researchers to quantitatively assess path dependencies between electoral incentives, regulatory decisions, and macroeconomic stability—advancing political science scholarship beyond conventional comparative case studies. By identifying institutional designs that mitigate politically induced economic shocks, findings will inform debates on constitutional engineering and multilateral governance frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the interaction between politics and economics in the formation of public policy. Includes instruction in microeconomics; macroeconomics; political theory; American, comparative, and international political economy; and quantitative methods.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the development of next-generation wireless communication systems and secure embedded computing architectures through computationally intensive modeling and optimization. The research addresses two critical challenges in electrical and computer engineering: (1) optimizing beamforming and resource allocation for millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive MIMO systems in 6G networks, and (2) designing energy-efficient hardware accelerators for post-quantum cryptographic protocols. Current limitations in simulating large antenna arrays (256+ elements) with realistic channel models and in evaluating lattice-based cryptography on FPGA-based systems require unprecedented computational resources. Our approach combines finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) electromagnetic simulations with deep reinforcement learning to optimize antenna configurations while accounting for multi-path fading and interference. Parallel Monte Carlo simulations will assess error rates across 10^6 channel realizations, while GPU-accelerated neural networks iteratively refine beamforming codebooks. For cybersecurity applications, we propose RTL-level simulations of NIST-standardized Kyber and Dilithium algorithms synthesized across Xilinx UltraScale+ FPGAs, benchmarking power-performance tradeoffs through cycle-accurate models of 7nm ASIC implementations. The computational workload necessitates sustained access to high-performance computing resources, including GPU clusters for training physics-informed neural networks and FPGA emulation platforms for pre-silicon verification. Expected outcomes include novel beamforming algorithms achieving 95%+ spectral efficiency in non-line-of-sight conditions, open-source hardware templates for post-quantum cryptography accelerators with 40% lower energy per bit than existing designs, and a public dataset of mmWave channel characteristics for 28-300 GHz bands. This work will directly contribute to scalable 6G network deployments and quantum-resistant cybersecurity infrastructure, addressing key gaps in wireless and embedded systems research.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and scientific principles to the design and development of computer systems. Includes instruction in computer architecture, cybersecurity, electronic circuits, electromagnetism, electronic materials and design, micro-fabrication methods and techniques, signal and image processing, and wireless communication networks.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the dynamics of cross-linguistic influence in multilingual digital communication environments, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model real-time language processing and adaptation. As global digital interactions increase, multilingual speakers often engage in code-switching, lexical borrowing, and syntactic blending across three or more languages—phenomena that remain understudied in computational frameworks due to the complexity of modeling fluid, context-dependent language use. Traditional approaches in applied linguistics have focused on bilingual contexts or isolated language pairs, but the rise of transnational online communities and AI-mediated communication tools necessitates scalable methods to analyze multi-directional language transfer. The research problem centers on developing a computational model that simulates how multilingual individuals negotiate competing linguistic systems during real-time discourse, with attention to cognitive load, sociopragmatic constraints, and platform-specific affordances. The project will employ transformer-based architectures fine-tuned on a novel corpus of multilingual social media interactions, video conference data, and gaming communities, incorporating temporal, acoustic-prosodic, and orthographic features. Computational experiments will combine neural machine translation, attention mechanism analysis, and agent-based modeling to track decision-making pathways in language selection and hybridity. Expected outcomes include 1) a scalable framework for predicting emergent hybrid language forms in digitally mediated contexts, 2) quantitative metrics for cross-linguistic permeability across typologically diverse language triads, and 3) open-source tools to inform adaptive language education technologies and inclusive digital communication policies. The HPC resources are critical for training multi-modal models on terabyte-scale interaction data, running parallelized simulations of language convergence scenarios, and optimizing real-time processing pipelines for heterogeneous linguistic inputs. Findings will advance theoretical understanding of multilingual cognition in technology-rich environments while addressing practical challenges in designing linguistically responsive digital infrastructures.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on language-related concerns in the everyday world, including language education, acquisition of first and additional languages, discourse analysis, language assessment, literacy, and language policy and planning. Includes instruction in linguistic theory; language teaching and learning; discourse analysis; language and cognition; and language, culture, and identity.

abstract: The study of morphogenesis and cell differentiation during embryonic development remains a central challenge in developmental biology. A critical gap exists in understanding how multicellular aggregates integrate biochemical signaling with mechanical forces to establish robust tissue architecture. This project aims to develop a computational framework to model the spatiotemporal dynamics of cell-cell interactions and force transmission during early embryogenesis, focusing on gastrulation events in vertebrate model systems. Current limitations in analyzing tissue-scale biomechanical feedback require high-resolution simulations of collective cell behaviors that are intractable with standard computing resources. We propose to implement a hybrid agent-based model coupled with continuum mechanics, parameterized by live-cell imaging data from avian and amphibian embryos. The computational approach will integrate cell polarity dynamics, adhesion receptor trafficking, and actomyosin contractility into a 3D viscoelastic model to predict emergent tissue deformation patterns. High-performance computing resources will enable simulations at biologically relevant scales (10^4-10^5 cells) with subcellular spatial resolution and minute-level temporal resolution across developmental time windows. Validation will leverage quantitative comparisons to in vivo perturbation experiments targeting cytoskeletal regulators and cell adhesion molecules. Expected outcomes include (1) identification of critical thresholds in mechanical coupling that ensure faithful germ layer segregation, (2) predictive maps of stress distribution during primitive streak formation, and (3) mechanistic insights into how local cell shape changes propagate to orchestrate global tissue remodeling. This work will establish a scalable computational platform for analyzing developmental robustness, with direct implications for understanding congenital malformations caused by disrupted morphogenetic processes. The requested resources will support iterative model refinement through parallelized parameter space exploration and high-throughput simulation analyses that exceed local computing capabilities.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of embryology, development, and growth of animals and human beings. Includes instruction in fertilization, oogenesis, histogenesis, gastrulation, and cell differentiation; embryological development including organ and pattern formation, morphogenesis, gene regulation, cell lineage, and fate maps; disease and defect studies; transgenic and evolutionary models of growth and development; and applications to specific organisms and phyla.

abstract: Cancer progression is driven not only by genetic mutations but also by dynamic interactions between tumors and host physiological systems. Despite advances in molecular oncology, the role of systemic physiological adaptation—such as altered vascular function, metabolic resource allocation, and hormonal signaling—in shaping tumor evolution and therapeutic resistance remains poorly understood. This project seeks to develop a multiscale computational framework to model how tumors co-opt physiological networks to sustain growth, evade immune detection, and metastasize. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will integrate tissue-level biomechanical models of tumor-vascular interactions with systemic physiological data, including circulatory dynamics, nutrient distribution, and stress-response pathways. Agent-based models will simulate tumor cell populations interacting with spatially heterogeneous microenvironments, while differential equation systems will capture systemic variables such as blood pressure, pH, and hormone gradients. The computational pipeline will be parameterized using experimental data from murine models of breast and pancreatic cancer, including intravital imaging, hemodynamic measurements, and metabolomic profiles. Key objectives include identifying physiological "tipping points" that trigger metastatic dissemination and predicting how perturbations to vascular remodeling or autonomic signaling alter therapeutic efficacy. By bridging organ-scale physiology with tumor biology, this work aims to reveal novel mechanisms by which host physiology constrains or enables cancer progression. The outcomes will provide a platform for testing hypotheses about non-cell-autonomous drivers of treatment resistance and inform the design of physiology-modulating adjuvant therapies. Successful implementation requires HPC capabilities to manage iterative simulations across parameter spaces, high-throughput analysis of multimodal datasets, and real-time visualization of complex, spatially resolved models. This resource allocation will directly support the development of translational strategies that exploit physiological vulnerabilities in cancer.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the scientific study of the functional dynamics, morphology, and biochemical and biophysical communications within organisms and between living systems at all levels of complexity and integration. Includes instruction in reproduction, growth, hormonal action, vascular function, respiration, digestion, sensory perception and processing, sensorimotor integration, signal encoding and conveyance, homeostasis, physical function and malfunction, evolutionary physiology, and disease processes.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze the evolution of rabbinic legal reasoning (Halacha) across temporal, geographic, and cultural contexts through computational text mining and network analysis. While traditional rabbinic scholarship relies on manual close reading of primary texts such as the Talmud, Midrash, and Responsa literature, this study addresses the challenge of systematically tracing patterns in legal argumentation, citation networks, and semantic shifts at scale. The research focuses on understudied Halachic debates concerning ethical dilemmas in communal leadership, pastoral care, and crisis response from the medieval period through early modernity. A corpus of approximately 50,000 digitized Hebrew and Aramaic texts—including rare manuscripts, printed commentaries, and epistolary responsa—will be processed using natural language processing (NLP) pipelines optimized for rabbinic Hebrew morphology and formulaic legal syntax. Computational methods will include transformer-based language models fine-tuned for semantic similarity detection in legal arguments, graph-theoretical analysis of cross-textual references, and time-series modeling of conceptual diffusion across Jewish diaspora communities. The project requires HPC capabilities to manage memory-intensive processing of non-Latin scripts, parallelize feature extraction across multilingual texts, and train domain-specific embeddings for rare lexical constructs. Expected outcomes include 1) quantitative maps of Halachic decision-making patterns correlated with historical crises, 2) identification of previously unrecognized interdisciplinary influences (e.g., medical ethics principles emerging from plague-era responsa), and 3) an open-source framework for computational rabbinics. This interdisciplinary nexus of Jewish law, digital humanities, and ethical philosophy aims to establish new methodologies for studying religious legal systems as dynamic, data-rich cultural artifacts while providing practical tools for contemporary rabbinic education and interfaith policy discourse.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for ordination as Rabbis. Includes instruction in Talmud, Halacha, Liturgy and Rituals, Rabbinical Thought, Jewish Ethics, Jewish Education, Pastoral Counseling and Homiletics.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to investigate the biomechanical drivers of osteoarthritis (OA) progression in the human knee joint through patient-specific computational modeling. Despite OA’s prevalence as a leading cause of chronic pain and mobility impairment, the dynamic interplay between joint mechanics, tissue degradation, and patient-specific anatomical factors remains poorly characterized. Current clinical tools lack the resolution to predict disease trajectories or optimize personalized interventions. To address this gap, we propose developing a multi-scale computational framework integrating finite element analysis (FEA), machine learning (ML), and biomechanical simulation to model knee joint stresses under real-world loading conditions. High-resolution MRI and motion capture data from a longitudinal cohort of OA patients will inform patient-specific models, capturing variations in cartilage morphology, ligamentous structures, and gait patterns. HPC resources will enable large-scale parameter sweeps to simulate thousands of activity scenarios, quantify stress distributions in articular cartilage, and correlate mechanical loading patterns with radiographic and symptomatic disease progression. Concurrently, ML algorithms will identify predictive biomechanical biomarkers from simulated and clinical datasets. This approach aims to establish causal links between mechanical stressors and OA pathogenesis while accounting for anatomical heterogeneity. The anticipated outcomes include a validated computational platform for stratifying OA risk, optimizing rehabilitative exercise regimens, and guiding surgical planning. By elucidating patient-specific mechanobiological pathways, this work could transform the management of OA from reactive to proactive, reducing the burden of invasive interventions. The project’s computational demands—particularly the parallel processing requirements for FEA simulations and ML training on multi-terabyte datasets—necessitate robust HPC infrastructure. Successful execution will advance interdisciplinary innovation at the intersection of orthopedics, biomechanics, and computational health sciences.
cip_title: Health Professions and Related Clinical Sciences, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in the health professions and related clinical sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop a high-resolution computational framework to evaluate the long-term effectiveness of renewable energy transition policies under climate change uncertainty, with a focus on grid reliability, cost equity, and emissions reduction targets. Current policy models often lack the spatial-temporal granularity needed to capture localized energy demand patterns, intermittent renewable generation profiles, and evolving climate risks—gaps that limit actionable insights for equitable decarbonization. We propose an integrated modeling approach combining agent-based simulations of energy market decisions with machine learning-enhanced climate-impact projections at 1km² resolution across three U.S. regions. The computational workflow will couple a modified version of the Global Change Analysis Model (GCAM) with regionally downscaled CMIP6 climate data and historical grid failure records. High-performance computing resources are critical for running millions of policy scenario iterations that vary renewable portfolio standards, carbon pricing mechanisms, and infrastructure adaptation timelines while accounting for probabilistic heatwave intensification and demand surge events. Anticipated outcomes include identification of policy packages that minimize energy poverty risks under +1.5°C to +3°C warming scenarios, quantification of storage capacity thresholds to offset renewable intermittency, and spatial vulnerability maps linking climate hazards to grid resilience investments. The 50TB dataset generated will support open-source policy tools for municipal planners, while model architectures will be optimized for GPU-accelerated clusters using PyTorch and Dask parallelization. This work directly addresses intergenerational equity challenges in energy transition planning through computationally intensive analysis of distributional impacts across socioeconomic groups—a capability previously constrained by coarse-resolution modeling approaches. Results will inform state-level implementation of the Inflation Reduction Act and international just transition frameworks.
detailed_field: Environmental/ natural resources management and policy
cip_definition: A program of study that focuses on the systematic analysis of public policy issues related to climate change, energy policy, environmental economics, global sustainability, and security. Includes instruction in climate change, clean energy technologies, environmental policy, environmental law, environmental economics, food security, fossil fuels, renewable and sustainable energy sources, and water issues.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the evolution of Mormon theological frameworks and their sociocultural implications through computational analysis of large-scale textual and demographic datasets. Despite extensive qualitative scholarship on the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS), quantitative studies of doctrinal development and its relationship to cultural adaptation remain limited. The research addresses this gap by employing natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning (ML) to analyze a curated corpus of over 100,000 LDS texts, including scriptures, sermons, administrative publications, and ethnographic records spanning 1830–present. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are critical to process this data at scale, enabling the training of transformer-based models for semantic analysis, topic modeling, and sentiment detection across historical periods. Concurrently, agent-based modeling will simulate demographic shifts in LDS communities to explore correlations between doctrinal emphasis and socioreligious behaviors. Expected outcomes include identifying patterns in theological prioritization (e.g., shifts in teachings on communal welfare or familial structures), mapping discursive networks linking doctrine to cultural practices, and visualizing longitudinal trends in religious rhetoric. These findings will advance scholarly understanding of how LDS theology negotiates modernity while retaining doctrinal continuity, offering a model for computational approaches in religious studies. The project’s computational workflows will be open-sourced, promoting interdisciplinary methodology development at the intersection of digital humanities and belief systems research. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this work aims to generate foundational insights into the dynamic interplay of belief, culture, and institutional adaptation in Mormonism, with implications for broader studies of religion in sociotechnical contexts.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on beliefs, practices, culture, and history of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormon). Includes instruction in Mormon culture, history, literature, philosophy, sociology, and theology.

abstract: This research project seeks to address the challenge of optimizing digital content distribution strategies for visual arts and media platforms through advanced computational modeling. As the volume and diversity of user-generated visual content grow exponentially, cultural institutions and media enterprises face significant barriers in predicting audience engagement, allocating platform resources efficiently, and mitigating algorithmic biases in content recommendation systems. Current manual or semi-automated approaches struggle to process multimodal data—including high-resolution imagery, user interaction metadata, and temporal viewing patterns—at the scale required for actionable insights. To bridge this gap, we propose developing a machine learning framework leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze terabyte-scale datasets from public art repositories, social media platforms, and streaming services. The computational pipeline will integrate convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for visual feature extraction, transformer-based models for cross-modal analysis of text and image data, and graph neural networks (GNNs) to map content dissemination patterns across digital networks. By training these models on heterogeneous datasets spanning contemporary digital art, design trends, and historical engagement metrics, the system will generate predictive models for audience reach, content virality, and resource allocation efficiency. The HPC infrastructure is critical for handling memory-intensive preprocessing of high-resolution visual assets, parallelized hyperparameter optimization, and real-time simulations of content distribution scenarios. Anticipated outcomes include an open-source toolkit for cultural organizations to simulate audience engagement strategies, evidence-based guidelines for equitable content promotion algorithms, and novel metrics for evaluating the cultural impact of digital visual media. This work aims to advance computational methods in arts management while addressing pressing industry needs in an era of algorithm-driven media consumption.
major_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design
detailed_field: Visual arts, media studies, and design nec
cip_title: Arts, Entertainment, and Media Management, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in arts, entertainment, and media management, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The development of advanced materials with tailored mechanical, thermal, and functional properties requires precise control over microstructural evolution during manufacturing processes. Current limitations in predicting phase transformations and defect dynamics in multicomponent alloys under non-equilibrium conditions hinder progress toward next-generation materials for energy-efficient industrial applications. This project seeks to address these challenges through a multiscale computational framework integrating quantum-mechanical calculations, phase-field modeling, and mesoscale dislocation dynamics simulations. The research will employ density functional theory (DFT) to parameterize interfacial energetics and diffusion coefficients in novel high-entropy alloy systems, coupled with GPU-accelerated phase-field methods to simulate microstructure evolution during rapid solidification and thermomechanical processing. Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations will investigate dislocation nucleation and propagation mechanisms in these complex alloys, with explicit incorporation of chemical short-range order effects. The computational workflow requires high-performance computing resources to manage the extreme resolution demands of capturing nanoscale defect interactions while maintaining macroscale-relevant simulation volumes. Expected outcomes include predictive models linking processing parameters to microstructural features and mechanical performance, enabling the design of alloys with enhanced strength-ductility trade-offs and corrosion resistance. These results will directly inform experimental synthesis efforts in our collaborative research group, accelerating the development of sustainable materials for additive manufacturing and high-temperature structural applications. The requested allocation of 500,000 node-hours on GPU-enabled clusters, supplemented by high-memory nodes for ab initio calculations, will support time-resolved simulations across 6-8 alloy compositions over a 12-month period. This work advances fundamental understanding of non-equilibrium microstructure formation while providing industry-relevant computational tools to reduce trial-and-error in materials development cycles.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply mathematical and materials science principles to the design, development and operational evaluation of materials and related processes used in manufacturing in a wide variety of settings; the synthesis of new industrial materials, including marrying and bonding composites; analysis of materials requirements and specifications; and related problems of system design dependent on materials factors.

abstract: This research project seeks to investigate the systemic risk dynamics of decentralized cryptocurrency markets, focusing on the emergent behavior of liquidity protocols and automated market makers (AMMs) in decentralized exchanges (DEXs). While traditional financial systemic risk models emphasize centralized intermediaries, decentralized finance (DeFi) ecosystems operate via algorithmic coordination, creating unique vulnerabilities that remain understudied. The core research problem lies in quantifying how network effects, protocol interdependencies, and liquidity fragmentation across blockchain-based DEXs propagate instability during market shocks. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework combining agent-based modeling (ABM) with real-time blockchain data ingestion. The ABM will simulate heterogeneous agents (e.g., liquidity providers, arbitrageurs, leveraged traders) interacting across multiple DEX protocols under varying market conditions, while on-chain transaction data will parameterize and validate model assumptions. Computational challenges include scaling simulations to replicate the Ethereum and Solana ecosystems’ transaction throughput (>1,000 TPS), modeling cross-chain liquidity flows, and analyzing high-dimensional time-series data to detect latent risk cascades. GPU-accelerated graph neural networks will be employed to map liquidity network topologies and stress-test protocol resilience. Expected outcomes include (1) a novel risk metric for DeFi liquidity fragmentation, (2) protocol design recommendations to mitigate reflexivity in AMM pricing, and (3) a publicly accessible dataset linking on-chain activity to systemic vulnerability indicators. This work bridges financial economics, distributed systems, and computational social science, offering policymakers and protocol developers tools to address stability challenges in algorithmically mediated markets. The requested HPC resources are critical for handling the combinatorial complexity of multi-chain simulations and achieving sub-second latency in real-time risk monitoring applications.
cip_title: Finance and Financial Management Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in financial management and services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Architectural design increasingly relies on computational tools to address complex challenges in sustainability, structural efficiency, and spatial optimization. However, current architectural drafting and CAD workflows struggle to perform high-fidelity simulations at scale due to computational limitations, particularly when analyzing large structures or integrating multiple performance criteria. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to enable advanced simulations and generative design processes that transcend the capabilities of standalone workstations. The research will focus on three computational domains: 1) parallelized finite element analysis for evaluating structural integrity under dynamic environmental loads, 2) machine learning-driven energy modeling that incorporates real-time climate data and material properties, and 3) multi-objective optimization algorithms for space planning and building systems integration. By distributing these compute-intensive tasks across HPC clusters, the project aims to reduce simulation times from days to hours while improving model resolution by an order of magnitude. Expected outcomes include novel methodologies for integrating HPC capabilities into mainstream architectural CAD workflows, validated through case studies of mid-rise mixed-use buildings. The results will advance the precision of performance-based design in architectural practice, enable data-driven material optimization strategies, and establish scalable frameworks for collaborative design iteration. This work will directly enhance instructional resources in architectural CAD/CADD programs by providing students with access to cutting-edge computational design techniques, while contributing to broader efforts in sustainable building practices through optimized energy and structural solutions.
cip_title: Architectural Drafting and Architectural CAD/ CADD
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply technical knowledge and skills to develop working drawings and electronic simulations for architectural and related construction projects. Includes instruction in basic construction and structural design, architectural rendering, architectural-aided drafting (CAD), layout and designs, architectural blueprint interpretation, building materials, and basic structural wiring diagramming.

abstract: The increasing complexity of biological systems demands advanced computational strategies to integrate multi-modal data and model dynamic interactions at scale. This project seeks to address the challenge of predicting emergent behaviors in cellular signaling networks using heterogeneous, high-dimensional datasets (e.g., proteomic, metabolomic, and single-cell transcriptomic data). Traditional methods often fail to capture non-linear interactions or scale to organism-level simulations, limiting their utility in identifying therapeutic targets. We propose a hybrid computational framework combining graph neural networks (GNNs) with agent-based modeling (ABM) to simulate signaling cascades across spatial and temporal resolutions. The GNN component will infer latent interaction rules from experimental data, while the ABM module will execute stochastic simulations of network perturbations. To overcome computational bottlenecks, we will implement distributed training of GNNs using PyTorch Geometric and optimize ABM parallelization via custom Message Passing Interface (MPI) protocols. The pipeline will leverage High-Performance Computing (HPC) resources for three critical tasks: (1) processing terabyte-scale datasets from public repositories like PRIDE and MetaboLights, (2) training memory-intensive neural architectures on >10,000 cellular subgraphs, and (3) running ensemble simulations to quantify uncertainty in pathway predictions. Expected outcomes include an open-source software package for scalable signaling network analysis and novel insights into cross-talk between metabolic and regulatory pathways in stress response scenarios. This work will establish a template for resource-efficient integration of machine learning and mechanistic modeling, directly addressing NIH-defined priorities for computational biology infrastructure. Successful implementation requires dedicated access to GPU-accelerated nodes with large memory capacity (>512 GB/node) and fast interconnects to manage communication-heavy ABM workloads. The proposed allocations will enable unprecedented resolution in systems-level biological simulations, with applications ranging from drug repurposing to synthetic biology design.
detailed_field: Bioinformatics, biostatistics, and computational biology nec
cip_title: Biomathematics, Bioinformatics, and Computational Biology, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in biomathematics, bioinformatics, and computational biology, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance research in Vietnamese dialectology and literary analysis through large-scale computational linguistics methods. Despite Vietnam’s rich linguistic diversity, comprehensive studies of regional dialect variations and their historical evolution remain limited due to the challenges of processing vast, unstructured datasets spanning text, audio, and historical records. Similarly, computational analyses of Vietnamese literary texts—critical for identifying stylistic trends, sociolinguistic influences, and intertextual connections—are hindered by the lack of scalable tools tailored to the language’s tonal and syntactic complexity. This project will address these gaps by developing and deploying machine learning models to classify dialect features from audio recordings and textual sources, map their geographic distribution, and analyze patterns in a corpus of premodern and modern Vietnamese literature. Computational workflows will include transformer-based models for dialect identification, neural topic modeling to trace thematic shifts in literature across periods, and graph-based algorithms to visualize intertextual networks. The scale of data—encompassing over 50,000 literary texts, 10,000 hours of dialect recordings, and orthographic records from archival materials—necessitates HPC infrastructure for parallel processing, distributed storage, and GPU-accelerated model training. Anticipated outcomes include the first open-access digital atlas of Vietnamese dialects, annotated literary corpora with computational metadata, and publicly available NLP tools optimized for Vietnamese. These resources will support scholarly research, language preservation efforts, and applications in education, translation technology, and cultural heritage management. By integrating computational methods with traditional philological expertise, this project aims to establish new frameworks for analyzing Vietnamese language dynamics and literary production, with broader implications for underrepresented languages in digital humanities.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the Vietnamese language. Includes instruction in philology; dialects; literature; and applications to business, science/technology, and other settings.
