Leveraging a novel integration of high-resolution geospatial datasets, agent-based modeling (ABM), and natural language processing (NLP) of community archives, the research will develop a computational framework to simulate decision pathways under varying scenarios of environmental communication and resource allocation. The computational workflow requires processing multi-terabyte datasets spanning satellite-derived land-use change maps (2000–2024), transcribed public meeting records from 142 municipal bodies, and fine-scale elevation models. High-performance computing resources are essential for three core tasks: (1) training transformer-based NLP models to detect evolving risk perception patterns in unstructured textual data, (2) running ensemble ABM simulations that incorporate stochastic cultural valuation parameters alongside hydrodynamic flood projections, and (3) performing sensitivity analyses across 15 coastal biogeomorphic subregions to identify leverage points for intervention. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for culturally attuned resilience planning, validated against 14 case study regions, that improves predictions of human response lags and maladaptive infrastructure investments by 40–60% compared to purely biophysical models. The resource request supports scaling the framework to handle continental-scale datasets while maintaining hyperlocal resolution—a computational challenge requiring parallelized GPU-optimized workflows for geospatial deep learning and distributed memory architectures for large-scale scenario testing. Results will advance methodological integration in critical geography while providing actionable insights for equitable adaptation policy design.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the systematic study of the spatial distribution and interrelationships of people, natural resources, plant and animal life. Includes instruction in historical and political geography, cultural geography, economic and physical geography, regional science, cartographic methods, remote sensing, spatial analysis, and applications to areas such as land-use planning, development studies, and analyses of specific countries, regions, and resources.

abstract: This research project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical gaps in the computational analysis of under-documented Southeast Asian languages, particularly those in the Malayo-Polynesian and Tibeto-Burman families. While these languages exhibit rich morphological and syntactic complexity, many remain understudied due to limited digital corpora and a lack of scalable tools for analyzing their structural features. The primary research problem centers on reconstructing historical language relationships and modeling contact-induced linguistic changes in mainland Southeast Asia and the insular regions, where centuries of multilingual interaction have generated intricate patterns of convergence and divergence. Current methods, often constrained by single-threaded processing, struggle to handle the combinatorial complexity of comparative datasets spanning dozens of languages with variable documentation quality. The proposed computational approach integrates phylogenetic inference algorithms with neural sequence-to-sequence models to simultaneously analyze lexical, phonological, and morphosyntactic features across 40+ languages. HPC resources will enable parallelized Bayesian phylogenetic analyses (using BEAST2 and RevBayes) to model language diversification timelines, while transformer-based architectures (e.g., fine-tuned BERT models) will process and align textual data from heterogeneous sources, including colonial-era manuscripts and modern speech recordings. Memory-intensive tasks, such as probabilistic alignment of cognate sets across 100,000+ lexical items, require distributed computing to achieve feasible runtimes. Expected outcomes include 1) a publicly accessible database of annotated linguistic features for Southeast Asian languages, 2) probabilistic models of language contact zones in the region, and 3) methodological advances in handling fragmentary historical data through hybrid machine learning/statistical approaches. This work will significantly enhance understanding of language diversification patterns in Southeast Asia while developing computational frameworks applicable to other under-resourced language families. The requested allocation of 200,000 CPU-hours and GPU nodes with 4 TB RAM capacity will support these large-scale comparative analyses over a 12-month period.
detailed_field: Foreign languages, literatures, and linguistics nec
cip_title: Southeast Asian Languages, Literatures, and Linguistics, General
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on one or more of the modern languages spoken in mainland Southeast Asia and the Indonesian and Philippines Archipelagoes, including, but not limited to, members of the Thai, Tibeto-Burman, and Malayo-Polynesian language families.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a scalable computational framework to optimize the integration, analysis, and security of heterogeneous healthcare datasets, including electronic health records (EHRs), genomic data, and real-time wearable device outputs. A critical challenge in health information technology is the efficient processing of large-scale, multi-modal data while maintaining compliance with privacy regulations such as HIPAA. Existing tools often struggle with interoperability, computational bottlenecks, and dynamic data validation, limiting their utility for predictive analytics and clinical decision support. To address this, we propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to deploy parallelized machine learning pipelines for real-time data harmonization and anomaly detection. Computational workflows will include federated learning architectures to train predictive models on distributed datasets without centralized data aggregation, thereby preserving patient confidentiality. Additionally, GPU-accelerated natural language processing (NLP) models will be applied to unstructured clinical notes to extract latent phenotypic features, enabling linkage with structured EHR fields. A key innovation involves simulating synthetic patient cohorts—generated via generative adversarial networks (GANs)—to stress-test data validation algorithms under diverse scenarios while avoiding exposure of sensitive information. The project will utilize HPC resources for 1) large-scale hyperparameter optimization of deep learning models, 2) cryptographic hashing and encryption protocols for secure data sharing, and 3) validation of data integrity across multi-institutional datasets. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for privacy-preserving health data analysis, benchmarks for computational efficiency in clinical data processing, and novel algorithms for automated error detection in medical records. This work will directly advance the scalability and security of health information systems, supporting applications in precision medicine, public health surveillance, and clinical research. By addressing computational barriers to data quality and interoperability, the project aligns with the program’s focus on preparing professionals to manage evolving technical demands in healthcare data infrastructure.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals, under the supervision of health information administrators and other professionals, to construct medical records and clinical databases, perform manipulations on retrieved data, control the security and quality of records, and supervise data entry and technical maintenance personnel. Includes instruction in clinical and biomedical science data and information requirements, database management, data coding and validation, information security, quality control, health information content and structure, medical business procedures, and legal requirements.

abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, with complex pathophysiology often influenced by genetic, molecular, and hemodynamic factors. A critical challenge in clinical cardiology lies in predicting individual patient trajectories and optimizing personalized treatment strategies for conditions such as heart failure, arrhythmias, and ischemic heart disease. This project seeks to address these challenges by developing multiscale computational models of cardiac function that integrate patient-specific imaging, electrophysiological data, and genomic profiles. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we aim to simulate cardiac electromechanics across spatially resolved myocardial tissues, model blood flow dynamics in coronary arteries under varying physiological conditions, and identify biomarkers of disease progression using machine learning-driven analysis of multi-omics datasets. The computational framework will employ finite element methods for biomechanical simulations, lattice Boltzmann methods for hemodynamics, and deep learning architectures for pattern recognition in high-dimensional clinical data. Key outcomes include predictive models of arrhythmia susceptibility, optimized stent placement strategies for coronary interventions, and classifiers for early detection of heart failure decompensation. These tools will be validated against clinical outcomes from retrospective cohorts and prospective pilot studies. The project’s computational demands—including large-scale parameter sweeps, real-time coupling of fluid-structure interactions, and training of neural networks on terabyte-scale datasets—necessitate access to HPC infrastructure with parallel processing capabilities, high-memory nodes, and GPU acceleration. Successful implementation will advance precision cardiology by enabling clinically actionable insights derived from complex, multi-modal data, ultimately bridging gaps between mechanistic research and bedside care. This work aligns with national priorities to reduce cardiovascular disease burden through innovation in data-driven healthcare solutions.
cip_definition: Research focused on Cardiology

abstract: This project seeks to optimize built environments for mitigating airborne pathogen transmission while balancing energy efficiency and human behavioral dynamics—a critical challenge at the intersection of architectural design, environmental engineering, and public health. Current guidelines for healthcare and public spaces rely on static ventilation standards, which inadequately address real-time fluctuations in occupancy, activity types, or emerging pathogen variants. We propose developing an adaptive computational framework that integrates high-fidelity airflow simulations with machine learning-driven occupancy pattern analysis to enable dynamic, context-aware ventilation strategies. The research employs large-scale agent-based modeling to simulate human movement and aerosol dispersion in complex indoor environments, coupled with reinforcement learning algorithms to optimize HVAC control policies. High-performance computing resources are essential for resolving turbulence models at spatial scales <1 cm³ across multi-room architectures and iteratively training neural networks on stochastic behavioral datasets. Expected outcomes include predictive metrics for infection risk reduction under variable occupancy scenarios, validated against experimental tracer gas data from partner healthcare facilities. This work will advance the evidence base for responsive building systems that autonomously adapt to epidemiological threats while minimizing energy waste—a dual imperative for sustainable health-focused design. By bridging computational fluid dynamics, building science, and behavioral epidemiology, the project establishes a novel methodology for evaluating design interventions that transcend conventional disciplinary boundaries in human-centered health research.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the impact of design and architecture on the health of individuals and larger populations, and how to create settings that promote health, healing, and well-being. Includes instruction in architecture, interior design, human health services, communication studies, medical and clinical innovations, behavioral and engineering sciences, hospitals and health systems, and environmental conditions that influence health.

abstract: This project seeks to advance the computational modeling of large-scale economic systems with heterogeneous agents, focusing on the dynamics of market resilience under stochastic shocks. Traditional equilibrium models often struggle to capture the nonlinear feedback loops and adaptive behaviors that characterize real-world economies, particularly during crises. To address this gap, we propose developing a high-dimensional agent-based model (ABM) that integrates microeconomic decision-making rules with macroeconomic network interdependencies. The ABM will simulate interactions among firms, households, and financial institutions across spatially linked markets, incorporating adaptive learning algorithms to model agent responses to supply chain disruptions, inflation volatility, and credit constraints. A core challenge lies in efficiently scaling the model to represent millions of agents with empirically calibrated parameters derived from global trade databases, central bank reports, and firm-level financial records. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to manage the combinatorial complexity of agent interactions, parallelize Monte Carlo simulations for robustness testing, and optimize parameter spaces via genetic algorithms. The project will leverage GPU-accelerated nodes for real-time visualization of emergent macroeconomic patterns and use distributed memory systems to handle high-frequency data assimilation. Expected outcomes include (1) novel insights into policy trade-offs for stabilizing interconnected markets, (2) open-source tools for scalable ABM development in economics, and (3) empirical validation of non-equilibrium recovery pathways post-shock. Results will inform adaptive regulatory frameworks and provide a computational testbed for stress-testing economic policies under diverse crisis scenarios. This work requires sustained access to HPC clusters with multi-core processors, large-memory nodes, and high-throughput storage to accommodate the petabyte-scale datasets generated during iterative simulations. The computational infrastructure will enable unprecedented resolution in modeling economic complexity, bridging theoretical innovation with applied policy design.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in economics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance predictive modeling of watershed resilience under climate change, addressing critical gaps in sustainable natural resource management. The research focuses on the dynamic interactions between hydrological systems, land-use changes, and climatic extremes in biodiverse regions vulnerable to droughts and flooding. Current models lack the spatial resolution and temporal granularity needed to simulate nonlinear feedbacks between precipitation patterns, soil erosion, and anthropogenic stressors, limiting actionable insights for conservation. To address this, we propose an integrated computational framework combining hydroclimatic simulations, geospatial machine learning, and ensemble modeling. The HPC environment will enable high-resolution (1 km² grid) simulations of watershed dynamics across decadal timescales, integrating multi-source data from satellite remote sensing, regional climate models, and field sensors. Parallelized workflows will optimize Bayesian calibration of hydrological parameters, while graph neural networks will analyze connectivity in erosion and sediment transport processes. This approach will quantify uncertainty in water availability projections under IPCC climate scenarios, identifying thresholds for ecosystem degradation. The outcomes will directly inform state and federal agencies on prioritizing conservation corridors and adaptive water allocation policies. By resolving fine-scale processes in heterogeneous landscapes, the project will generate open-access datasets and modular code for reproducibility in similar ecosystems. The requested resources are essential to overcome memory and processing bottlenecks in handling >50 TB of multi-temporal geospatial data and running 10⁶+ model iterations. This work bridges gaps between climatology, hydrology, and computational sustainability, offering a scalable toolset to mitigate conflicts between ecological preservation and human water demands.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of biological, chemical, and physical principles to the study of the physical environment and the solution of environmental problems, including subjects such as abating or controlling environmental pollution and degradation; the interaction between human society and the natural environment; and natural resources management. Includes instruction in biology, chemistry, physics, geosciences, climatology, statistics, and mathematical modeling.

abstract: The increasing prevalence of complex, multifactorial chronic conditions in adult populations—such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and obesity—demands innovative approaches to optimize care delivery and health outcomes. Current clinical decision-making frameworks often struggle to integrate high-dimensional patient data, including electronic health records (EHRs), biomarker profiles, and socio-behavioral determinants, into actionable care plans. This project seeks to address this gap by developing a computational framework to model patient-specific risk trajectories and simulate the impact of targeted nursing interventions. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we will analyze large-scale EHR datasets from diverse adult populations (n ≈ 500,000) to identify patterns in disease progression, treatment adherence, and care coordination barriers. Machine learning models, including recurrent neural networks and ensemble classifiers, will predict individualized risks of complications or hospital readmissions. Concurrently, agent-based simulations will test hypothetical intervention strategies—such as tailored education protocols or remote monitoring schedules—to quantify their potential efficacy under varying clinical scenarios. The computational pipeline will prioritize scalability to accommodate heterogeneous data types and real-time validation against prospective clinical data from partner health systems. Expected outcomes include (1) validated predictive algorithms for early identification of high-risk patients, (2) a simulation toolkit to prioritize resource allocation for nurse-led interventions, and (3) open-access dashboards to support clinical decision-making. By integrating computational modeling with nursing expertise, this work aims to advance precision health strategies in adult care, reduce preventable hospitalizations, and establish a replicable framework for data-driven resource optimization in nursing practice. The HPC infrastructure is critical to managing the computational burden of multi-modal data integration, hyperparameter tuning for machine learning models, and parallel execution of large-scale simulations.
cip_definition: A program that prepares registered nurses to provide general care for adult patients. Includes instruction in adult primary care, adult pathophysiology, clinical management of medication and treatments, patient assessment and education, patient referral, and planning adult health maintenance programs.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a computational framework to optimize the resilience and sustainability of urban construction projects under dynamic environmental and operational stressors. Construction engineering faces critical challenges in balancing structural integrity, material efficiency, and project timelines, particularly as climate change intensifies weather-related risks and regulatory demands evolve. Current design practices often rely on simplified models that inadequately capture multi-physics interactions—such as coupled thermal-structural behavior in concrete or soil-structure dynamics during excavation—leading to over-engineering or vulnerabilities. To address this, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled approach integrating finite element analysis (FEA), discrete event simulation, and machine learning to model complex construction systems at unprecedented scales. The research will simulate (1) time-dependent material degradation in composite structures under variable humidity and load cycles, (2) real-time resource allocation for robotic and human workflows on constrained urban sites, and (3) probabilistic risk assessment of supply chain disruptions using geospatial and economic datasets. Computational workflows will leverage GPU-accelerated solvers for FEA and graph neural networks to optimize 3D-printed structural components, reducing material waste by an estimated 15–25%. By parallelizing Monte Carlo simulations across 10,000+ scenarios, we will quantify climate adaptation strategies for transport infrastructure, directly informing revised ASTM and AASHTO codes. The HPC resources are essential to handle petascale datasets from LiDAR-scanned construction sites and IoT sensor networks, enabling near-real-time digital twin updates. Outcomes will include open-source tools for automated Building Information Modeling (BIM) validation and a decision support system prioritizing low-carbon materials without compromising safety margins. This work bridges critical gaps in data-driven construction lifecycle management, offering scalable methods to reduce costs and embodied carbon in next-generation smart cities.
detailed_field: Civil, environmental, and transportation engineering nec
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply scientific, mathematical, and management principles to the planning, design, and building of facilities and structures. Includes instruction in civil engineering, structural principles, site analysis, computer-assisted design, geology, evaluation and testing, materials, contracting, project management, graphic communications, and applicable laws and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to develop an integrated computational framework to evaluate the economic trade-offs and environmental outcomes of land-use policies aimed at balancing agricultural productivity, biodiversity conservation, and carbon sequestration. Current models in environmental economics often simplify spatial heterogeneity or assume static agent behavior, limiting their capacity to inform regionally adaptive policies. To address this gap, we propose an agent-based model (ABM) coupled with high-resolution geospatial data to simulate land-use decisions under varying climate scenarios, market conditions, and regulatory interventions. The ABM will incorporate heterogeneous decision-making by agricultural producers, incorporating bounded rationality, risk preferences, and responses to subsidy structures. A dynamic computable general equilibrium (CGE) component will link local land-use changes to broader market feedbacks. The computational complexity of simulating millions of agent interactions across multi-decadal time horizons, combined with high-dimensional parameter spaces for policy testing, necessitates high-performance computing (HPC) resources. Key tasks include parallelized Monte Carlo simulations to assess policy robustness under uncertainty, calibration using Bayesian methods with historical land-use data, and real-time visualization of spatial-economic outcomes. Expected outcomes include a scalable tool for policymakers to quantify cost-benefit ratios of conservation incentives, predict leakage effects, and optimize spatial targeting of interventions. By leveraging HPC capabilities, this project will advance the resolution and predictive accuracy of environmental-economic models, directly addressing the program’s focus on evaluating resource management strategies through rigorous economic analysis. Results will be disseminated through open-source model repositories and policy briefs to support evidence-based decision-making in natural resource economics.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of economic concepts and methods to the analysis of issues such as air and water pollution, land use planning, waste disposal, invasive species and pest control, conservation policies, and related environmental problems. Includes instruction in cost-benefit analysis, environmental impact assessment, evaluation and assessment of alternative resource management strategies, policy evaluation and monitoring, and descriptive and analytic tools for studying how environmental developments affect the economic system.

abstract: This project seeks to develop scalable computational methods for analyzing high-dimensional stochastic processes with complex dependency structures, a problem central to advancing statistical theory but hindered by prohibitive computational demands. Traditional approaches to inference in such settings—particularly for infinite particle systems, non-Markovian processes, and Banach space-valued stochastic systems—rely on simplifying assumptions that limit their applicability to real-world data. We propose a framework combining measure-theoretic probability, Bayesian hierarchical modeling, and resampling techniques to address these limitations. The core computational challenges involve (1) approximating high-dimensional integrals in posterior distributions arising from Bayesian nonparametric models, (2) simulating particle system trajectories with long-range dependencies, and (3) validating asymptotic properties of estimators under weaker regularity conditions than current limit theory permits. High-performance computing resources will enable parallelized Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling with adaptive preconditioning, distributed computation of exchangeable sequences via tensor decomposition methods, and large-scale numerical studies comparing frequentist and Bayesian uncertainty quantification in non-Donsker function classes. Expected outcomes include new convergence guarantees for sequential Monte Carlo methods in Banach spaces, optimized algorithms for stochastic partial differential equation parameter estimation, and open-source software implementing robust inference tools for non-ergodic processes. This work will directly impact statistical theory by bridging gaps between abstract probabilistic results and computationally feasible implementations, while providing methodological advances for applications requiring inference on complex stochastic systems, such as spatially interacting particle models in epidemiology and functional time series analysis in climate science.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the mathematical theory underlying statistical methods and their use. Includes instruction in probability theory parametric and non-parametric inference, sequential analysis, multivariate analysis, Bayesian analysis, experimental design, time series analysis, resampling, robust statistics, limit theory, infinite particle systems, stochastic processes, martingales, Markov processes, and Banach spaces.

abstract: The design and optimization of next-generation engineering systems, such as adaptive smart grids and autonomous manufacturing platforms, are increasingly constrained by the limitations of conventional computational resources in handling multi-scale, multi-physics simulations. These systems integrate heterogeneous data streams and require real-time decision-making under uncertainty, posing significant challenges for traditional serial computing approaches. This project proposes the development of a scalable, high-fidelity computational framework utilizing high-performance computing (HPC) to enable the simultaneous analysis of structural, thermal, and fluid dynamic interactions within complex engineering environments. By implementing a hybrid approach that combines finite element methods (FEM) with deep reinforcement learning (DRL) algorithms, the research aims to dynamically optimize system parameters across varying temporal and spatial scales. The computational workflow will leverage distributed memory parallelism via MPI and GPU-accelerated tensor operations to efficiently process large datasets generated by embedded IoT sensors and high-resolution simulations. Key deliverables include an open-source software module for adaptive mesh generation and a validated DRL model for predictive maintenance scheduling in industrial settings. The successful execution of this project will provide critical insights into the co-design of resilient and energy-efficient infrastructure, directly addressing national priorities in sustainable manufacturing and smart city development. Access to HPC resources is essential to achieve the required computational throughput for training machine learning models on terabytes of operational data and conducting parameter sweeps across 10^5+ design configurations. The outcomes will advance the integration of AI-driven analytics with physics-based modeling, establishing a paradigm shift in engineering system design for rapidly evolving technological landscapes.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in engineering technologies and engineering-related fields, not elsewhere classified

abstract: Sterilization of surgical instruments is a critical component of healthcare safety, yet current protocols face challenges in scalability, adaptability, and precision. Emerging pathogens, biofilm resilience, and variability in instrument design complicate the validation of sterilization cycles, risking incomplete decontamination or unnecessary equipment degradation. This project proposes a computational approach to model and optimize sterilization processes using high-performance computing (HPC) resources. We will develop agent-based simulations to map microbial survival thresholds under varying thermal, chemical, and mechanical conditions, integrating genomic data from antibiotic-resistant strains and structural analyses of surgical instruments. Machine learning models trained on sterilization logs, material degradation datasets, and real-time sensor outputs from autoclaves will identify risk factors for process failure and predict optimal parameter combinations (e.g., temperature, pressure, cycle duration) for heterogeneous instrument loads. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations will further analyze steam penetration efficacy in complex instrument geometries, such as laparoscopic or robotic tools. By coupling these models into an adaptive decision-support framework, the project aims to generate dynamic sterilization protocols tailored to specific pathogen threats, instrument materials, and operational constraints. Anticipated outcomes include validated predictive tools for clinical technicians, evidence-based revisions to sterile processing standards, and a repository of open-access simulation templates for microbial inactivation kinetics. This work addresses a pressing need for data-driven sterilization strategies in an era of evolving antimicrobial resistance and technologically advanced surgical tools. The requested HPC resources are essential to manage the high-throughput analysis of multi-modal datasets, parallelize large-scale CFD simulations, and deploy deep learning architectures for real-time operational recommendations. Successful implementation could reduce healthcare-associated infections, extend instrument lifespans, and inform regulatory policies for sterile processing technologies.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to clean, sterilize, and assemble surgical instruments, equipment, and supplies for use in operating rooms and other medical and surgical facilities. Includes instruction in sterilization; infection control; decontamination; and surgical instrumentation processing, distribution, and record-keeping.

abstract: This project seeks to investigate the interplay between microbial community dynamics in urban aquatic ecosystems and localized climate resilience, leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to model complex, cross-domain interactions. Urban water systems—such as reservoirs, constructed wetlands, and stormwater networks—host dynamic microbial communities that influence nutrient cycling, pollutant degradation, and greenhouse gas fluxes. However, the feedback loops between microbial metabolic processes, hydrological variability, and extreme weather events remain poorly quantified, limiting predictive models for climate adaptation. We propose an integrative computational framework combining metagenomic data, high-resolution climate projections, and hydrodynamic simulations to resolve these interactions at city-relevant scales. Metagenomic datasets from longitudinal sampling across diverse water bodies will be processed using custom bioinformatics pipelines to characterize microbial functional traits and phylogenetic networks. These outputs will be coupled with physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) trained on 3D hydrodynamic models of water flow, temperature, and solute transport, validated against sensor networks in partner cities. Agent-based models will then simulate microbial community responses to stochastic precipitation events and heatwaves under varying urban land-use scenarios. The HPC environment is critical for parallelizing genome annotation, scaling PINN training across spatially nested domains, and running ensemble climate-microbiome simulations at hourly temporal resolution. Expected outcomes include (1) a novel open-source framework for microbial-climate system modeling, (2) predictive maps of ecosystem service thresholds under future climate scenarios, and (3) evidence-based guidelines for engineering bioenhanced water infrastructure. By bridging microbial ecology, urban hydrology, and climate science, this work addresses a critical gap in adaptive urban planning while advancing computational methods for cross-scale interdisciplinary research.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in data science, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to develop scalable numerical algorithms for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) arising in multiphysics systems, such as coupled fluid-structure interaction problems. Traditional discretization methods suffer from prohibitive computational costs and memory requirements when applied to such systems, particularly in three dimensions or with dynamic boundary conditions. The research problem centers on overcoming these limitations by designing hybrid tensor decomposition and adaptive sparse grid techniques optimized for modern high-performance computing (HPC) architectures. The proposed computational approach integrates low-rank tensor approximations with parallelizable multilevel iterative solvers to reduce the dimensionality of parameter spaces while preserving solution accuracy. Key innovations include the development of a distributed-memory framework for hierarchical tensor operations and the implementation of dynamic load-balancing strategies to address irregular computational workloads inherent to adaptive sparsity patterns. The project will validate these methods using benchmark problems from biomechanics and aerospace engineering, comparing results against conventional finite element solutions. Expected outcomes include a 40-60% reduction in memory usage and a 3-5x speedup for targeted problem classes, enabling simulations at scales previously impractical on existing systems. Successful implementation will provide an open-source software toolkit for the computational mathematics community, with direct applications in optimizing medical device design and turbulent flow analysis. The requested HPC resources—including GPU-accelerated nodes and high-bandwidth interconnects—are critical for testing weak and strong scaling properties of the algorithms up to 10^6 core-hours, as well as for managing the communication overhead of distributed tensor computations. This work bridges algorithmic innovation with practical engineering challenges, advancing the state of computational mathematics in data-sparse representations for complex physical systems.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of mathematics to the theory, architecture, and design of computers, computational techniques, and algorithms. Includes instruction in computer theory, cybernetics, numerical analysis, algorithm development, binary structures, combinatorics, advanced statistics, and related topics.

abstract: Cutaneous diseases, including psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, and melanoma, involve complex interactions between genetic, immunological, and environmental factors. Current gaps in understanding disease heterogeneity and treatment resistance limit the development of personalized therapies. This project seeks to address these challenges by leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) to analyze multi-omics datasets and simulate molecular pathways underlying dermatologic pathologies. The research will integrate bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data from patient-derived skin biopsies, genomic variant databases, and spatially resolved proteomic profiles to identify disease-specific cellular states and dysregulated signaling networks. Machine learning models will be trained on these datasets to classify subtypes of chronic inflammatory skin conditions and predict drug response variability. Concurrently, molecular dynamics simulations will model interactions between therapeutic agents (e.g., biologics, small-molecule inhibitors) and target proteins under varying inflammatory microenvironments, enabling in silico screening of optimized compounds. A parallel computational pipeline will employ agent-based modeling to study immune cell trafficking and keratinocyte dynamics in lesional skin, parameterized by longitudinal clinical imaging data. The HPC infrastructure is critical for managing petabyte-scale data storage, accelerating genome-wide association studies via parallelized statistical frameworks, and performing real-time analysis of high-resolution histopathology images using deep learning architectures. Expected outcomes include the identification of novel biomarkers for early disease detection, computationally validated drug candidates for refractory cases, and predictive algorithms to guide therapeutic selection. These results will be disseminated through open-source tools for dermatological data analysis, fostering reproducibility in computational dermatology. By bridging large-scale data science with mechanistic modeling, this work aims to advance precision dermatology and improve outcomes for patients with complex or treatment-resistant skin diseases.
cip_definition: Research focused on diseases of the skin, hair, nails and mucous membranes. May also include research on dermatologic surgical procedures, cutaneous allergies, sexually transmitted diseases, and diagnostic and therapeutic techniques.

abstract: This project seeks to address inefficiencies in dynamic resource allocation for next-generation communication networks, particularly as demand surges for high-bandwidth applications such as augmented reality, ultra-high-definition streaming, and distributed teleconferencing. Current protocols struggle to adapt to fluctuating user densities, heterogeneous device capabilities, and variable latency thresholds, resulting in suboptimal bandwidth distribution and service degradation. The research employs high-performance computing (HPC) to develop adaptive algorithms that optimize real-time resource allocation across large-scale, decentralized networks. Using simulated environments replicating 5G/6G edge networks, the project will model traffic patterns, device interactions, and QoS requirements under diverse scenarios. Machine learning techniques—including graph neural networks and reinforcement learning—will be trained on these simulations to predict congestion points and preemptively allocate computational and spectral resources. Additionally, the project will prototype hybrid protocols that integrate centralized orchestration with decentralized decision-making, balancing scalability and responsiveness. By leveraging parallel computing architectures, the team will iteratively test algorithmic performance across millions of simulated network states, varying parameters such as node density, data payload size, and mobility patterns. Anticipated outcomes include a framework for intelligent resource distribution that reduces median latency by 30-50% in high-density scenarios compared to existing standards, alongside benchmarks for protocol adaptability in underprovisioned environments. This work directly supports the development of robust communication infrastructures capable of sustaining emerging immersive technologies, offering actionable insights for network operators and standards bodies. The computational scale required—processing terabyte-scale network logs, training deep learning models on heterogeneous data streams, and running real-time simulations—necessitates access to HPC resources with GPU acceleration and distributed memory architectures.
cip_title: Communications Technologies and Support Services, Other
cip_definition: Any instructional program in communications technologies and support services, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to advance understanding of the formation and evolution of compact galactic nuclei in low-mass dark matter halos, a critical but unresolved aspect of hierarchical structure formation. Current cosmological simulations lack the resolution to model the complex interplay between dark matter dynamics, baryonic cooling, and feedback mechanisms at sub-kiloparsec scales in these environments. We propose a suite of high-resolution, N-body + hydrodynamical simulations using the adaptive mesh refinement code ENZO, optimized to resolve gravitational collapse, gas fragmentation, and star formation in nascent nuclear star clusters within dwarf galaxy analogs. The simulations will incorporate radiative cooling, metal enrichment from supernovae, and radiation pressure feedback, with dark matter modeled as a dynamically active component. Computational demands are substantial, requiring ~5 million CPU-hours on a Tier 2 HPC system to achieve 0.1 pc spatial resolution across 50 simulated halos spanning redshifts z = 10–2. Memory-intensive tracer particles will track chemical evolution, while high-frequency output (Δt ≈ 0.1 Myr) will capture rapid dynamical processes. Expected outcomes include (1) statistically robust predictions for the mass function of nuclear star clusters in low-mass galaxies, (2) constraints on dark matter density profiles through dynamical friction modeling, and (3) synthetic observables (e.g., metallicity gradients, velocity dispersions) testable against JWST and upcoming Extremely Large Telescope surveys. The resulting public data products will provide critical benchmarks for interpreting high-redshift galaxy observations and testing alternatives to cold dark matter cosmologies.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in astronomy and astrophysics, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance epidemiological modeling of zoonotic disease transmission at the human-animal interface, a critical challenge in veterinary medicine and public health. Current limitations in predicting outbreak dynamics stem from the computational complexity of integrating heterogeneous datasets—including livestock movement patterns, wildlife migration, genomic surveillance, and climate variables—into spatially explicit, multiscale models. Existing tools struggle to handle the scale and resolution required for actionable insights, particularly in resource-limited agricultural settings where data granularity and latency further complicate real-time analysis. To address this, we propose developing an adaptive, agent-based modeling framework optimized for parallel computing architectures. This framework will simulate pathogen spread across species and landscapes, incorporating stochastic drivers of transmission, host immunity dynamics, and intervention scenarios such as targeted vaccination or movement restrictions. Machine learning techniques will be embedded to refine parameter estimation from incomplete field data and improve model accuracy iteratively. The HPC environment is essential for running ensemble simulations at scale, enabling sensitivity analyses across thousands of parameter combinations and geospatial resolutions (1–10 km granularity). Expected outcomes include predictive tools to identify high-risk zones for cross-species spillover, optimize resource allocation for outbreak prevention, and evaluate trade-offs between livestock productivity and disease control measures. By coupling veterinary health data with computational innovation, this work will directly inform One Health strategies, enhance preparedness for emerging zoonoses, and support sustainable agricultural practices. The resulting models and datasets will be disseminated through open-access platforms to foster collaboration across veterinary and computational research communities.
major_field: Agricultural, animal, plant, and veterinary sciences
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals for the independent professional practice of veterinary medicine, involving the diagnosis, treatment, and health care management of animals and animal populations and the prevention and management of zoonosis. Includes instruction in the veterinary basic sciences, infectious and noninfectious disease, diagnostic procedures, veterinary clinical medicine, obstetrics, radiology, anesthesiology, surgery, toxicology, animal health and preventive medicine, clinical nutrition, practice management, and professional standards and ethics.

abstract: This research project seeks to develop a computational framework to model and predict emergent dynamics in microbial-metabolic networks within soil ecosystems, integrating principles from biogeochemistry, systems biology, and nonlinear dynamics. Soil microbiomes drive critical planetary-scale processes, including carbon sequestration and nutrient cycling, yet their functional resilience under climate-driven perturbations remains poorly quantified. Current models either oversimplify metabolic interactions or lack the spatiotemporal resolution to capture community-scale feedbacks with abiotic factors like moisture gradients and redox potential. To address this gap, we propose a hybrid computational approach combining lattice Boltzmann methods for simulating pore-scale fluid dynamics and reactive transport with genome-informed agent-based metabolic network models. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve microbe-mineral interfaces at micrometer scales while simulating hectare-level ecosystem processes over decadal timeframes. The codebase will leverage adaptive mesh refinement and parallelized reaction-diffusion solvers to dynamically couple physicochemical parameters with stochastic microbial population dynamics. Machine learning surrogates will be trained on simulation outputs to identify tipping points in methane emission pathways under varying temperature and precipitation regimes. Expected outcomes include (1) a publicly accessible library of optimized GPU kernels for coupled biogeochemical-agronomic simulations, (2) quantitative metrics linking microbial functional diversity to soil carbon stability across climatic regions, and (3) predictive models informing land-use strategies that balance agricultural productivity with carbon-negative soil management. By bridging scales from enzymatic processes to landscape-level impacts, this work will establish new computational paradigms for analyzing complex biological systems in heterogeneous environments.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply advanced computational methods and analysis to science, mathematics, and engineering practice. Includes instruction in applied mathematics and statistics, data science, numerical analysis and scientific computing, computational mechanics and physics, parallel computing and computer architecture, and mathematical modeling.

abstract: Clinical cytogenetics faces growing challenges in analyzing complex genomic datasets generated by high-resolution techniques such as fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), next-generation sequencing, and whole-genome cytogenetic profiling. These methods produce vast amounts of imaging, sequencing, and structural variation data, necessitating advanced computational resources to detect subtle chromosomal abnormalities, resolve ambiguous structural rearrangements, and correlate findings with clinical outcomes. This project seeks high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop and deploy scalable bioinformatics pipelines for integrated analysis of multi-omics data in the context of hematologic malignancies, congenital disorders, and transplant compatibility. The computational workflows will leverage machine learning models to identify predictive biomarkers from cytogenetic, epigenomic, and transcriptomic datasets, with a focus on improving the resolution of karyotype interpretation and minimizing diagnostic turnaround times. Key tasks include parallelized processing of whole-genome sequencing data to detect cryptic translocations, GPU-accelerated image analysis of FISH and photomicrography datasets for automated anomaly detection, and dynamic visualization of 3D chromatin conformation changes associated with leukemogenesis. The HPC environment will enable large-scale simulations of clonal evolution in cancer to model the impact of chromothripsis and chromoplexy on therapeutic resistance. Expected outcomes include optimized algorithms for distinguishing pathogenic variants from benign polymorphisms, validated predictive models for post-transplant chimerism analysis, and open-source tools for reproducible cytogenomic data integration. By enhancing the precision and scalability of clinical cytogenetic analyses, this work aims to directly inform treatment stratification for hematologic cancers, reduce graft rejection risks in transplant recipients, and uncover novel mechanisms of genomic instability. The requested resources will support critical advancements in translating complex cytogenetic data into actionable clinical insights, bridging gaps between research discoveries and patient care in precision medicine.
cip_definition: The clinical research and diagnosis of genetic diseases and defects, in preparation for organ transplants, and in support of treatments for cancers and leukemias. Includes chromosome analysis, fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), molecular genetic techniques, cytotechnology, and photomicrography.

abstract: Mental health disorders are characterized by complex interactions between biological, psychological, and socio-environmental factors, leading to significant variability in treatment responses. Current approaches in psychiatric nursing often rely on generalized intervention strategies, which may not adequately address individual patient needs. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to develop predictive models that identify patient-specific factors influencing treatment outcomes in individuals with severe mental illnesses, such as schizophrenia and major depressive disorder. By integrating large-scale electronic health records (EHRs), genomic data, and longitudinal behavioral assessments, we aim to disentangle multidimensional predictors of symptom remission, medication adherence, and crisis recurrence. Computational workflows will include machine learning algorithms to classify risk profiles, agent-based modeling to simulate the impact of nursing interventions in virtual patient cohorts, and network analysis to map dynamic relationships between psychosocial stressors and clinical trajectories. The scale and resolution of these analyses—encompassing thousands of variables across diverse datasets—necessitate parallel processing, large-memory nodes, and GPU acceleration for real-time optimization of models. Expected outcomes include the identification of biomarkers and contextual factors that predict responsiveness to specific nursing interventions, such as tailored psychoeducation or crisis de-escalation techniques. These insights will inform the development of decision-support tools for psychiatric nurses, enabling personalized care plans that improve patient stabilization and reduce hospital readmissions. By bridging computational psychiatry and nursing science, this work advances precision mental health strategies while highlighting the critical role of HPC in translating complex data into actionable clinical frameworks.
cip_definition: A program that prepares registered nurses to promote mental health and provide nursing care to patients with mental, emotional or behavioral disorders, in mental institutions or other settings. Includes instruction in psychopathology, behavioral health, counseling and intervention strategies, psychoeducation, mental health assessment and dual diagnosis, stabilization and management of psychotic illness, psychiatric care and rehabilitation, substance abuse, and crisis intervention.

abstract: This project seeks to develop a novel computational framework to optimize decentralized decision-making in multi-agent supply chain networks under dynamic, uncertain conditions. Traditional centralized optimization models struggle to address real-time disruptions, such as sudden demand shifts, supplier failures, or logistical bottlenecks, due to computational latency and incomplete information. We propose an agent-based reinforcement learning (RL) approach embedded within a high-performance computing (HPC) environment to simulate and resolve these challenges. The research problem focuses on balancing local autonomy among supply chain agents (e.g., suppliers, distributors) with global coordination to minimize systemic risk while maintaining operational efficiency. The computational methodology integrates asynchronous Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) with graph neural networks (GNNs) to model interdependencies and enable adaptive, distributed decision protocols. By leveraging parallelized simulations across GPU clusters, the framework will evaluate millions of stochastic scenarios—incorporating probabilistic demand forecasts, geopolitical disruptions, and sustainability constraints—to identify robust coordination strategies. Expected outcomes include a scalable library of hybrid RL-GNN algorithms optimized for HPC architectures, validated against real-world datasets from semiconductor and pharmaceutical supply chains. This work will advance management science by providing a computational paradigm for resilient, self-organizing business networks, with direct applications to crisis response planning and ESG (environmental, social, governance)-aligned resource allocation. The requested HPC resources are critical to achieving the necessary scale and speed for training multi-agent systems in hyper-realistic virtual environments, which is infeasible with conventional cloud computing infrastructure.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the application of statistical modeling, data warehousing, data mining, programming, forecasting and operations research techniques to the analysis of problems of business organization and performance. Includes instruction in optimization theory and mathematical techniques, data mining, data warehousing, stochastic and dynamic modeling, operations analysis, and the design and testing of prototype systems and evaluation models.

abstract: Healthcare systems face escalating challenges in balancing operational efficiency, equitable resource allocation, and adaptability to dynamic public health needs. This project seeks to develop a computational framework for simulating and optimizing service delivery networks under varying policy constraints, demographic shifts, and crisis scenarios. Leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources, we propose to build agent-based models (ABMs) that integrate multi-source data—including electronic health records, workforce distribution patterns, and regional health inequity metrics—to simulate patient flow, facility-level decision-making, and system-wide outcomes. The models will incorporate machine learning algorithms to dynamically adapt resource allocation strategies based on emergent patterns in simulated scenarios, such as pandemic surges or Medicaid policy changes. Computational demands arise from modeling large-scale networks (5,000+ interdependent healthcare entities), stochastic patient agents (10^6+ concurrent agents), and multi-objective optimization across competing priorities (cost, wait times, health outcomes). The HPC environment will enable parallelized scenario testing, sensitivity analyses, and real-time visualization of cascading system effects. Expected outcomes include an open-source toolkit for health administrators to stress-test allocation strategies, predictive metrics for service bottlenecks, and policy briefs on resilient resource distribution frameworks. This work directly addresses critical gaps in evidence-based health services management by providing computational methods to evaluate tradeoffs in care delivery design, particularly for underserved populations. Results will advance both methodological capabilities in public health operations research and practical strategies for implementing equity-focused administration practices.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the application of policy analysis, public administration, business management, and communications to the planning and management of health services delivery systems in the public and private sectors, and prepares individuals to function as health services administrators and managers. Includes instruction in health systems planning, public health organization and management, pubic health policy formulation and analysis, finance, business and operations management, economics of health care, organizational and health communications, marketing, human resources management, and public health law and regulations.

abstract: This project seeks to address challenges in optimizing industrial metal manufacturing processes through advanced computational modeling of microstructure evolution and defect formation during solidification and thermal treatment. A critical barrier in metallurgical applications is the unpredictable emergence of voids, inclusions, and phase inhomogeneities that compromise component durability, particularly in high-stress environments. Traditional trial-and-error methods to mitigate these defects are resource-intensive and lack the resolution to capture nanoscale interactions influencing macroscopic material properties. To overcome this, we propose a multiscale simulation framework combining phase-field modeling, finite element analysis, and machine learning techniques to predict defect nucleation under varying process parameters. High-performance computing (HPC) resources are essential to resolve multiphysics phenomena across temporal and spatial scales, including solute diffusion dynamics, interfacial energy effects, and thermal stress distributions during rapid cooling cycles. The computational workflow will integrate experimental data from partner industrial laboratories to validate models against real-world alloy systems and processing conditions. Expected outcomes include predictive tools for minimizing defect densities in cast alloys and heat-treated components, with direct applications in automotive and heavy machinery manufacturing. By establishing correlations between computational signatures and quality control metrics, this work will enable data-driven adjustments to production parameters, reducing material waste by an estimated 15–20% in target industrial use cases. The resulting open-access simulation templates will enhance metallurgical technology education, providing students with hands-on training in computational materials process design. Successful implementation requires sustained access to GPU-accelerated nodes for parallelized phase-field calculations and distributed memory systems for ensemble machine learning training on heterogeneous microstructure datasets.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply basic engineering principles and technical skills in support of engineers and metallurgists engaged in developing and using industrial metals and manufacturing processes. Includes instruction in principles of metallurgy, related manufacturing systems, laboratory techniques, testing and inspection procedures, instrument calibration, system and equipment maintenance and repair, applications to specific processes, and report preparation.

abstract: The study of strongly correlated quantum systems remains a central challenge in modern physics due to the exponential growth of computational complexity with system size. Classical simulations of such systems—particularly those involving out-of-equilibrium dynamics or high-dimensional entanglement—are often intractable with conventional methods. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to advance numerical simulations of quantum many-body systems using tensor network algorithms optimized for parallel architectures. The research will focus on two interconnected objectives: (1) simulating non-equilibrium phases in one- and two-dimensional spin lattices under time-dependent perturbations, and (2) characterizing entanglement growth and thermalization processes in disordered quantum systems. These investigations will employ matrix product states (MPS) and projected entangled pair states (PEPS) frameworks, combined with density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) methods, adapted for GPU-accelerated clusters. A key innovation involves developing hybrid CPU-GPU workflows to manage memory-intensive tensor contractions and optimize scalability for systems exceeding 100 qubits. The computational demands are substantial, requiring multi-node parallelism, distributed memory management, and petascale storage for wavefunction snapshots. Expected outcomes include new insights into dynamical phase transitions in quantum spin systems, quantitative predictions of thermalization timescales in engineered quantum materials, and benchmarks for near-term quantum simulators. By pushing the boundaries of simulable system sizes, this work will provide foundational data for testing theoretical conjectures in quantum statistical mechanics and guide experimental efforts in quantum computing platforms. The requested allocation of 500,000 node-hours, supplemented by high-memory nodes and fast interconnects, is critical to achieving the necessary numerical precision and temporal resolution. Results will be disseminated through open-source code releases, enabling broader community access to the optimized algorithms developed during this project.
cip_definition: A general program that focuses on the scientific study of matter and energy, and the formulation and testing of the laws governing the behavior of the matter-energy continuum. Includes instruction in classical and modern physics, electricity and magnetism, thermodynamics, mechanics, wave properties, nuclear processes, relativity and quantum theory, quantitative methods, and laboratory methods.

abstract: Palliative care research faces significant challenges in predicting patient trajectories and optimizing individualized care plans due to the complex interplay of biological, psychosocial, and clinical factors influencing outcomes. Current approaches often rely on static models that inadequately capture dynamic symptom evolution, treatment responses, and heterogeneous patient needs. This project seeks to address these limitations by developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-enabled framework to integrate multimodal data—including electronic health records, genomic profiles, real-time symptom reports, and social determinants of health—into predictive models for personalized palliative care. The research will employ machine learning techniques such as recurrent neural networks and Bayesian hierarchical models to analyze longitudinal datasets from 15,000+ patients across six palliative care cohorts. These models will identify critical predictors of symptom burden, quality-of-life trajectories, and end-of-life decision-making patterns while accounting for missing data and temporal dependencies. Computational demands include large-scale parallel processing for model training, stochastic simulations of care pathways, and sensitivity analyses across demographic subgroups. The HPC infrastructure will enable rapid iteration of complex algorithms that would be infeasible with standard clinical computing resources. Expected outcomes include validated predictive tools to guide early interventions for high-risk patients, dynamic decision-support systems for clinicians, and stratification frameworks for clinical trial enrollment. By elucidating modifiable factors in palliative care outcomes, this work aims to reduce preventable suffering, optimize resource allocation, and establish scalable computational methodologies for future research in patient-centered care. The proposed models and pipelines will be disseminated through open-source platforms to foster collaboration across palliative care research networks.
cip_definition: Research focused on Palliative Care

abstract: Advances in genomic technologies have revolutionized the identification of genetic variants underlying clinical disorders, yet challenges persist in distinguishing pathogenic mutations from benign variants, integrating multi-omics data, and predicting clinical outcomes in heterogeneous populations. This project seeks to address these gaps by developing scalable computational frameworks to enhance the precision and accessibility of clinical genetic services. We propose leveraging high-performance computing (HPC) resources to analyze large-scale genomic datasets from diverse patient cohorts, including whole-exome sequencing, RNA-seq, and epigenetic profiles, alongside clinical phenotyping data. Machine learning models, including graph neural networks and ensemble classifiers, will be trained to prioritize pathogenic variants, predict genotype-phenotype associations, and model gene-gene interaction networks. A key focus is the integration of population-specific allele frequencies and environmental covariates to reduce disparities in variant interpretation for underrepresented groups. Additionally, we will simulate population genetic dynamics under different inheritance models to optimize risk prediction algorithms for complex disorders. Computational workflows will be parallelized to process terabytes of data efficiently, with iterative model validation using cloud-native tools. Expected outcomes include open-source software for variant prioritization, risk stratification templates for rare diseases, and predictive models for therapeutic response in genetic syndromes. These tools will directly inform clinical workflows, reducing diagnostic odysseys and improving counseling accuracy for families. The requested HPC resources—particularly GPU-accelerated nodes and high-memory compute instances—are critical for training deep learning architectures, managing distributed genomic databases, and conducting real-time simulations during patient consultations. By bridging computational innovation with clinical genetics practice, this work aims to advance equitable, evidence-based care for individuals with genetic disorders.
cip_definition: Research on how to provide comprehensive diagnostic, management, and counseling services for individuals and families at risk for clinical disorders with a genetic basis.

abstract: This project seeks to develop advanced computational models to optimize the design and application of insulation materials for industrial systems, addressing challenges in thermal management, fire resistance, and acoustic dampening. Current insulation practices rely heavily on empirical testing and standardized material specifications, which often fail to account for dynamic environmental conditions, complex geometries, or interactions between multiple physical phenomena (e.g., heat transfer coupled with mechanical stress). To overcome these limitations, we propose a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven approach integrating multi-physics simulations, machine learning, and uncertainty quantification. Finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) will model heat flow, material degradation, and airflow in insulated systems under variable operational scenarios, including extreme temperatures and mechanical vibrations. Machine learning algorithms will analyze simulation outputs to identify optimal material compositions and installation configurations, while Monte Carlo methods will assess performance reliability across stochastic conditions. The computational framework will also evaluate the safety and efficiency of novel asbestos-free insulation materials and robotic application techniques. By leveraging HPC resources, this work will enable high-resolution simulations of large-scale industrial systems—such as power plant boilers and HVAC networks—that are infeasible with laboratory-scale experiments. Anticipated outcomes include predictive models for insulation lifespan, energy loss reduction strategies, and risk assessments for asbestos abatement workflows. These results will directly inform curriculum updates in the Insulator program, providing trainees with data-driven insights into modern insulation technologies. The project aligns with broader industrial goals of energy efficiency and workplace safety, offering a scalable computational toolkit to advance sustainable infrastructure practices.
cip_definition: A program that prepares individuals to apply insulation materials to pipes, boilers, ducts, refrigeration systems, and related equipment to reduce the passage of heat, cold, sound, or fire. Includes instruction in insulation specifications, measuring and cutting insulating material, applying and securing insulation, installing vapor barriers, insulation system maintenance, asbestos removal and abatement, and safety training.

abstract: The proposed research investigates the emergent dynamics of decentralized information processing in colonial marine invertebrates, a novel interdisciplinary niche bridging organismal biology, complex systems theory, and distributed computing. While neuronal computation is well-studied, many sessile marine colonies (e.g., bryozoans, tunicates) exhibit coordinated group behaviors—such as synchronized feeding currents or colony-wide threat responses—without centralized neural control. This project addresses the critical knowledge gap in understanding how these systems achieve distributed decision-making through localized cell-to-cell signaling and hydrodynamic interactions. We will develop a high-resolution 3D agent-based model integrating individual zooid behavior, mechanochemical signaling cascades, and fluid dynamics at colony scales. The computational framework will employ smoothed particle hydrodynamics coupled with stochastic reaction-diffusion processes to simulate signal propagation through both biological tissue and surrounding water. High-performance computing resources are essential to resolve the nonlinear interactions across 10^4-10^5 individual zooids in realistic flow regimes, requiring parallelized simulations across thousands of cores. Validation will leverage published experimental data on response thresholds and propagation speeds in Botryllus schlosseri colonies. Expected outcomes include: 1) identification of critical parameters enabling reliable distributed computation in noisy aquatic environments, 2) quantitative comparison of efficiency trade-offs between neural and non-neural biological computing systems, and 3) bio-inspired design principles for robust decentralized networks in marine robotics. This work establishes a new paradigm for studying computation in non-neural multicellular systems while advancing fundamental knowledge about the evolutionary constraints and capabilities of biological distributed intelligence.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in the biological and biomedical sciences, not elsewhere classified

abstract: The development of effective therapeutics targeting G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) remains a central challenge in molecular pharmacology due to the dynamic interplay between ligand binding, receptor conformational states, and downstream signaling bias. While experimental techniques provide critical structural insights, they often lack the temporal resolution to map the full energy landscape of receptor-ligand interactions or predict how subtle molecular variations influence signaling outcomes. This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to perform large-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and free energy calculations aimed at resolving the mechanistic basis of signaling bias in adenosine A1 and A2A receptors—GPCRs with therapeutic relevance in cardiovascular and neurological disorders. We will employ all-atom MD simulations in explicit lipid bilayers to characterize ligand-induced conformational changes across receptor subtypes, followed by Markov state modeling to identify metastable states associated with G protein vs. β-arrestin coupling. Alchemical free energy perturbation (FEP) methods will quantify the energetic contributions of specific receptor residues to ligand selectivity and bias. These computational workflows will be integrated with experimental validation data from collaborators, including radioligand binding assays and BRET-based signaling profiles. The scale of sampling required to resolve rare transitions between signaling states (hundreds of microseconds of aggregate simulation time per system) necessitates GPU-accelerated HPC resources. Expected outcomes include (1) predictive models linking ligand chemistry to receptor conformation and signaling bias, (2) identification of allosteric sites amenable to bias-encoded drug design, and (3) a computational framework adaptable to other therapeutically relevant GPCRs. By bridging molecular-scale dynamics with pharmacological function, this work aims to advance rational strategies for developing safer, more selective GPCR-targeted therapies.
cip_definition: A program that focuses on the scientific study of the biochemical and biophysical characteristics of drugs at the molecular level and their interaction with, and effects on, biological macromolecules and cellular structures and processes. Includes instruction in molecular biology and biophysics; pharmacology of signal transduction, transmitters, and protein synthesis and release; receptors, protein interaction and binding; drug discovery and recognition; molecular toxicology; drug design; pharmacodynamics; developmental genetics; and studies of therapeutic strategies.

abstract: This project seeks to leverage high-performance computing (HPC) resources to address critical challenges in contemporary journalism, specifically the rapid analysis of large-scale, unstructured digital media datasets. As newsrooms increasingly rely on social media, multimedia content, and real-time audience engagement metrics, traditional computational tools struggle to process these heterogeneous data streams efficiently. The research problem centers on developing scalable methods to analyze evolving media ecosystems, detect misinformation patterns, and model audience behavior across platforms—tasks requiring advanced computational capacity. The proposed work integrates natural language processing (NLP), network analysis, and machine learning techniques to examine multi-terabyte datasets comprising text, video, and user interaction logs from public social media APIs and news archives. HPC resources will enable parallel processing of linguistically diverse content, training of transformer-based models for cross-lingual misinformation detection, and dynamic visualization of information diffusion networks. Expected outcomes include an open-source framework for real-time media ecosystem mapping, predictive models of viral content spread, and computational workflows tailored to investigative journalism needs. By quantifying biases in algorithmic content curation and identifying emerging narrative patterns, this research aims to enhance journalists’ capacity to verify information at scale, track disinformation campaigns, and adapt to shifting audience dynamics. The project bridges computational methods with journalistic practice, offering empirically grounded insights into digital information flows while maintaining strict ethical protocols for data anonymization and source protection. Results will be disseminated through academic partnerships with media organizations, fostering evidence-based approaches to address credibility challenges in 21st-century journalism.
cip_definition: Any instructional program in journalism, not elsewhere classified

abstract: This project seeks to enhance the precision and safety of diagnostic imaging through advanced computational modeling of radiation transport and tissue interaction dynamics. Current clinical protocols for X-ray, gamma-ray, and ultrasonic imaging rely on generalized safety thresholds and image reconstruction algorithms, which may not fully account for patient-specific anatomical variability or optimize the trade-off between image quality and radiation dose. To address this, we propose developing a high-performance computing (HPC)-driven framework to simulate radiation and acoustic wave propagation in heterogeneous biological tissues. The research will integrate Monte Carlo methods for stochastic modeling of photon and acoustic energy deposition with finite element analysis to predict tissue-specific responses. Patient-derived CT and MRI datasets will be used to construct anatomically accurate computational phantoms, enabling personalized simulations of radiation dose distribution and image artifact formation. Concurrently, machine learning models trained on these simulations will identify optimal imaging parameters to minimize dose while maintaining diagnostic fidelity. A key innovation is the parallelization of these workflows across GPU clusters to enable rapid, large-scale simulations that are infeasible on conventional systems. Expected outcomes include validated predictive models for patient-specific dose optimization in radiography, fluoroscopy, and ultrasound, as well as open-source tools for simulating novel hybrid imaging modalities. This work directly supports radiation safety advancements by quantifying tissue-specific risk thresholds and refining equipment calibration protocols. The requested HPC resources are critical for managing the computational intensity of multi-modal, high-resolution simulations, which require petabytes of memory allocation and thousands of GPU core hours.
